build: original Durell Software release, a tape image made with Ramsoft MakeTZX; a BASIC program loads a 190-byte turbo loader to $FAF2, which loads 49,000 bytes to $4000-$FF67 and returns to $EFD8

exclude: empty on the tape: the display list and the stack grow into it in play
empty on the tape: part of the frame buffer in play
the tape utility's copy of the ROM's cassette routines and the top of BASIC's memory: not the game's, never run by it, and not listed because it is the machine's ROM

comments.text: Sprite shift table for an offset of 1 pixel, the first of seven 256-byte pages at $5B00-$61FF; the page for an offset of s pixels is at $5A00 + $100*s. Odd offsets hold a right shift and even offsets a left shift: byte L is L>>1 when L is odd and (L<<6) AND $FF when L is even. A sprite byte v is looked up at v OR 1 for the part that stays in the first screen byte (v>>1) and at (v<<1) AND $FF for the bit that spills into the next byte ((v<<7) AND $FF), so one page gives both halves. The pages arrive on the tape already filled: the loop that makes them, $EC19-$EC59, belongs to the mastering routine at $EB9C, which the game does not run. They are read by the four masked sprite loops at $B6DF, $B760, $B8C3 and $B9A8. Each is entered with the page number in a register, made from the low three bits of the x coordinate by ADD A,$5A ($B6DB, $B75A, $B8BC, $B9A1); when those bits are 0 a byte-aligned loop is used instead and no page is read.

Sprite shift table for an offset of 2 pixels (page $5C of the seven described at sprite_shift_1). Byte L is L>>2 when L is odd and (L<<5) AND $FF when L is even: offset $FF holds $3F and offset $FE holds $C0. Looked up at v OR 1 it gives v>>2, the part of a sprite byte that stays in the first screen byte; looked up at (v<<1) AND $FF it gives (v<<6) AND $FF, the 2 bits that spill into the next byte.

Sprite shift table for an offset of 3 pixels (page $5D of the seven described at sprite_shift_1). Byte L is L>>3 when L is odd and (L<<4) AND $FF when L is even: offset $FF holds $1F and offset $FE holds $E0. Looked up at v OR 1 it gives v>>3, the part of a sprite byte that stays in the first screen byte; looked up at (v<<1) AND $FF it gives (v<<5) AND $FF, the 3 bits that spill into the next byte.

Sprite shift table for an offset of 4 pixels (page $5E of the seven described at sprite_shift_1). Byte L is L>>4 when L is odd and (L<<3) AND $FF when L is even: offset $FF holds $0F and offset $FE holds $F0. Looked up at v OR 1 it gives v>>4, the part of a sprite byte that stays in the first screen byte; looked up at (v<<1) AND $FF it gives (v<<4) AND $FF, the 4 bits that spill into the next byte.

Sprite shift table for an offset of 5 pixels (page $5F of the seven described at sprite_shift_1). Byte L is L>>5 when L is odd and (L<<2) AND $FF when L is even: offset $FF holds $07 and offset $FE holds $F8. Looked up at v OR 1 it gives v>>5, the part of a sprite byte that stays in the first screen byte; looked up at (v<<1) AND $FF it gives (v<<3) AND $FF, the 5 bits that spill into the next byte.

Sprite shift table for an offset of 6 pixels (page $60 of the seven described at sprite_shift_1). Byte L is L>>6 when L is odd and (L<<1) AND $FF when L is even: offset $FF holds $03 and offset $FE holds $FC. Looked up at v OR 1 it gives v>>6, the part of a sprite byte that stays in the first screen byte; looked up at (v<<1) AND $FF it gives (v<<2) AND $FF, the 6 bits that spill into the next byte.

Sprite shift table for an offset of 7 pixels (page $61 of the seven described at sprite_shift_1). Byte L is L>>7 when L is odd and L itself when L is even: offset $FF holds $01 and offset $FE holds $FE. Looked up at v OR 1 it gives v>>7, the part of a sprite byte that stays in the first screen byte; looked up at (v<<1) AND $FF it gives (v<<1) AND $FF, the 7 bits that spill into the next byte.

Bit-reversal table, 256 bytes: byte L is L with its eight bits in the opposite order, so offset $01 holds $80 and offset $0F holds $F0. It arrives on the tape already filled; the loop that makes it, $EBF0-$EC17 (eight SLA C, RR A pairs for each L), is part of the mastering routine at $EB9C. Three places read it. The mirrored sprite loops at $B748 and $B760 keep $62 in D' and fetch both bytes of every sprite row through it, which draws the sprite flipped left to right; the second of them then shifts each reversed byte through a sprite_shift page. The halt screen keeps $62 in B ($D08A) and, for each of the eight pixel rows at $5002-$5702, copies 14 bytes (columns 2-15) to columns 29 down to 16, each byte reversed through this table and rotated left one bit through the carry ($D092-$D09B).

Perspective curve, 128 bytes, indexed by height/2: the first of three tables that share page $63. $80EB takes a height in A, loads entry A>>1 into B and has $811E multiply each of four projected coordinates by (128+B)/128, so an entry is the extra magnification, in 128ths, of anything at that height above the board. The entries never fall as the index grows: 0 at height 0, $40 at height $80, $80 at height $C0 and $FA at height $FE. They stay within 1.2 of 128*i/(192-i), which makes the magnification about 384/(384-height), as seen from 384 units above the board; the exact rule that produced the bytes is not established. $80EB has two callers, both in $81DB, which calls it with the bottom height of the item it is drawing (unless that is 0) and then with the top height; $8584-$858D reads the table the same way to scale the constant 10.

Sixty-four bytes: entry i is 256/sqrt(1+(i/64)^2) rounded down and held to $FF, that is 256 times the cosine of the angle whose tangent is i/64. It runs from $FF at i=0 to $B6 at i=63. Read at $AA8B and $AAC7, in the routine at $A9A2 that $A926 calls while it turns the worm's speed and heading into velocities. Both reads use offset $80 + (t>>2) on page $63, where t is the low byte of the slope word the caller loaded from ($8005), and each multiplies a magnitude by entry/256. $A9A2 returns before either read when t is 0.

Quarter sine wave, 64 bytes, read at $A8D6 by the sine routine $A8C4. Of the five instructions that load H with $63 ($80EB, $8584, $A8C4, $AA89, $AAC5) it is the one whose offset runs from $C0 up. $A8C4 takes an angle in A with 256 steps to the circle, folds it into the first quadrant (index A AND $3F, or 63 minus that when bit 6 of A is set), returns the entry in A and leaves bit 7 of the angle, the sign, in the carry of AF'. Entry 0 is 0 and the rest climb to $FF, within 1.1 of 255*sin((i+0.5)*90/64 degrees); the exact rule that produced the bytes is not established. $A8C4 has 16 callers; the cosine is taken by adding $40 to the angle first, as at $A928.

Starting contents of cell_grid: 25 words, five rows of five, each the address of a cell record or 0. The LDIR at $7617-$7620 copies these 50 bytes to cell_grid when a game starts, and no other instruction names $6400. The centre word, at $6418, is cell_64ae, the cell the worm starts in; 16 of the 25 words hold a cell address and 9 are 0. The first word of the last row, at $6428, is cell_7382, the same cell as the word after it. The links in the cell records put cell_73ea there instead (it is the west link of cell_7382 and the south link of cell_73cc). That corner of the grid is outside the nine cells drawn, and the first time the grid moves the word is either dropped or rebuilt from the links.

The cell grid: 25 words, five rows of five, each the address of a cell record or 0 where the board has no cell. The entry for row r, column c is at $6432 + 10*r + 2*c; rows run north to south, columns west to east, and the centre entry at $644A (current_cell) is the cell the worm is in. A game start fills it from cell_grid_template. When the worm crosses a cell edge, $9F92 (east), $A035 (west), $A1D7 (north) or $A275 (south) slides the whole grid one column or row the other way with LDIR or LDDR, fills the row or column that opens up from the link words of the cells next to it, and has $A0EB and $A313 follow links again along the outer columns and rows. $ADD2-$AE3B passes the nine entries round the centre to $AEF9 for drawing; $A192 searches all 25 for a cell address and returns its column and row; $DF9F fetches the entry for a column and row; $D551 scans all 25 for blocks of type $E8-$EB; the insert map at $CE2E reads them from the last entry backwards.

Centre entry (row 2, column 2) of cell_grid: the address of the cell the worm is in. $ADD2 takes it first when the nine cells round the worm are listed for drawing; $CE1D compares it with the copy at $CE06 to decide whether the insert map needs redrawing; $A3C0 tests its high byte at $644B, and when that is 0 the worm has moved onto a square with no cell: $80 is added to the heading at $8001 to turn it round and the sparky count at $805D drops by one, stopping at 0. The 12 words after it are the rest of cell_grid: columns 3 and 4 of row 2, then rows 3 and 4.

First in memory of the board's 129 cell records, which run from $6464 to $7579 and are followed by board_end. A cell is a 256 by 256 square of the circuit board. Its record is four link words, the addresses of the cells to the east, north, west and south in that order (0 for none), then a list of 7-byte items closed by a 0 byte (see cell_6464_items). East is +x, right on the screen; south is +y, down the screen. The grid code at $9F92-$A3B2 follows the links, as do the object code at $DFF7-$E0D1 and the insert map at $CE61. Counting them as the game-start loop at $759F walks them (8 bytes of links, 7 an item, a 0 ends a list) gives 129 cells and 459 items. In the comments on these records a cell's place is counted in cells from the start cell cell_64ae along the links, leaving out the two links that do not fit a flat map (cell_670e east to cell_7571, cell_68eb east to cell_6c25, and their return links). This cell is 1 south of the start cell. Links: east cell_64cc, north cell_64ae, west cell_7364, south cell_654b. It holds 6 items (6 blocks).

Item list of cell_6464: six items and the 0 that ends the list at $6496. Every item on the board is 7 bytes: +0 top height, +1 bottom height, +2 x, +3 x size, +4 y, +5 y size, +6 type. x and y are 0-255 inside the cell and a size may carry the item past the cell's edge; +0 is never 0, because a 0 there ends the list. $AF73 reads the seven bytes in that order into a 15-byte display record and gives up early when +1 is $FF or the item lies wholly outside the 256 by 128 window round the worm. Bits 7-6 of the type give the shape: $C0 a block, $80 a ramp along x, $40 a ramp along y, $00 a wedge, a block cut along a diagonal; in the ramps, none of which has bit 5 set on this board, bit 4 says which end is high, and in the wedges bits 5-4 say which corner is kept. Bits 1-0 pick one of four 8-byte shading sets at $80CB ($825F). Block types with bit 5 set are picked out by value at $89BF-$8A0F: on this board $E0 (the sprites from $CC0B and $CC6B are drawn on its top), $E1 (drawn as a pyramid), $E2 (its own shading, $89A6), $E3 ($8833), $E8-$ED (shading $FFAA; $E8-$EB are also the blocks $D55A picks to start a train of objects from), $F4 ($874C), $F5 (not drawn), $F6 ($BB06) and $F7. Type $F7 with $0C at +5 is a spindle: $75BE sets its +1 to its +0 less one when a game starts, $A5B3 sets +1 to $FF when the worm touches it, and bit 0 of +0 decides whether its four-frame sprite runs forwards or backwards ($8611). Type $F7 with anything else at +5 is a handler record, never drawn: +4 and +5 hold the address of a routine that $AF49 calls just before it lists the item after the record. Here: 1: block, x $72-$A2, y $40-$70, height $00-$30, type $C5. 2: block, x $72-$A2, y $40-$70, height $30-$70, type $E1. 3: block, x $A2-$150, y $50-$60, height $00-$30, type $E2. 4: block, x $82-$92, y $70-$150, height $00-$30, type $E2. 5: block, x $82-$92, y $10-$40, height $00-$30, type $E2. 6: block, x $00-$72, y $50-$60, height $00-$30, type $E2.

Handler word of the record at $660E in cell_65e3: the four parameter bytes $64 $46 $02 $14 come before it and the $F7 tag after it. The tape image holds $BD90 here. Whenever the nine cells round the worm are listed for drawing (once a frame in play) and this cell is one of them, $AF49 calls the address held here just before it lists the next item ($6615, a type $F4 block at x $6C-$94, y $18-$40), with HL pointing at the record. $BD90 takes $02 off that item's top each call until it would fall below $14, sets it to $14 and, because the item is type $F4, writes $BE07 here and a random 5 to 36 into the record's first byte. $BE07 counts that byte down by one a call; when it runs out it adds $02 to the top each call up to $46, and once there, if ($8066) is not 0 and ($7C71) is below $0C, it takes one off ($8066), adds a type $F3 object over the middle of the item and writes $BD90 back. The first byte's value in the image, $64, is replaced before $BE07 ever reads it.

End of the board, two bytes: $00 and $FF. After the 0 that ends a cell's item list, the game-start loop ($75C7-$75CF) and the mastering loop ($EBE6-$EBEE) step IX on by two and stop if the byte there is $FF; otherwise they add 7 and are at the next cell's first item. After the last cell (cell_7571, list ending at $7579) that byte is the $FF at $757B. Neither loop reads the $00 at $757A, which stands where a further cell's first byte would be. The other walkers do not come here: they take one cell at a time from a cell address.

A single `JP $EB9C` between the end of the board data (the `$FF` at `$757B`) and the code that starts a game. No instruction in the image jumps to or calls `$757C`, and the word `$757C` occurs nowhere in the image, so nothing reaches it, and it has not been seen to run. Its target `$EB9C` is also the address the display list starts at in play (`$AB00` and `$AEDC` load it as a list address), so once a game is running the bytes there are no longer the code this jump was written for.

Starts a game. One reference: the `JP NC,$757F` at `$E521`, taken when the menu finds key code `$23` (the 0 key) held. It resets the stack to `$F000`, starts the sound list at `$E4C2` (pointer `$E4AE`, with `$E4B0` and `$E4B1` both 1), fills the 512 attribute bytes of character rows 0 to 15 (`$5800-$59FF`) with `$44` and zeroes the spindle count `$805B`. It then walks every board record from `$646C` in 7-byte steps: a zero first byte ends a cell's list, the next cell's records begin 9 bytes after that zero, and `$FF` two bytes after it ends the board. For each record whose byte 6 is `$F7` and byte 5 is `$0C` it writes byte 0 minus 1 into byte 1. Those records are the spindles: collecting one sets its byte 1 to `$FF` (`$A5B3`), so this puts every collected spindle back. Run against the image, the walk covers 129 cells and 459 records, 58 of them spindles, and stops at `$757B`; it also changes byte 1 in 36 of the 58 as they stand in the image, where some hold a lower value (the record at `$666D` has `$32` and 0). Next it zeroes the score `$8060`, the three bytes `$BD6C-$BD6E` and the frame counter `$8059`, and calls `$BD12` with A, B and C all 0; copies the four 16-byte worm segment records from `$7FA4` to `$7F54`; sets the heading `$8001` to `$83`, the speed `$8003` to `$0A`, the head's x `$7FF5` to 8, y `$7FF7` to 5 and height `$7FFF` to `$10` (each with a zero low byte, and `$8000` = 0); zeroes `$8004`, `$8058` and `$BAAD`; copies the 50-byte cell window from `$6400` to `$6432`; empties the object list (`$7C71` = 1, `$7C72` = `$7C74`); gives the worm `$14` (20) sparkies in `$805D`; builds the display list once (`$AAF3`) and enters the frame loop at `$7638`. It does not touch the hi-score `$8064`, the shown score `$8062` or the budget byte `$8066`.

One pass of play; `$7635` enters it and `$779D` jumps back to it. It adds 1 to the 16-bit frame counter `$8059`, cuts the speed `$8003` to `$0A` if it is `$0B` or more, calls `$7925` when the counter's low byte equals `$64` (once in 256 passes) and stores (counter AND 3) + 1 in `$8067`. Then, in order: `$9CF1` moves the worm (its head, then its segments), `$D438` updates the objects, `$AAF3` builds the display list, `$EAA9` clears the frame buffer and draws the floor, `$B2F4` draws the list and `$E9E8` copies the buffer to the screen. After that a non-zero `$8055` is raised by 1 and zeroed once it reaches 5, `$8056` is zeroed, the byte at `$7F43` is copied to the attribute at `$5800`, and four more routines run: `$77A0` (bugs on the worm), `$7C13` (controls into `$8057`), `$CE0A` (the map) and `$7A30` (panel lights and counters). Bit 7 of `$8057` leaves for the menu at `$E508`. If `$8058` is non-zero the controls are discarded (`$8057` = 0) and, unless its bit 7 is set, `$8058` is cleared. If it is zero, bit 0 of `$8057` subtracts `$0C` from the heading `$8001`, bit 1 adds `$0C`, `$8067` is zeroed, bit 2 adds 1 to the speed when the result is below `$0C`, bit 3 subtracts 3 from it with a floor of 0, and `$8058` is cleared. A fire request in `$8053` is then consumed. It is refused when `$805D` minus 1 is negative as a signed byte, which is the case at 0 and also at `$81` or more, and when the object count `$7C71` is `$12` or more. Otherwise it takes one sparky, adds one to the count, sets `$8055` to 2 and writes a 30-byte record at the list end `($7C72)`: byte 0 = `$F1`, bytes 2 and 3 = 2 (the centre cell of the window), bytes 4 to 7 = the head's x and y with 5 taken off each high byte (left alone if that would borrow), bytes 8 and 9 = `$0A`, bytes 10 and 11 = the head's height, bytes 12 and 13 = the same with `$12` added to the high byte, byte 14 = minus the heading, byte 15 = 4 and byte 16 = `$37`. With bit 6 of `$8057` set it instead adds `$80` to the worm's own heading and writes byte 14 = `$A0` and byte 15 = 0. Bytes 1 and 17 to 29 are left as they were, and `$7C72` moves on by 30. Last, if bit 4 of `$8057` is set it re-reads the controls until the bit clears and then calls the halt screen at `$D05E`.

Called once a pass from `$7688`. The bytes `$7F5A`, `$7F6A`, `$7F7A` and `$7F8A` (byte 6 of the four worm segment records, head first) count the bugs riding each segment. While `$8058` is not negative: if all four counts are 1 or more it starts the sound list at `$E4B7` (`$E4FC`) and sets `$8058` to `$FF`, which begins the worm's death; otherwise it moves bugs towards the tail, one segment a pass. A bug steps from a segment into the next one when that one is empty, and a segment other than the first that then holds 2 or more keeps all but one and hands one back to the segment before it. For example, counts (1,0,0,0) become (0,1,0,0), (2,0,1,0) become (1,1,0,1), and (1,1,1,1) give `$8058` = `$FF` with `$E4AE` = `$E4B7`. While `$8058` is negative it instead subtracts 1 from it each pass and returns as long as the result is still negative and at least one of the four counts is non-zero. When the result reaches `$7F`, or all four counts are zero, it continues into the end sequence at `$783B`.

Entered only from the code above it (`$7825` and the fall-through after `$783A`). It first discards the return address into the frame loop, so play does not resume. It tests bit 7 of the spindle count `$805B`, which `$9E70` sets by writing `$C0` there when the head touches a type `$F6` object, then writes `$E6` to `$EB9B`, `$EBAA`, `$EBB9` and `$EBC8` and `$7900` to `$EB97`, `$EBA6`, `$EBB5` and `$EBC4`. Those are the type byte (+14) and source pointer (+10) of the display-list entries at `$EB9C`, `$EBAB` and `$EBBA`, the first three of the worm's four segments, and the same two offsets of a 15-byte slot at `$EB8D` that the list builder does not use (`$AAF3` and `$AED8` load `$EB8D` and at once overwrite the register). The fourth segment's entry at `$EBC9` is left as it is. Type `$E6` is drawn by `$870F` as the sprite whose address is at source + 15, which with source `$7900` is the word at `$790F`. With bit 7 set it jumps to `$78C9`. Otherwise it starts the sound list at `$E4EE` if none is playing (`$E4F7`) and shows eight passes of explosion through `$7911` and `$7914`: sprite `$C5B3` twice, `$C5EF` twice, `$C5B3`, `$C5EF`, then `$C62B` twice, with `$8056` stepping from 2 to 23 in threes, and continues into `$788F`.

The end of both end-of-game paths: reached by falling through from `$788C` and by the jumps at `$78F8` and `$78FE`. If the hi-score `$8064` is at least the score `$8060` it jumps straight to the menu at `$E508`. Otherwise it copies the score into `$8064`, splits it with `$7B2E` and draws five digits at `$52BB`, `$52BA`, `$52B9`, `$52B8` and `$52B7` (character columns 27 down to 23 of row 21, starting two pixel lines into the cell) before jumping to `$E508`. The last two digits are taken from B after the digit routine has already been called three times, and that routine leaves B = 0, so the thousands and ten-thousands are always drawn as 0. Run on a score of 12345, this code stores 12345 in `$8064` and draws 0, 0, 3, 4, 5; the panel's own score code at `$7ADF` saves BC first and draws 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Reached from `$785E` when bit 7 of `$805B` is set, that is after the head touched a type `$F6` object. It is described here from the code alone and has not been seen to run. First loop: while the head's y high byte `$7FF7` is 2 or more it subtracts 2 from it, calls `$EAA9` (clear and floor), rebuilds the display list (`$AAF3`), writes `$FF` over the type bytes of all four worm-segment entries (`$EBAA`, `$EBB9`, `$EBC8`, `$EBD7`) so that the worm is not drawn, then draws the list (`$B2F4`) and copies it to the screen (`$E9E8`). Second loop: once a pass, with the same three calls but without rebuilding the list, it steps the byte at `$BAAD`, which the type `$F6` drawing code at `$BB06` reads. A value from 0 to `$7F` goes up by 1 and the loop ends when it reaches `$80`; a value of `$80` or more goes down by 3 and the loop ends when it drops below `$80`. Both exits go to `$788F`.

Two bytes holding the address of the sprite that the end-of-game explosion shows. `$7911` is the only instruction that names it. It is read through IX: `$783B` gives the worm's display-list entries the source pointer `$7900`, and the type `$E6` drawing routine at `$870F` takes the sprite address from source + 15 and + 16, which are these two bytes. The image holds `$C5B3`, the first value the sequence loads.
Stores HL in `$790F` and continues into `$7914`. Called five times, from `$786B`, `$7874`, `$787D`, `$7883` and `$7889`, with HL = `$C5B3`, `$C5EF`, `$C5B3`, `$C5EF` and `$C62B`.

Shows one pass of the end-of-game explosion. It stores A in `$8056` (the click spacing `$EAA9` uses while it clears the frame buffer), calls `$EAA9`, `$B2F4` and `$E9E8` (clear and floor, draw the display list, copy to the screen) without rebuilding the list, and returns with A raised by 3. Called three times directly, from `$786E`, `$7877` and `$788C`, and entered five more times by falling through from `$7911`.

Called by the frame loop when the frame counter's low byte is `$64`, with HL still holding the counter. It returns at once if bit 0 of the counter's high byte `$805A` is set, so it acts once in 512 passes. If the high byte is a multiple of 4 it sets `$8066` to `$0C`. Then, if the object count `$7C71` is below `$0A`, it adds 6 to the count and copies the 180 bytes at `$7951` (six 30-byte records) to the end of the object list at `($7C72)`, moving that pointer on by 180. One caller, `$7650`.

Six ready-made 30-byte object records, 180 bytes (`$7947` loads the length `$B4`), which `$7925` appends to the object list. Their types (byte 0) are `$F0`, `$F1`, `$F1`, `$F0`, `$F1`, `$F1`. All six have bytes 2 and 3 = `$64`, `$64`; a byte 3 of 5 or more makes the pair a cell address, here `$6464`, the first cell of the board data. All six also have bytes 8 and 9 = `$0A`, byte 11 = `$30` and byte 15 = `$FF`. Bytes 5 and 7 (x and y inside the cell) are `$85,$B0`, `$85,$70`, `$A4,$53`, `$85,$10`, `$85,$30` and `$64,$53`; byte 14 (the heading) is `$40`, `$40`, `$00`, `$C0`, `$C0`, `$80`; byte 13 is `$30` in the two `$F0` records and `$3A` in the four `$F1` records. Type `$F1` is the type the firing code gives a sparky and the type the worm collects for one (`$9E19`, `$A626`); type `$F0` is skipped by the display-list builder (`$AE5A`), so those two are never drawn. `$7940` holds the only reference.

Sixteen attribute bytes: the colours of the column of lights in the bottom panel, character columns 10 and 11 of rows 16 to 23. Each pass `$7A30` overwrites the entry numbered by the low four bits of `$E470` with a colour from `$7A15`, fills all sixteen with `$41` if the object count `$7C71` is `$12` or more, and copies them to the attribute file: entries 0, 6, 10 and 12 each colour both cells of rows 16, 19, 21 and 22, and the pairs 2-3, 4-5, 8-9 and 14-15 colour the two cells of rows 17, 18, 20 and 23. Entries 1, 7, 11 and 13 are written but never copied to the screen. Three instructions load the address (`$7A3D`, `$7A49`, `$7A56`) and `$7A4C` loads `$7A06` for the fill.

Sixteen attribute values that the panel lights take their colours from, indexed by a 4-bit number in `$7A25`: `$03 $43 $04 $05 $44 $05 $45 $43 $06 $04 $46 $07 $47 $45 $04 $07`. All have black paper; the ink numbers are 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, and seven of the sixteen have the BRIGHT bit set. One instruction names it, `$7A2A`.
Returns A = the byte at `$7A15` + (A AND `$0F`), leaving the index in DE. One caller, `$7A33`. For example A = `$FF` returns `$07`.

Called once a pass from `$7691`. Lights: it takes a random byte from `$E472`, picks a colour with `$7A25` and stores it in the entry of `$7A05` numbered by the low four bits of `$E470`; then, if the object count `$7C71` is `$12` or more, it overwrites all sixteen entries with `$41`; then it copies the table to the attributes at `$5A0A`, `$5A2A` and so on down to `$5AEA`, two cells in each of rows 16 to 23. Counters: when the spindle count `$805B` differs from its copy `$805C` it updates the copy and draws three digits at `$5659-$565B`; when the score `$8060` differs from the shown score `$8062` it moves the shown score towards it, by at most 3 a pass upwards and all at once downwards, and draws five digits at `$5097-$509B`; when the sparky count `$805D` differs from its copy `$805E` it updates the copy and draws three digits at `$5439-$543B`. The digits come from `$7B2E` and are drawn by `$7B63` and `$7B6B`. The two leading digits of the sparky and spindle rows are never drawn here.

Splits the 16-bit number in HL into five decimal digits by repeated subtraction: it calls `$7B5D` with DE = -10000, -1000, -100 and -10 in turn. Returns B = ten-thousands in the high four bits and thousands in the low four, C = hundreds and tens packed the same way, and A = L = units. For example HL = `$3039` (12345) gives B = `$12`, C = `$34`, A = 5. Four callers: `$78A1`, `$7AA8`, `$7ADF` and `$7B16`. The `INC A` at `$7B5C`, after this routine's `RET`, is the loop step of the routine that follows.

Adds DE, a negative power of ten, to HL for as long as the addition carries, adding 1 to A for each such step through the `INC A` at `$7B5C`, then takes the last addition back. On return A has gained one decimal digit and HL holds the remainder. Called four times, all from `$7B2E`. For example HL = `$3039`, DE = `$D8F0`, A = 0 returns A = 1 and HL = `$0929`.

Draws the digit held in the low four bits of A: four `SLA A` move it to the high four bits and execution continues into `$7B6B`. Ten callers: `$78A7`, `$78AE`, `$78BC`, `$7AAE`, `$7AB5`, `$7AE6`, `$7AED`, `$7AFD`, `$7B1C` and `$7B23`.

Draws the digit held in the high four bits of A at screen address HL: eight bytes from `$CDB6` + 8 times the digit, one per pixel line. It steps H for each line and, when H reaches a multiple of 8, moves to the next character row by setting H to `$50` and adding `$20` to L, which is only right in the bottom third of the screen, where all its callers draw. It returns with B = 0. Six direct callers (`$78B5`, `$78C3`, `$7ABC`, `$7AF4`, `$7B04`, `$7B2A`) and the fall-through from `$7B63`. For example A = `$35`, HL = `$565B` writes the glyph for 3 to `$565B`, `$575B` and then `$507B` to `$557B`.

Scans the eight keyboard half-rows with `IN A,(C)` at `$7B91` (ports `$FEFE`, `$FDFE`, `$FBFE` and so on to `$7FFE`) and returns only when exactly one key is down, with its code in A. The code is 8 times (4 minus the key's bit number in the half-row) plus the row number, where the row runs from 7 for `$FE` down to 0 for `$7F`: B is 0, SPACE is `$20` and CAPS SHIFT is `$27`. If two half-rows show a key, or one half-row shows two keys, or no key is down, it starts the scan again. One caller, the key redefiner at `$E593`. Run against a model of the keyboard matrix, each of the 40 keys returns the code whose entry in `$7BB0` is that key, and two keys held together never return.

Forty bytes, one for each key code that `$7B8B` returns: the character the key redefiner shows for that key. Codes 0 to 7 are `B H Y 6 5 T G V`, 8 to 15 `N J U 7 4 R F C`, 16 to 23 `M K I 8 3 E D X`, 24 to 31 `$82 L O 9 2 W S Z` and 32 to 39 `$81 $84 P 0 1 Q A $83`. The four bytes `$81` to `$84` are message numbers for the text printer at `$E95D`, whose table at `$E795` gives `<SPACE>`, `<SYM SHIFT>`, `<CAPS SHIFT>` and `<ENTER>` for them. One instruction names the table, `$E5A8`.

Eight bytes, one for each key row of the redefiner in screen order (BLASTER, BURPER, FASTER, SLOWER, RIGHTER, LEFTER, BOUNCER, ABORTER): the index in `$7BE0` at which that row's key code is stored. The values are 2, 1, 5, 4, 7, 6, 3, 0. One instruction names it, `$E59D`, which indexes it with the row number in `$8034`; the ninth row, EXIT, leaves at `$E57F` before the lookup.

Eight key codes, in the numbering of `$7B8B` and `$7BE8`, one for each control. `$7C13` tests them in order; the first sets bit 7 of the control byte `$8057` and the last bit 0. As loaded: `$06` G (bit 7, leave the game), `$24` 1 (bit 6, lay a burper), `$20` SPACE (bit 5, fire), `$01` H (bit 4, halt), `$26` A (bit 3, slower), `$25` Q (bit 2, faster), `$1A` O (bit 1, heading plus `$0C`) and `$22` P (bit 0, heading minus `$0C`). The redefiner stores a new code into one entry at `$E5A6`. Two instructions load the address, `$7C16` and `$E5A2`.

Tests one key. A is a key code: its low three bits select the half-row (0 for `$7F`, 1 for `$BF`, up to 7 for `$FE`; the routine rotates `$FE` right that many times plus one to make the high byte of the port address) and the next three bits select the key in it (0 for bit 4, up to 4 for bit 0; it rotates the byte it read right 5 minus that many times). It reads the half-row with `IN A,($FE)` at `$7BFC` and returns carry clear when the key is down and carry set when it is up. Six callers: `$7C1D` in the control reader and `$E51E`, `$E526`, `$E52E`, `$E55C` and `$E575` in the menu and the redefiner. Run against a model of the keyboard matrix it agrees with `$7B8B` for all 40 codes.

Sixteen bytes indexed by the low four bits read from port `$1F`: the control bits those four joystick lines set. Port bits 0 and 1 map to control bits 0 and 1, port bit 2 sets control bit 3 and port bit 3 sets control bit 2, so the table reads `00 01 02 03 08 09 0A 0B 04 05 06 07 0C 0D 0E 0F`. One instruction names it, `$7C35`.

Builds the control byte `$8057`; HL, DE and BC are saved and restored. It tests the eight key codes at `$7BE0` in order with `$7BE8`, shifting a 1 into E for each key that is down, so the first code ends in bit 7 and the eighth in bit 0. If `$E868` holds `$0E` (the menu flips that byte between `$0D` and `$0E` at `$E533`) it also reads the joystick with `IN A,($1F)`: the low four bits go through the table at `$7C03` and are ORed in, and bit 4 of the port adds `$20`, or `$40` when bit 2 of the port is set as well. Then the fire latch: when either of bits 5 and 6 is set and `$8054` is 0 it sets `$8054` and `$8053` to `$FF`; when neither bit is set it zeroes `$8054`. `$8053` is therefore raised once for each press. Two callers: `$768B` in the frame loop and `$7790`, where the loop waits for the halt key to be released. With the keys as loaded, G, 1, SPACE, H, A, Q, O and P give `$80`, `$40`, `$20`, `$10`, `$08`, `$04`, `$02` and `$01`, and port values `$04`, `$08`, `$10` and `$14` give `$08`, `$04`, `$20` and `$48`.

One byte: the number of 30-byte records in the object list plus 1, counting records that have been promised but not yet written. A new game sets it to 1 with the list empty. 32 instructions name it, 17 reads and 15 writes. The adders test it first: firing needs it below `$12` (`$770D`), `$7925` below `$0A` before adding 6, `$BE2A` below `$0C`, `$D450` below `$0D` before adding 2 (one marker record and the record that marker writes later at `$DE5A`), `$D494` below 9 and `$D53E` below `$0B` before adding up to 5. Eight removals subtract 1 (`$9E4E`, `$9E98`, `$A60E`, `$A658`, `$D885`, `$DBFA`, `$DD57`, `$DEEA`). `$7A42` turns the panel lights to `$41` when it is `$12` or more. The image holds 2, which matches the one record at `$7C74`.

The address of the first free byte after the last record of the object list at `$7C74`. A new game sets it to `$7C74`. Each record written moves it on by 30 (`$7786`, `$BEC4`, `$D48E`, `$D520`, `$D681`, `$DEAF`) and the wave at `$794C` by 180; each removal takes 30 off and copies the record it then points at over the one removed (`$9E5A`, `$9EA4`, `$A61A`, `$A664`, `$D891`, `$DC06`, `$DD71`, `$DEF6`). Loops over the list start from this address and step down by 30 until they pass `$7C74` (`$9FEC`, `$A09A`, `$A226`, `$A2C6`, `$AE3E`, `$D691`, `$E119`). 39 instructions name it, 23 reads and 16 writes. The image holds `$7C92`, one record.

The object list: 30-byte records for the things that move on the board apart from the worm, packed from `$7C74` up to the address in `$7C72`. The count byte `$7C71` never passes `$12`, so at most 17 records exist and the list ends by `$7E71`; from its second record on it lies over the code and text of the first screen (`$7C92-$7F2F`), which has finished by then. Layout, as the firing code at `$7722` and the display-list builder at `$AE57` use it: byte 0 is the type (`$F1` a sparky, `$F3` a bug that can climb onto the worm, and `$F0`, `$E3`, `$E5`, `$E6` and `$FB`, each with its own branch in the dispatcher at `$D6A0`; `$F0` and `$E3` are not drawn). Bytes 2 and 3 are the cell: a column and row from 0 to 4 in the 5 by 5 window at `$6432` when byte 3 is below 5, the cell's address otherwise (`$A192` converts). Bytes 4-5 and 6-7 are x and y inside the cell, low byte first, with the position in the high byte; bytes 8 and 9 are width and depth; bytes 10-11 and 12-13 are the heights of its bottom and top; the meaning of bytes 14 onward depends on the type. Eight instructions load the address `$7C74`. The 30 bytes in the image are one type `$F3` record, with `$7C71` = 2 and `$7C72` = `$7C92` to match: a state left in memory when the image was saved, which a new game discards.

The first code the game runs after the entry stub: `JP $7C92` at `$EFF6` is its only reference. If the byte at `$FC00` is zero it goes straight to `$7F30`; the tape image holds `$FF` there, so a load from tape shows the warning, and what the test was for is not established. Otherwise it prints the text at `$7CE0` one byte at a time through `$7CB3` until a zero byte, waits until any key is down (`IN A,($FE)` at `$7CA9` with A = 0, which selects all eight half-rows) and jumps to `$7F30`. Nothing comes back here afterwards, and in play the object list, from its second record on, is written over this code and its text.

Prints one byte of the warning text. Code 1 is a line break: it sets the low five bits of the cursor's low byte, so the step that follows moves to the start of the next line. Any other code is drawn as the eight bytes at `$3C00` + 8 times the code, the ROM's character set, down the eight pixel lines of the cell. The cursor is the operand of the `LD DE,nn` at `$7CCA` (bytes `$7CCB` and `$7CCC`), a screen address that the routine advances itself: by 1 after each character, and by `$0800`, one third of the screen, when the low byte wraps to zero. The tape image holds `$4000` there; following the routine through the 592-byte text leaves `$50F7`. One caller, `$7CA1`.

The text of the first screen, 592 bytes: character codes for `$7CB3`, with code 1 as a line break (11 of them) and a zero byte at `$7F2F` to end it. It is a notice headed `£100 REWARD` (`$60` is the pound sign in the Spectrum character set) that describes a genuine cassette, asks for suspected forgeries to be sent to Durell Software's address in Taunton and promises a replacement and the reward. Lines that fill all 32 columns run on without a break, which is why some words are joined in the bytes. Two references: `$7C99` loads the address, and the tenth word of the message table at `$E795` (`$E7A7`) also holds it, as message `$89`, though no `LD A,$89` exists in the image and no message text embeds that code. In play the object list can grow over the first part of the text, up to `$7E71`.

Copies the bottom-panel picture to the screen from the memory that later becomes the frame buffer: 2,048 bytes from `$F000` to the pixel lines of the bottom third (`$5000-$57FF`), then 256 bytes from `$F800` to the attributes of character rows 16 to 23 (`$5A00-$5AFF`). It then jumps to the menu at `$E508`. Reached only from the first screen, by `$7C96` and `$7CB0`, so it runs once after each load.

One byte, `$44` in the image. The frame loop copies it to the attribute of the top-left character cell (`$5800`) once a pass at `$7682`, the only instruction that names it, and nothing writes it. `$44` is bright green ink on black paper, the value a new game fills rows 0 to 15 with. Why that one cell is rewritten every pass is not established.

Eight zero bytes with no reference found: no instruction names any of them, none of the indexed accesses to the worm records that follow reaches this far down, and none has been seen read or written in play.

Eight bytes, all `$80`, standing where a record before the first worm segment record would end. Each segment record ends with four screen points (x, then y plus `$40`), and the routine that draws a segment, `$851C`, joins two points of the record before it to two of its own, reading the earlier pair at IX-8, IX-7, IX-4 and IX-3. For the first segment those offsets land here, on `$7F4C`, `$7F4D`, `$7F50` and `$7F51`, and give the point (`$80`, `$40`): the centre of the 256 by 128 view, where the worm's head is. Nothing writes these bytes, and `$7F4E`, `$7F4F`, `$7F52` and `$7F53` are never read.

The first of four 16-byte worm segment records (`$7F54`, `$7F64`, `$7F74`, `$7F84`), head first; `$809F` holds the count. Layout: bytes 0-1, 2-3 and 4-5 are signed 16-bit x, y and height offsets, in units of 1/256, from the previous point (for this record, the head) to the end of the segment; byte 6 is the number of bugs riding the segment; byte 7 is the height of the segment's end, written at `$A550`; bytes 8 to 15 are four screen points (x, y plus `$40`) for the end of the segment, written by the display-list builder at `$ACEA-$ADB9`, of which the drawing routine `$851C` reads the first and third. A new game copies all four records from `$7FA4`. The head update subtracts the head's step from this record's three offsets (`$9F78`, `$A1BC`, `$A3B7`), which is what makes the body trail behind. `$A3E9` then walks the four records through IX: a segment whose three offsets, taken as magnitudes, add up to 11 units or more hands a quarter of its x and y offsets, and a quarter or an eighth of its height offset, to the next record, its end is dropped or raised to the surface that the probe at `$9A89` finds, and things it touches are collected (`$A5A4-$A66D`). `$AB1C` walks them through HL to build the display list. Byte 6 of this record is `$7F5A`: `$9E81` adds 1 to it when the head touches a type `$F3` object, and `$77A0` passes bugs on down the worm. Five instructions name `$7F54` and five name `$7F5A`.

The second worm segment record, in the layout given at `$7F54`; its offsets run from the end of the first segment. Its bug count is `$7F6A`, which three instructions name, all in `$77A0` (`$77B2`, `$780C`, `$782C`). The rest of the record is reached only through IX (`$A405` onward, and `$851C` when it is drawn) and through HL in the display-list builder.

The third worm segment record, in the layout given at `$7F54`. Its bug count is `$7F7A`, named by `$77BB`, `$7801` and `$7831` in `$77A0`; a bug arriving from the second segment is stored here and moved on to the fourth on the next pass if that one is empty.

The fourth and last worm segment record, the tail, in the layout given at `$7F54`. Its bug count is `$7F8A`, named by `$77C4`, `$77F6` and `$7836` in `$77A0`: bugs collect here first, and when this count and the other three are all non-zero the worm dies. The segment loop's hand-on for this record (IX+`$10` to IX+`$15`) falls in the slot at `$7F94`.

A fifth 16-byte slot after the four segment records. The segment loop at `$A489-$A50B` adds the fourth segment's hand-on to the first six bytes here, reading and writing them as IX+`$10` to IX+`$15` with IX = `$7F84`, but the loop stops after four records, so nothing consumes those offsets and nothing draws this slot. The image holds `$0700`, 0 and `$0500` there, the same starting offsets as the records at `$7FA4`; a new game does not rewrite them, since its copy to `$7F54` is `$40` bytes long. The ten bytes from `$7F9A` have no reference.

The starting state of the four worm segment records: 64 bytes that a new game copies to `$7F54` (`$75E8-$75F1`, the only reference). Each 16-byte record holds an x offset of `$0700`, a y offset of 0, a height offset of `$0500` and ten zero bytes, so the worm starts as a straight line of four segments, each ending 7 units further along x and 5 units higher than the one before.
Sixteen more bytes in the pattern of the records before them (`$0700`, 0, `$0500`, then zeros). The copy at `$75EE` moves `$40` bytes, which stops just short of these, and no instruction names them.

The x position of the worm's head on the board, 16 bits: the high byte `$7FF5` is the position inside the current cell, a cell being 256 units across, and the low byte is the fraction. A new game sets `$0800`. `$9F80-$9F84` adds the pass's x step `$7FF8` to it, and a carry or borrow out of the high byte scrolls the 5 by 5 cell window at `$6432` (`$9F92`, `$A035`). The firing code copies it into the new sparky (`$7730`), and `$9DA8` adds its low byte to the step to find how many whole units the head moves. `$7FF5` on its own is read five times (`$AF02`, `$AF85`, `$D472`, `$D947`, `$DC76`) to place cells and objects relative to the head. Ten instructions name the two bytes: two writes and eight reads.

The y position of the worm's head, in the same form as `$7FF4`; a new game sets `$0500`. `$A1C5-$A1C9` adds the y step `$7FFA` to it and a carry or borrow scrolls the cell window the other way (`$A1D7`, `$A275`). The high byte `$7FF7` is read at `$AF18`, `$AFB8`, `$D478`, `$D965` and `$DCC3`, and the sequence at `$78C9` counts it down in twos. Twelve instructions name the two bytes: three writes and nine reads.

The head's x movement for the current pass of the frame loop, signed 16 bits in units of 1/256: half of the x component `$803D` that `$A926` works out from the heading and speed (`$9D05-$9D0C`). `$9DA4` and `$9DAC` read its two bytes to find the whole units moved, `$9F74` uses it to move the head and to pull the first segment the other way, and `$A3F3` takes it as the starting x for the segment loop. Five instructions name the two bytes: one write and four reads.

The head's y movement for the current pass, half of the y component `$803F` from `$A926` (`$9D0F-$9D16`). Read at `$9DB4` and `$9DBC` for the whole units moved, at `$A1B8` to move the head and the first segment's y offset, and at `$A3F9` as the starting y for the segment loop. Five instructions name the two bytes.

The head's change of height for the current pass, signed 16 bits. `$9D19-$9D35` sets it to half of (the height component `$803B` from `$A926`, minus 256 times the fall speed `$8004`). `$9DE8` replaces it with minus the height when the head would go below zero. When the head lands on or climbs a surface, `$9F59-$9F6B` sets the high byte `$7FFD` to the rise and the low byte to 0. `$9DC7` adds it to the height and `$A3B3` subtracts it from the first segment's height offset. Six instructions name the two bytes: four writes and two reads.

The height of the worm's head above the board, 16 bits with the whole part in `$7FFF`; a new game sets `$1000`. While the head is in the air `$9E04` stores the height plus the pass's change; when it lands on or climbs a surface `$9F67` sets the high byte to the surface height the probe found. Read by the firing code (`$7752`), as the starting height for the segment loop (`$A3FF`) and the display-list builder (`$AB16`), and by the bug code at `$D729` and `$D804`, which compares the worm's height with a bug's. Eleven instructions name the two bytes: three writes and eight reads.

Zeroed at the start of each head update (`$9CF2`) and set to `$0C` when an obstacle turns the head aside (`$9ECD`). `$9EC4` tests it: after one deflection in a pass the update is run again from `$9CF5` with the new heading, and if the head is blocked a second time the worm is stopped at `$9F4C` and not turned again. A new game writes 0 here as the low byte of the word it stores at `$8000`. Four instructions name it.

The worm's heading, one byte, 256 steps to a full turn; a new game sets `$83`. On flat ground `$00` moves the head towards higher x, `$40` towards lower y, `$80` towards lower x and `$C0` towards higher y. 17 instructions name it, 9 reads and 8 writes. The frame loop subtracts or adds `$0C` for the two turn controls (`$76B5-$76C9`) and adds `$80` when a burper is laid (`$7771`). `$9CFC` passes it with the speed to `$A926`, which turns the pair into the pass's x and y steps. Collecting a sparky adds a random amount from -15 to +16 (`$9E2E`, `$A638`); an obstacle replaces it with one of eight headings 3 steps either side of `$00`, `$40`, `$80` and `$C0` (`$9EF6-$9F31`) or reverses it (`$9F3A`); running off the board adds `$80` (`$A3C6`). The firing code stores its negative in the new sparky's byte 14 (`$7761`).

The low byte of the 16-bit speed whose high byte is `$8003`. Seven instructions name it, all as the pair: a new game sets the pair to `$0A00`; while the head is not falling fast (`$8004` below 3), `$9D4A-$9DA1` adds or subtracts an amount worked out from the height component `$803B`, so the worm slows going up and gains going down; a bounce off an obstacle divides the pair by 4 (`$9F3D-$9F48`); a stop zeroes it (`$9F52`). The clamp at `$9D98`, for a result whose high byte is `$0C` or more, has not been seen to run.

The worm's speed in whole units, 0 to `$0B`; a new game sets `$0A`. The frame loop cuts it to `$0A` when it is `$0B` or more (`$763F`), adds 1 for the faster control while the result stays below `$0C` and subtracts 3 for the slower one down to 0. `$9CF8` passes it to `$A926` as the length of the pass's step. `$9DFE` sets bit 0 while the head is in the air, collecting a sparky sets bits 0 and 1 (`$9E3A`, `$A644`), the death throes count it down (`$A442`), and `$AC55` adds it to the width index of one segment each pass, which draws that segment narrower, a different one each pass. 16 instructions name it, 9 reads and 7 writes, besides the four 16-bit writes through `$8002`.

The downward speed of the head, built up while nothing holds it. `$9D19-$9D35` takes 256 times this value off the pass's change of height; `$9D38-$9D43` then adds 2 to it unless that change is already below -9 units; landing (`$9E0B`), stopping (`$9F4F`) and a new game zero it. At 5 or more, `$9D22-$9D2B` sets bit 0 of `$8058`, which makes the frame loop ignore the controls for that pass, and at 3 or more the slope adjustment of the speed is skipped (`$9D46`). Six instructions name it.

The slope of the surface the head last landed on or climbed: a copy of the probe's result word `$8039`, stored at `$9F71`. The low byte is the gradient as 256 times the smaller of rise and run over the larger (`$9CCC`). The high byte carries the probe's flags from `$8040`: bit 1 for a ramp that runs along y (`$9C66`), bit 0 when the probe swapped the ramp's two heights (`$9C19`, `$9C7F`) and bit 7 when the rise is larger than the run (`$9CD4`). `$9CF5` loads it into HL for `$A926`, which uses it to produce the height component `$803B` of the step. Two instructions name it; on flat ground it is zero.
Four zero bytes between the slope word and the projection workspace. No instruction names them and none has been seen read or written in play.

Screen x of the left edge of the current object's bottom rectangle, a signed 16-bit value. For each display-list entry, `$81DB` takes the entry's four extents relative to the head (`$802B-$8031`) and scales them once for the height of its bottom and once for the height of its top (`$80EB`), giving two rectangles: the bottom one here and in `$800D`, `$800F` and `$8011` (x1, x2, y1, y2) and the top one in `$8013-$8019`. It then adds `$80` to every x and `$40` to every y, which puts the head at the centre of the view. When the bottom height is 0, or the type is `$E5`, the bottom rectangle is the extents unscaled. 30 instructions name this word: 3 writes, all in `$81DB` (`$81EA`, `$8207`, `$8236`), and 27 reads by the face routines at `$82B0-$8310` and the drawing code for the various types up to `$8DBF`.
Screen x of the right edge of the bottom rectangle described at `$800B`. 27 instructions name it: the three writes in `$81DB` (`$81F0`, `$820D`, `$823D`) and 24 reads.
Screen y of the upper edge of the bottom rectangle described at `$800B`. 26 instructions name it: three writes in `$81DB` (`$81F6`, `$8213`, `$8255`) and 23 reads.
Screen y of the lower edge of the bottom rectangle described at `$800B`. 22 instructions name it: three writes in `$81DB` (`$81FC`, `$8219`, `$825C`) and 19 reads.

Screen x of the left edge of the current object's top rectangle: the entry's left extent scaled for the height of its top by `$80EB` (`$80F7`), plus `$80` (`$8228`). The type `$E1` routine at `$8482` replaces both x values with their mean (`$848E`) and does the same to the y values, which shrinks the top to a point. 52 instructions name it, 3 writes and 49 reads; six of the reads are in the type `$F6` drawing code at `$BB65-$BC4F`.
Screen x of the right edge of the top rectangle: written by `$80EB` at `$8100`, offset at `$822F` and averaged with x1 at `$8491`. 48 instructions name it, 3 writes and 45 reads.

Screen y of the upper edge of the top rectangle: written by `$80EB` at `$8109`, offset by `$40` at `$8247` and averaged with y2 at `$84A0`. The type `$F6` drawing code also rewrites it (`$BB41`, `$BB55`), in code that has not been seen to run. 51 instructions name it, 5 writes and 46 reads.

Screen y of the lower edge of the top rectangle: written by `$80EB` at `$8112`, offset at `$824E`, averaged at `$84A3` and rewritten by the type `$F6` drawing code at `$BB4C` and `$BB5C`. 44 instructions name it, 5 writes and 39 reads.

The first of eight 16-bit words, `$801B` to `$802A`, that carry the coordinates of whatever shape is being drawn or tested: four x, y pairs for the four-cornered fill at `$9819`. This word is the first x. It is the left edge for the rectangle fill at `$8E13`, the left end of the first edge for the trapezoid fill at `$8FF5`, and the x of the first upright edge for `$9579`. The object code reuses it for an object's left edge with the cell overflow in the high byte (`$DF59`; tested at `$E1FF`, `$E272`, `$E2CC` and `$E3F0`) and copies its low byte back as the object's new x (`$D752`, `$DA50`). The halt screen writes single bytes here (`$D2A3`), having zeroed the high bytes it needs at `$D0A3-$D0B2`. 73 instructions name it, 30 writes and 43 reads.

The high byte of `$801B`, named on its own twice: the halt screen zeroes it at `$D0A3`, so that its 8-bit writes to `$801B` make valid words, and the object probe reads it at `$E19D` as the object's cell overflow in x.

The first y of the shape workspace: the top row for the rectangle fill (`$8E24`), the row of the first edge for the trapezoid fill (`$9001`, `$9014`), and the upper end of the first upright edge for `$9579` (`$9588`). The object code stores an object's near edge in y here with the cell overflow in the high byte (`$DF7D`) and copies the low byte back as the object's new y (`$D75E`, `$DA5C`). 69 instructions name it, 31 writes and 38 reads.
The high byte of `$801D`, named on its own twice: zeroed by the halt screen at `$D0AF` and read by the object probe at `$E1A3` as the object's cell overflow in y.

The second x of the shape workspace: the right edge for the rectangle fill (`$8E1E`), the right end of the first edge for the trapezoid fill (`$9008`, `$9027`), and the x of the second upright edge for `$9579`. The object code stores an object's right edge, left edge plus width, here (`$DF65`). 66 instructions name it, 29 writes and 37 reads.
The high byte of `$801F`, named on its own twice: zeroed by the halt screen at `$D0A6`, and read by the object probe at `$DFE8` to tell whether the object's right edge has crossed into the next cell.

The second y of the shape workspace: the upper end of the second upright edge for `$9579` (`$957C`) and the second corner's y for `$9819`. The rectangle and trapezoid fills do not use it. `$8444` stores byte 8 of a bug's record (its width) here and `$B39D` tests it for 7 to choose between the two ways of drawing a bug; `$DF9B` stores an object's cell (its bytes 2 and 3) here for `$DFDF`. 36 instructions name it, 14 writes and 22 reads.

The third x of the shape workspace: the left end of the second edge for the trapezoid fill (`$8FF8`, `$902F`) and the third corner's x for `$9819`. `$842C` stores byte 14 of a bug's record, its heading, here, and the bug drawing code reads it seven times (`$B411-$B580`) to turn the body and legs. `$DF92` stores an object's bottom and top heights in this byte and the next for the probe (`$DFD3`). The halt screen keeps the left end of the band it is drawing here. 63 instructions name it, 30 writes and 33 reads.

The high byte of `$8023`, used on its own by three pieces of code. `$8432` copies byte 15 of a bug's record here, and `$B3A5` and `$B3B4` take its low and high halves as the angles of one pair of legs. `$DFD8` stores an object's height, top minus bottom, here, and the probe adds it to a surface height at `$E3AE` and `$E446`. The halt screen zeroes it at `$D0A9`. Seven instructions name it.

The third y of the shape workspace: the bottom row for the rectangle fill (`$8E2A`), the row of the second edge for the trapezoid fill (`$8FF5`, `$9011`), the lower end of the first upright edge for `$9579` (`$958C`) and the third corner's y for `$9819`. `$8438` stores byte 16 of a bug's record here for a second pair of legs (`$B3C9`, `$B3D8`); `$DF89` stores an object's far edge in y, near edge plus depth; the halt screen keeps the row of the band it is drawing here. 73 instructions name it, 35 writes and 38 reads.

The high byte of `$8025`, named on its own six times: `$843E` copies byte 17 of a bug's record here for the third pair of legs (`$B3ED`, `$B3FC`); the object probe reads it at `$DFEE` and `$E020` to tell whether the object's far edge has crossed into the next cell in y; the halt screen zeroes it at `$D0B2`.

The fourth x of the shape workspace: the right end of the second edge for the trapezoid fill (`$8FFC`, `$9037`) and the fourth corner's x for `$9819`. The map routine at `$CE0A` keeps the screen column of the map cell it is drawing here (`$CE41-$CE5B`, read at `$CEC2` and `$CFF6`). The object probe stores the address of the cell an object stands in here (`$DFE5`, `$E1B3`, `$E1CA`), and the object code turns it back into a window position at `$D764` and `$DA62`. The halt screen keeps the right end of a band here. 54 instructions name it, 30 writes and 24 reads.

The high byte of `$8027`, named on its own ten times. The map routine keeps the screen row of the map cell it is drawing here: it starts from `$C8`, steps down by `$10` and stops below `$78` (`$CE2B-$CE3C`, read at `$CF4B` and `$D003`). After the object probe it is the high byte of the object's cell address, and four places test it for zero, meaning no cell there (`$D6FA`, `$DA21`, `$DB6D`, `$DD3E`). The halt screen zeroes it at `$D0AC`.

The fourth y of the shape workspace: the lower end of the second upright edge for `$9579` (`$9580`) and the fourth corner's y for `$9819`. The map routine keeps its pointer into the cell window here (`$CE31`, `$CE44`, `$CE4D`). The object step code stores the new low byte of an object's x here (`$DF5C`), which the object code reads back at `$D74C` and `$DA4A`. 45 instructions name it, 17 writes and 28 reads.
The high byte of `$8029`, named on its own three times: the object step code stores the new low byte of an object's y here (`$DF80`) and the object code reads it back at `$D758` and `$DA56`.

The first of four 16-bit words, `$802B`, `$802D`, `$802F` and `$8031`, with two main uses. The draw loop at `$B2F4` loads them with a display-list entry's x1, x2, y1 and y2 relative to the head (`$B320-$B33B`) for `$81DB` to project. The fill routines then reuse them as working copies for clipping: x1, x2, y1, y2 for the rectangle fill (`$8E1B-$8E2D`), and for the trapezoid fill at `$90F9` the left and right x on the first row (`$802B`, `$802D`) and on the last row (`$802F`, `$8031`). This word has two more uses: the display-list builder keeps the previous point's position in whole units here while it boxes a worm segment (x at `$AB39` and `$AB5C`, then y at `$AB9F` and `$ABC2`), and the bug drawing code keeps the x of the bug's centre here (`$B389`). 45 instructions name it, 26 writes and 19 reads.

The high byte of `$802B`, named on its own four times: the trapezoid fill tests it at `$9062` and `$9327` to see whether the first row's left x is off the screen, and the display-list builder stores the third byte of the worm's running position here (`$AB53`, `$ABB9`) so that `$802B` reads as a signed 16-bit number of whole units.

The second extent word: the entry's x2 for `$81DB` (`$B329`), the right edge for the rectangle fill and the right x on the first row for the trapezoid fill. The bug drawing code keeps the y of the bug's centre here (`$B390`). 41 instructions name it, 24 writes and 17 reads.
The high byte of `$802D`, read on its own twice, at `$9042` and `$9349`, where the trapezoid fill tests whether the first row's right x is off the screen.

The third extent word: the entry's y1 for `$81DB` (`$B332`), the top row for the rectangle fill and the left x on the last row for the trapezoid fill. The bug drawing code stores the bug's width here as one byte (`$B37A`) and reads it nine times to size the body and legs. 41 instructions name it, 23 writes and 18 reads.

The high byte of `$802F`, named on its own six times: the trapezoid fill's clip test reads it at `$9069`, `$9073` and `$907A`, and the bug drawing code stores one and a half times the bug's width here (`$B39A`) as the reach of its legs (`$B49A`, `$B4BB`).

The fourth extent word: the entry's y2 for `$81DB` (`$B33B`), the bottom row for the rectangle fill and the right x on the last row for the trapezoid fill. 31 instructions name it, 22 writes and 9 reads.
The high byte of `$8031`, read on its own three times by the trapezoid fill's clip test (`$9049`, `$9052`, `$905A`).

The first byte of a 20-byte block, `$8033` to `$8046`, that several routines use as parameters and scratch; the worm's probe at `$9A89` addresses it through IY. For that probe this byte is the x of the point to test, in whole units from the head: the head update stores it at `$9DB1` and the segment loop at `$A51C`, `$A6BC` and `$A7A0`, and the probe reads it as IY+0. Its other uses, each as the 16-bit word `$8033-$8034`: the y of the highest corner in the four-cornered fill (`$9941`, read at `$9889` and `$98F4`); a partial product in `$A926`, which returns the word in HL (`$AAEF`); in the display-list builder a worm segment's x offset (`$AB40`) and then one component of its half-width (`$AC7A`); in the object code an object's x step for the pass (`$DF41`, `$DCB4`), zeroed at `$D8BF` and `$D9B5`. 33 instructions name it: 17 writes, 15 reads and the `LD IY,$8033` at `$9A89`.

For the worm's probe, the y of the point to test in whole units from the head (stored at `$9DC1`, `$A52D`, `$A6C8` and `$A7A6`; read as IY+1). As the high byte of the word at `$8033` it is also the sign that `$AA9C` and `$AC6C` test and the whole part of an object's x step (`$DF49`). The key redefiner borrows it for the number of the row the cursor is on, 0 to 8 (`$E54D`, read at `$E561`, `$E569`, `$E57A` and `$E597`). Twelve instructions name it on its own.

For the worm's probe, the height of the point to test (stored at `$9DD0`, `$9DDA`, `$A553` and `$A7AC`; read at `$9AAC` and `$9B6C`). As a word it is the y of the second corner in the four-cornered fill (`$9957`, `$99EC`), a partial product in `$A926`, a worm segment's y offset and then the other component of its half-width in the display-list builder (`$ABA6`, `$AC90`), and an object's y step (`$DF21`, `$DD29`). After the object probe at `$DFB8` the byte holds the type of the board record or object that the moving object met (`$E3A0`, `$E3D3`, `$E43A`, `$E46B`), which the object code tests ten times, for instance for `$F1` at `$D848`. 50 instructions name it, 22 writes and 28 reads.

The height of the surface at the probed point. The worm's probe starts it at the probe height (`$9AAF`) and replaces it with the top of whatever stands in the way (`$9B61`); the head update compares it with the head's height to choose between climbing and being blocked (`$9EB0`) and climbs to it (`$9F5D`, `$9F64`); the segment loop does the same for each segment (`$A674`, `$A686`). The object probe uses it the same way for a moving object (`$DFDC`, `$E3C3`, `$E45B`, read six times by the object code). As the high byte of the word at `$8035` it is also a sign byte (`$AADA`, `$AC82`) and the whole part of an object's y step (`$DF6D`). 25 instructions name it on its own, 6 writes and 19 reads.

A 16-bit address: what the probe found. The worm's probe zeroes it (`$9A90`) and stores the address of the display-list entry that the point touches or rests on (`$9B3C`, `$9B76`); the head update loads it into IX to read the entry's type (`$9E0E`) and the segment loop into IY (`$A599`). The object probe stores the address of a board record or an object record here instead (`$E393`, `$E3C6`, `$E42D`, `$E45E`), and the object code reads it eight times, for example to remove a sparky that a bug ran into (`$D894`). Other uses: the y of the third corner in the four-cornered fill; a partial product in `$A926`; a word the display-list builder sets to 0 at `$AC21` and adds into each segment corner; the sign byte of an object's x step (`$DF3E`, `$DCC0`, read at `$DF4D`). 46 instructions name it, 19 writes and 27 reads.

The high byte of `$8037`. Four instructions test it for zero to see whether the worm's probe found anything (`$9E12`, `$9EB9`, `$A59D`, `$A6CB`); the object step code uses it as the sign byte of an object's y step (`$DD35`, read at `$DF71`).

A 16-bit result of the probe: the slope of the surface found, a gradient in the low byte and flags in the high byte, copied from `$803F` (`$9B43`, `$9B7D`). The head update copies it to `$8005` when the head lands or climbs (`$9F6E`). The object probe writes it five times and nothing reads it there. Other uses: the y of the lowest corner in the four-cornered fill; a partial product in `$A926`; the height of a worm segment's end in the display-list builder (`$ACA3`, read at `$ACDC` and `$AD5E`). 23 instructions name it, 14 writes and 9 reads.

The probe's verdict, in the low byte: `$FF` when the point is on or inside something, otherwise the height of the highest surface below it. The worm's probe zeroes it (`$9A96`), sets `$FF` at once when the probe height is 0 (`$9ABA`) and updates it as it tests entries (`$9B39`, `$9B5B`); the head update and the segment loop compare it with `$FF` (`$9DF2`, `$A573`). The object probe keeps the same convention (`$E0DD`, `$E390`, `$E3BD`, `$E42A`, `$E455`) and the object code reads it seven times. As a word it is also the height component of the worm's step returned by `$A926` (`$A9AF`, `$AAE8`; read at `$9D19` and `$9D4A`), the x of the highest corner in the four-cornered fill, and a corner's x before scaling in the display-list builder. 36 instructions name it, 18 writes and 18 reads.

For both probes, the height of the top of the thing under test at the probed point (`$9BF4`, and through IY+`$0A` at `$9C44` and `$9CAA`; `$E293`, `$E2F4`, `$E362`). As a word it is the x component of the worm's step from `$A926` (`$A95A`, halved into `$7FF8` at `$9D05`), the left x on the second corner's row in the four-cornered fill, a corner's y before scaling in the display-list builder, and a bug's x distance to the head (`$D950`). 33 instructions name it, 15 writes and 18 reads.

For both probes, the height of the bottom of the thing under test (`$9BFA`, `$9C41`, `$9CA7`; `$E299`, `$E2F0`, `$E35E`); the object probe compares it with the surface height plus the object's own height at `$E3A6`. As the high byte of the word at `$803D` it is the sign of a bug's x distance to the head, read at `$D81C`. Ten instructions name it on its own.

The slope of the thing under test: zeroed for each one (`$9B86`, `$E233`) and, for a ramp, set from the divide at `$9CCC` (`$9C61`, `$9CC7`, `$E307`, `$E375`), with the gradient in this byte and the flags in `$8040`. The probes copy it to `$8039` when the thing becomes the one found. As a word it is also the y component of the worm's step from `$A926` (`$A992`, halved into `$7FFA` at `$9D0F`), the right x on the second corner's row in the four-cornered fill, the height of a segment's end in the display-list builder (`$ACB5`), and a bug's y distance to the head (`$D96E`). 23 instructions name it, 12 writes and 11 reads.

The high byte of `$803F`. The worm's probe sets bit 0 here through IY+`$0D` when a ramp's high end is the other one (`$9C19`, `$9C7F`) and bit 1 for a ramp that runs along y (`$9C66`), then passes the byte in A to the divide at `$9CCC`, which adds bit 7 when the rise is larger than the run (`$9C5B`, `$9CC1`). The object probe does the same with direct stores (`$E2B6`, `$E30F`, `$E324`). `$D820` reads it as the sign of a bug's y distance to the head. Ten instructions name it on its own.

For the worm's probe, two sign bytes written together at `$9AA9`: `$8041` is 0 or `$FF` to extend the probe's x (`$8033`) to 16 bits and `$8042` does the same for its y; the probe reads them as IY+`$0E` and IY+`$0F`. As a word it is the left x on the third corner's row in the four-cornered fill (`$99B3`, `$99CC`, `$9A30`, `$9A7B`). Ten instructions name it, 6 writes and 4 reads.

The right x on the third corner's row in the four-cornered fill at `$9819`, which splits the shape into three trapezoids at its corners' rows. Nine instructions name it, all in that routine: 5 writes and 4 reads.

The x of the lowest corner in the four-cornered fill, where its third trapezoid ends in a point. Five instructions name it, all in that routine: four writes (`$999A`, `$99C0`, `$9A24`, `$9A56`) and one read (`$992E`). The byte after it, `$8046`, is its high byte.

The address of the next free 15-byte entry in the display list. `$AAF3` sets it to `$EB9C` (`$AB03`), stores it again after the four worm-segment entries (`$ADCA`), and `$B003` moves it on by 15 each time a board record or an object is accepted. `$AB25`, `$AE9C` and `$AF69` load it into IX to fill the entry. Six instructions name it.

A signed count of cells in x. While the display-list builder projects a board record or an object, it is the x offset of that thing's cell from the cell under the head: `$AEF9` stores -1, 0 or 1 for each of the nine visible cells (`$AEFA`), `$AE74` stores an object's window column minus 2, `$AF06` and `$AF80` use it as the high byte of an x coordinate, and the record handler at `$BE40` adds 2 to it to give a new object its window column. Earlier in the same routine it is the third byte of the worm's running x (`$AB07`, `$AB50`, `$AB57`). The object probe stores the offset of the cell it is testing here (`$E1D2`, `$E3D9`, as the low byte of BC). 14 instructions name it.

The y counterpart of `$8049`: the y offset in cells of the board record or object being projected (`$AEFE`, `$AE6C`; read at `$AF1C`, `$AFB4` and by the handler at `$BE47`), the third byte of the worm's running y (`$AB0A`, `$ABB6`, `$ABBD`), and the y offset of the cell under test in the object probe, which writes it as the high byte of the word at `$8049` and reads it at `$E20F`, `$E256`, `$E32B` and `$E3FE`. Twelve instructions name it on its own.

The address of the display-list entry being drawn. The draw loop at `$B2F4` starts it at the list head `$EB7E` (`$B303`) and replaces it with each entry's link in turn (`$B310`) until the link's high byte is 0. Six drawing routines reload IX from it to reach the entry and its source record (`$841C`, `$851C`, `$860A`, `$863F`, `$8667`, `$870F`). Eleven instructions name it.
Used by the list insert at `$B008`: the address of the entry after which the new entry will be linked (`$B00C`), read back at `$B02B` once the place is found. Two instructions name it.

The high byte of `$804D`, used on its own as a flag. Before the display-list builder projects an object it zeroes this byte (`$AEA7`); if the object is accepted, the insert at `$B008` stores an entry address at `$804D`, which makes this byte non-zero; `$AEB2` then tests it. For an object that was not accepted the builder goes on to `$AEB9`, where a type `$FB` object has its byte 1 counted down.

The type byte of the entry being drawn, stored by `$81DB` at `$81DC`. Its low two bits choose one of the four pattern sets at `$80CB` (`$825F`) and its top two bits choose the drawing routine (`$8278`); the routines read it again to tell the types apart (`$89B8`, `$8A12`, and nine reads between `$8ABC` and `$8C84`). 14 instructions name it, 1 write and 13 reads.

A counter in the trapezoid fill for its right-hand edge, the one that runs from `$802D` on the first row to `$8031` on the last. `$9323` sets it to the low byte of the x distance between those two, plus 1; the code that walks an edge which moves more than a pixel a row loads it (`$9452`, `$949E`), takes 1 off for each pixel stepped and stores it back (`$9475`, `$94C2`). Five instructions name it.

The same counter for the trapezoid fill's left-hand edge, from `$802B` on the first row to `$802F` on the last: set at `$92C8`, loaded at `$94F6` and `$953A`, stored back at `$951A` and `$955D`. Five instructions name it.

The number of rows the trapezoid fill has still to draw in the current run. The row loop at `$93E1` takes 1 off at `$956D-$9571` and repeats until it is zero; `$9397`, `$93A5`, `$93C2` and `$93DE` set it for a first row, the rows between and a last row. Six instructions name it.

Set to `$FF` by `$7C13` on the pass in which a fire control is first found down (`$7C63`), and read and zeroed by the frame loop (`$76FA`, `$7702`), which then tries to fire one sparky. Three instructions name it.

The latch behind `$8053`: `$FF` while either fire control has been down since it was last seen up (`$7C60`), 0 otherwise (`$7C6A`). `$7C59` tests it so that holding the control does not fire again. Three instructions name it, all in `$7C13`.

Sound for the pass. While `$E9E8` copies the frame buffer to the screen it flips bits 3 to 7 of the byte it writes to port `$FE`, of which bits 3 and 4 are the MIC and speaker lines, once every `$8055` pixel rows (`$EA19`), so a small value gives a buzz and 0 gives silence, since the 128 rows end before the counter comes round. That routine first steps the sound list at `($E4AE)`, when one is playing, and stores the list's current byte here (`$E9F6`). After the copy the frame loop adds 1 to a non-zero value and zeroes it once it reaches 5 (`$766E-$767B`). Other writers: firing (2, `$771F`), a deflection (`$0C`, `$9ED0`), a collected spindle (8, `$A5B7`), an explosion (8, `$DE35`), a type `$FB` marker counting down (`$21`, `$DE54`) and the halt screen (`$D0EC`, `$D10F`, `$D127`, `$D33A`). 13 instructions name it, 11 writes and 2 reads.

The same kind of value for the other long loop of a pass: while `$EAA9` fills the frame buffer with `$FF` it flips the same bits of port `$FE` once every `$8056` rows (`$EAB3`). The frame loop zeroes it after every pass (`$767F`). Writers: the end-of-game explosion (`$7914`), a sparky collected by the head (`$10`, `$9E23`) or by a segment (`$11`, `$A62D`), running off the board (9, `$A3E6`), a collected spindle (8, `$A5BA`), a type `$E5` object within 20 units of the head in x and y (2, `$DCE6`) and an explosion (8, `$DE38`). The two writes made while a bug is drawn (`$B36C`, `$B4E2`) come after the frame loop's clear and are zeroed at `$767F` before its next one. 11 instructions name it, 10 writes and 1 read.

The control byte built by `$7C13`: bit 7 leave the game, bit 6 lay a burper, bit 5 fire, bit 4 halt, bit 3 slower, bit 2 faster, bit 1 heading plus `$0C`, bit 0 heading minus `$0C`. The frame loop reads it eight times (`$7694` to `$7793`) and zeroes it for the pass when `$8058` is non-zero (`$76A5`). 12 instructions name it, 3 writes and 9 reads, all in the frame loop and `$7C13`.

Zero in normal play. Bits 0 and 1 make the frame loop ignore the controls for one pass and are then cleared (`$769C-$76F7`): bit 0 is set while the head falls fast (`$9D2B`), bit 1 when the head is over no cell (`$A3D3`) or a segment's height offset is 20 units or more (`$A565`). A value with bit 7 set means the worm is dying or the game is won: `$77A0` writes `$FF` when all four segments carry a bug (`$781D`), `$9E6D` writes `$C0` when the head touches a type `$F6` object, and `$7822` then counts the byte down each pass until it is positive, while the segment loop slows the worm and jitters its segments (`$A43B-$A469`). A new game zeroes it. 14 instructions name it, 8 writes and 6 reads.

A 16-bit count of passes of the frame loop: zeroed by a new game and incremented at `$7638-$763C`. The low byte paces things: `$764B` calls `$7925` when it equals `$64`, `$7653` takes its low two bits for `$8067`, and drawing code uses single bits of it to animate (`$84A6`, `$860E`, `$8833`, `$B4E8`, and `$8786` and `$BC77`, which have not been seen to run). `$DE91` copies it into a new bug as its heading, and two record handlers read it (`$BDD4`, `$BE73`, neither seen to run). The high byte `$805A` is read on its own twice: `$7925` tests its bit 0, and the record handler at `$BE6C` compares it with `$11` before choosing a new bug's size. 16 instructions name the two bytes.

The number of spindles collected in this game; a new game zeroes it (`$759C`) and `$A5C5-$A5C9` adds 1 for each spindle a segment touches. `$7A9C` shows it on the panel, `$BED5` compares it with `$32` (50), and the map routine reads it together with `$805C` (`$CE0D`) to see when to redraw. `$9E70` writes `$C0` here when the head touches a type `$F6` object, and `$783C` tests bit 7 to choose the end sequence. Eight instructions name it; the three at `$9E70`, `$A5C5` and `$A5C9` and the one at `$BED5` have not been seen to run.

The spindle count as last drawn on the panel. `$7A98-$7AA2` compares it with `$805B` and redraws the three digits when they differ. Two instructions name it; the map routine also reads it as the high byte of the word at `$805B`.

The number of sparkies the worm holds. A new game sets `$14` (20). Firing takes 1 (`$7705-$771A`), and is refused at 0 and at `$81` or more because the test is a signed one. The head or a segment touching a type `$F1` object adds 1 (`$9E3D`, `$A647`), a collected spindle adds 5 (`$A5BD`), and each pass the head spends over no cell takes 1 off, stopping at 0 (`$A3D6-$A3E2`). `$7B0B` shows it on the panel. Twelve instructions name it, 6 reads and 6 writes.

The sparky count as last drawn on the panel. `$7B07-$7B10` compares it with `$805D` and redraws the three digits when they differ. Two instructions name it. The byte after it, `$805F`, has no reference.

The score, 16 bits. A new game zeroes it. `$A5CC-$A5D3` adds the new spindle count for each spindle, so the first is worth 1 and the fiftieth 50; `$D84D` adds `$14` (20) when a sparky hits a bug; `$DD5A` adds `$23` (35) when a type `$E5` object meets a sparky. `$7ABF` moves the shown score towards it and `$7892` compares it with the hi-score at the end of a game. Nine instructions name it, 4 writes and 5 reads.

The score as drawn on the panel. `$7AC2-$7ADC` moves it towards `$8060` by at most 3 a pass when the score is higher, or sets it equal at once when the score is lower, and redraws the five digits. Two instructions name it; a new game does not reset it, so the opening pass of a game brings it down to 0.

The best score since the game was loaded. `$788F-$789C` replaces it with the score at the end of a game when the score is higher. Two instructions name it and nothing else writes it, so it lasts until the game is loaded again.

The number of bugs that the record handler at `$BE07` may still create: it does nothing when this is 0 (`$BE24`) and takes 1 off for each type `$F3` object it adds (`$BE36`). `$7932` sets it to `$0C` once in 1,024 passes, the first time on pass `$0064` of a game, `$D77A-$D77E` gives 1 back when a bug that has spent 40 passes outside the cell window is removed, and `$DB00-$DB06` adds byte 22 of an expiring type `$E3` object. A new game does not reset it; the image holds `$0C`. Seven instructions name it, 4 writes and 3 reads.

Chooses which worm segment is drawn narrower in the current pass. The frame loop stores (frame counter AND 3) + 1 here before the display list is built (`$7659`); the builder takes 1 off for each of the four segments and, for the one that brings it to 0, adds the speed `$8003` to the index into the table at `$E48C` that sets a segment's width (`$AC4C-$AC59`). The table's entries fall as the index rises (`$FF`, `$E6`, `$D2`, `$C5` and so on downward), so the chosen segment's two side points are placed closer together. The frame loop also zeroes it at `$76CD` on passes when the controls are read; that write is overwritten at `$7659` before the builder next runs. Four instructions name it.

A count of the board records and objects that the display-list builder accepted in the current pass: zeroed at `$ADCF` and incremented at `$AFF4-$AFF8`. `$D43B` reads it on the next pass: only when it is 0 does the code at `$D442` count down towards adding a type `$FB` marker at the head's position. Four instructions name it.

Nine 6-byte entries, 54 bytes, one for each cell of the 3 by 3 block around the cell under the head. An entry is three words: the screen x of the cell's origin (256 times the cell's x offset, minus the head's x inside its cell `$7FF5`, plus `$80`), the screen y of its origin (the same with the y offset, `$7FF7` and `$40`), and the cell's address from the window at `$6432`, or 0 where there is no cell. In address order the entries are the cells at offsets (-1,-1) `$8069`, (0,-1) `$806F`, (1,-1) `$8075`, (-1,0) `$807B`, (0,0) `$8081`, (1,0) `$8087`, (-1,1) `$808D`, (0,1) `$8093` and (1,1) `$8099`.
