The display-list builder fills each through `$AEF9` (nine calls, `$ADD8-$AE3B`), and `$EAA9` hands each to `$EB2B` (nine calls, `$EAF4-$EB27`), which draws that cell's 256-unit square of floor: filled with the rectangle fill when the address is 0, and otherwise marked with 7 to 14 single pixels (`$B9F2`) at positions produced by applying `$B350` (HL times 1509 plus 41) again and again to the cell's address. Each entry's address is loaded by exactly those two instructions; the other bytes are reached through DE and HL.
The number of worm segment records, 4. Nothing writes it; `$A3ED` and `$AB1F` copy it to the loop counter `$80A0` before walking the records at `$7F54`.

The count of worm segments still to process, loaded from `$809F` and counted down to 0 by the two loops over the segment records: the segment update (`$A3F0`, `$A7CA-$A7CE`) and the display-list builder (`$AB22`, `$ADC0-$ADC4`). Six instructions name it.

A 16-bit running value with three uses. In the head update it is the head's new height (`$9DCC`, `$9DE3`; copied to `$7FFE` at `$9E01`). In the segment update it is the x of the current segment's end relative to the head: it starts from the head's step `$7FF8` (`$A3F6`) and each record's x offset is added in turn (`$A518`), with corrections when a segment is pushed back (`$A73D`, `$A762`). The display-list builder uses it the same way starting from 0 (`$AB10`, `$AB4C`) and reads it for each corner of a segment. 18 instructions name it, 8 writes and 10 reads.

The high byte of `$80A1`, read on its own twice: at `$9DEE` as the whole part of the head's new height, and at `$A79D` to give the probe back the segment's x in whole units after a collision has been resolved.

The y of the current worm segment's end relative to the head, 16 bits: the segment update starts it from the head's step `$7FFA` (`$A3FC`) and adds each record's y offset (`$A529`), with corrections at `$A70B` and `$A794`; the display-list builder starts it from 0 (`$AB13`, `$ABB2`). 15 instructions name it, 6 writes and 9 reads.
The high byte of `$80A3`, read on its own once, at `$A7A3`, to give the probe back the segment's y in whole units.

The height of the current worm segment's end, 16 bits: both loops start it from the head's height `$7FFE` (`$A402`, `$AB19`) and add each record's height offset (`$A54C`, `$AC0A`); the segment update also puts back the height it had handed on to the next record when the segment's end is blocked (`$A68E`). 11 instructions name it, 5 writes and 6 reads.

The high byte of `$80A5`, the height in whole units, named on its own five times in the segment update: `$A56F` and `$A670` compare it with what the probe found, `$A588-$A58C` add the amount the segment's end falls or climbs in the current pass, and `$A7A9` gives it back to the probe.
Two zero bytes with no reference: no instruction names them and none has been seen read or written in play.

The first of four cell addresses, `$80A9`, `$80AB`, `$80AD` and `$80AF`, that the object probe at `$DFB8` collects before it tests a moving object against the board: the 2 by 2 block of cells that the object's footprint can touch. `$80AF` is the cell holding the footprint's far corner, `$80AD` the cell next to that one towards lower x, `$80AB` the cell next to it towards lower y, and this word the cell diagonal to it. A word is 0 where there is no cell. The probe zeroes all four (`$DFBB-$DFC4`), stores the object's own cell in one of them according to which way the footprint overlaps the next cells (`$DFF4`, `$E00A`, `$E026`, `$E038`) and fills the others by following the link words in the cells' headers (`$DFFA`, `$E010`, `$E04A-$E0D1`). Eight instructions name this word.

The second of the object probe's four cell addresses: the cell next to `$80AF` towards lower y. It is reached from `$80A9` through that cell's link word 0 (`$E077`) or from `$80AF` through its link word 2 (`$E087`), and tested with the y offset reduced by 1 (`$E0F5`). Nine instructions name it.

The third of the object probe's four cell addresses: the cell next to `$80AF` towards lower x. It is reached from `$80AF` through that cell's link word 4 (`$E09A`) or from `$80A9` through its link word 6 (`$E0AC`), and tested with the x offset reduced by 1 (`$E0EA`). Eight instructions name it.

The fourth of the object probe's four cell addresses: the cell that holds the far corner of the object's footprint, tested first (`$E0E0`). When the object has moved, `$E1AC-$E1CA` picks the object's new cell from the four by stepping back from this word's address, 2 bytes for x and 4 for y, and stores it in `$8027`. Eleven instructions name it.

Two bytes set together at `$E0D2`: how many cells the far-corner cell `$80AF` lies from the object's own cell, in x (`$80B1`) and in y (`$80B2`), each 0 or 1. The probe loads the pair into BC before each of its four cell tests and before each test against another object (nine reads, `$E0E3-$E199`), reducing one or both by 1 for the other three cells. Ten instructions name it.

A scratch byte of the trapezoid fill at `$90F9`. It holds the first row's number (`$921C`), from which `$9372` works out the address in the frame buffer; it keeps a copy of `$80B4` while a one-row shape is passed to the rectangle fill (`$9256`, `$9261`); and it holds the row count while the first row is drawn (`$9392`, `$93A1`). Seven instructions name it.

Tells the fill routines how to treat a shape's first and last rows. With bit 7 set they are drawn solid, which gives the shape an outline; with 0 every row takes the pattern (`$8EE5`, `$8FB1`, `$938B`). The rectangle fill and the trapezoid entry at `$8FF5` store `$81` (`$8E15`, `$900E`), the upright-edge fill at `$9579` stores 0 (`$9592`), the four-cornered fill stores `$81` for the middle one of its three trapezoids, which it draws first, and 0 for the other two (`$98BF`, `$98EE`), and the floor stores 0 (`$EB4C`). 13 instructions name it, 9 writes and 4 reads. The byte after it, `$80B5`, has no reference.

The first of four pattern words that `$81DB` copies from the table at `$80CB` for each object it draws, 8 bytes chosen by the low two bits of the object's type (`$826D-$8276`). Each word is a pattern byte and a toggle byte, in the form `$80BE` and `$80BF` take. This word is the pattern for the two side faces that join the upper and lower edges of the top and bottom rectangles (`$82B0`, `$82D0`). Type-specific code overrides it: `$84CB` stores `$FFAA`, `$89AF` stores `$AADD`, and `$84AD-$84B8` swaps it with `$80BA` on passes when bit 2 of the frame counter is clear. 11 instructions name it.

The second pattern word: the pattern for the top face, the rectangle that `$828F` fills. Besides the copy from `$80CB`, it is written at `$84CE`, `$8890`, `$89A9` and in code that has not been seen to run (`$875B`, `$8797`), and the ramp drawing code reads it eight times between `$8B25` and `$8DF2`. 18 instructions name it.

The third pattern word: the pattern for the two side faces that join the left and right edges of the top and bottom rectangles (`$82F0`, `$8310`). Written by the copy from `$80CB` and at `$84B8`, `$84D1`, `$889D`, `$8915` and `$89B2`. Eight instructions name it.
The fourth word of the 8 bytes that `$8276` copies from `$80CB`. No instruction reads it: the copy is its only access, so the last two bytes of each pattern set are never used.

The pattern byte for the fill routines. Its complement is what a fill writes to the frame buffer on rows of one parity (`$8E30`, `$8F9E`, `$93AB`, `$93CB`), so a set bit here becomes a cleared pixel in a buffer that starts each pass as all `$FF`. Almost every writer stores it together with `$80BF` as one word: the five face routines at `$828F-$8313` copy one of the words at `$80B6-$80BA` here, and other code loads constants such as `$AAAA` (`$8568`), `$FF55` (`$857C`) and `$00FF` (`$EB52`). 44 instructions name it, 36 writes and 8 reads.

The byte the fills XOR into the pattern from one row to the next (`$8FA7`, `$8FD8`, `$93B6`, `$93D6`, `$9567`), so that `$FF` alternates a pattern with its complement, and a toggle equal to the pattern leaves every other row untouched. When it is 0 the rectangle fill takes a shorter path that writes the same byte on every row (`$8ECE`). The halt screen complements it for each band it draws (`$D150-$D154`, `$D294-$D298`). 12 instructions name it on its own, 9 reads and 3 writes, besides the word stores through `$80BE`.
Six zero bytes with no reference: no instruction names them and none has been seen read or written in play.

A word that the draw loop sets to `$0040` at the start of every pass (`$B2F7`) and nothing reads. The image already holds `$0040`. `$40` is the y of the view's centre that `$81DB` adds as a constant, so this may be a left-over setting; what it was for is not established.
A word that the draw loop sets to `$FFC0` (-`$40`) at the start of every pass (`$B2FD`) and nothing reads; the image already holds that value.
One zero byte between the two unread words and the pattern table, with no reference.

Four sets of fill patterns, 8 bytes each, 32 bytes in all. `$81DB` picks a set with the low two bits of the object's type (`$825F-$8270`) and copies it to `$80B6-$80BD`. A set is four pairs of a pattern byte and a toggle byte: the first pair for the two faces drawn by `$82B0` and `$82D0`, the second for the top, the third for the two faces drawn by `$82F0` and `$8310`, and a fourth that is never read. Set 0 is `55 FF`, `AA FF`, `88 AA`, `AA AA`; set 1 is `FF 00`, `CC FF`, `00 00`, `AA FF`; set 2 is `44 EE`, `AA 55`, `AA AA`, `00 00`; set 3 is `EE 55`, `11 55`, `20 22`, `0A 0F`. One instruction names the table, `$826D`.

Scales an object's four extent words for one height. A is a height byte: the routine reads the byte at $6300 + A/2, one of the 128 entries of the perspective curve, into B, then passes each of the words at $802B, $802D, $802F and $8031 through the multiply at $811E and stores the results at $8013, $8015, $8017 and $8019. Each word in range comes back multiplied by (128+B)/128, so the greater the height, the further the point is pushed from the view centre. Called twice, both times from $81DB: at $8201 with the base height and at $821E with the top height.

Second entry to the multiply at $811E, for callers whose value is in the high byte of HL: it replaces HL by that byte sign-extended to 16 bits (-128 to 127) and falls into $811E, which multiplies it by (128+B)/128. Called eight times, at $ACE3, $ACF0, $AD23, $AD30, $AD65, $AD72, $ADA5 and $ADB2, all in the loop at $AB29 that builds the type $FA records of the display list. Each call there takes B from the high byte of a word, not from the curve at $6300, and stores the low byte of the result plus $80.

Multiplies the signed word in HL by (128+B)/128, the magnification for one height, and returns the result in HL. Only values from -192 to 191 are scaled: a positive value whose high byte is not zero or whose low byte is $C0 or more, and a negative value below $FF40, come back unchanged. A value in range is multiplied by twice B with eight shift-and-add steps (C takes a copy of B and is used up, B is kept), 256 times the value is added, and the sum is divided by 256, which drops the fraction. The negative path at $817A negates the value, does the same eight steps and negates the result, so negative results are rounded toward zero as well. The running sum is kept in 16 bits, so when the magnitude times B reaches 32768 one carry is lost and the result is 256 too small in magnitude. That takes a B of 171 or more, which the curve holds for height bytes of $DC and up, and with the values in the curve the shortened result is never below 133, still outside the 256 by 128 view. Six references: the four calls in $80EB, the JR at $811B inside $8116, which also falls through into it, and the call at $858D.

Draws one record of the display list. The walker at $B2F4 has copied the record's x1 (+2), x2 (+6), y1 (+4) and y2 (+8) to $802B, $802D, $802F and $8031, signed distances from the view centre, and passes the type (+$0E) in A, the base height (+$0D) in B and the top height (+$0C) in C. The routine stores the type at $804F and makes two copies of the extent: the base copy at $800B (x1), $800D (x2), $800F (y1) and $8011 (y2), scaled for height B by $80EB, or copied unscaled when B is zero or the type is $E5; and the top copy at $8013, $8015, $8017 and $8019, scaled for height C. It adds $0080 to all four x words and $0040 to all four y words, which puts the view centre at pixel (128, 64) of the frame buffer, then copies the eight bytes at $80CB + 8 * (type AND 3) to $80B6-$80BD: the pattern words for the y walls ($80B6), the top ($80B8) and the x walls ($80BA), and a fourth word at $80BC that no instruction reads. In each word the low byte is the pattern and the high byte the row toggle. Last it jumps on bits 7 and 6 of the type: both set to $89B8 (boxes and the special types), bit 7 alone to $8ABC (wedges sloping along x), bit 6 alone to $8BC3 (wedges sloping along y) and neither to $8C84 (boxes cut along a diagonal). Called from one place, $B347.

Draws an object's top face: the rectangle from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2) of the top copy at $8013-$8019, outlined and filled with the pattern word at $80B8. It copies $80B8 to the working pattern at $80BE, puts x1, x2, y1 and y2 in $801B, $801F, $801D and $8025 and jumps to the rectangle routine at $8E13. Ten callers: $84E0, $84E4, $875E and the seven face lists of $8A12 at $8A25, $8A36, $8A47, $8A51, $8A62, $8A6C and $8A76.

Draws the side wall that hangs from the y1 edge of an object, in the pattern word at $80B6. The wall is the trapezoid between two horizontal edges: the base copy's, at y1 ($800F) from x1 ($800B) to x2 ($800D), and the top copy's, at $8017 from $8013 to $8015. Both edges are passed in the two register sets to $8FF5, which returns without drawing unless the first edge is higher on screen than the second. So this wall shows only when the top copy's y1 lies below the base copy's, which is when that edge is below the view centre and the wall faces the viewer. Twelve callers: $84BB, $84D4, $84E7, $874C, $8A28, $8A39, $8A54, $8A65, $8A79, $8BD2, $8D5E and $8DB7.

Draws the side wall that hangs from the y2 edge of an object, in the pattern word at $80B6: the trapezoid between the top copy's edge at y2 ($8019, from $8013 to $8015) and the base copy's ($8011, from $800B to $800D), through $8FF5. Here the top edge is passed first, so the wall is drawn only when the top copy's y2 is higher on screen than the base copy's, which is when the edge is above the view centre. Eleven callers: $84BE, $84D7, $84EA, $874F, $8A2B, $8A3C, $8A68, $8A7C, $8C2C, $8CA2 and $8D00.

Draws the side wall that hangs from the x1 edge of an object, in the pattern word at $80BA. The wall is the trapezoid between two vertical edges: the base copy's, at x1 ($800B) from y1 ($800F) to y2 ($8011), and the top copy's, at $8013 from $8017 to $8019. They go in the two register sets to $9579, which returns without drawing unless the first edge is left of the second, so the wall shows only when the top copy's x1 is right of the base copy's: the edge is right of the view centre. Twelve callers: $84C4, $84DD, $84F0, $8755, $88A0, $8A3F, $8A57, $8A72, $8A7F, $8AD0, $8C9D and $8D59.

Draws the side wall that hangs from the x2 edge of an object, in the pattern word at $80BA: the trapezoid between the top copy's vertical edge at x2 ($8015, from $8017 to $8019) and the base copy's ($800D, from $800F to $8011), through $9579. The top edge is passed first, so the wall is drawn only when the top copy's x2 is left of the base copy's, which is when the edge is left of the view centre. Twelve callers: $84C1, $84DA, $84ED, $8752, $8918, $8A2E, $8A5A, $8A6F, $8A82, $8B4D, $8CFB and $8DBC.

Two RET instructions. The first is a routine that does nothing; the only CALLs to it are at $83D8 and $8AB8, both inside routines that nothing reaches, and the address occurs nowhere else in the image. The RET at $8331 has no reference of any kind.

Four words of storage between routines. The unreached routine at $833A saves the top copy's x1, x2 and y1 at $8332, $8334 and $8336 and reads them back from $83C1 on; $8338 has no reference. Nothing else in the image names these addresses, and all eight bytes are zero in the loaded image.

A drawing routine that nothing reaches: no instruction and no word in the image refers to $833A, and the bytes before it are a RET and the save area at $8332. It saves the top copy's x1, x2 and y1 at $8332-$8337, replaces both base x words by their mean and both base y words by their mean so that the base shrinks to its centre point, moves each side of the top copy a quarter of the top's width or depth toward the middle so that the top halves in size, and draws the result through the face-code box routine at $8A12. Then it copies the three saved words to $802B, $802D and $802F, clears $80BE and calls the empty routine at $8330. The top copy itself is not put back. What the routine was for is not established.

Draws an object of type $F1 as one sprite whose size follows the object's size on screen. Its corner is the mean of the base and top copies' x1 ($800B, $8013) and the mean of their y1 ($800F, $8017); its size is the low byte of the mean x2 less the mean x1. The routine jumps to $B797 with x in DE, y in HL and the size in B; that picks a sprite address from the table at $BF27, whose sprites are spiky bursts of growing size, and draws it. Reached only by the jump at $89D3.

Sets up an object of type $F3 and passes it to the figure routine at $B36A. It copies the base copy's x1, x2 and y1 to $801B, $801F and $801D, takes the list record's address from $804B, follows the pointer at +$0A to the entity record, and copies entity bytes +$0E, +$0F, +$10 and +$11 to $8023, $8024, $8025 and $8026 and byte +$08 to $8021. If entity byte +$12 is zero or positive it jumps straight to $B36A. If it is negative, with n its magnitude, the figure is first made smaller and turned: n/4 is added to x1 and to y1 and subtracted from x2 (one more is subtracted when the addition to x1 carries, because the SBC at $8473 takes that carry), and (n AND 3) * 64 is added to the byte at $8023, which $B36A passes to the lookup at $A8C4 as an angle of 256 to the turn. $B36A takes the figure's size from the low byte of x2 - x1. Reached only by the jump at $89CE.

Draws an object of type $E1 as a pyramid. Both x words of the top copy are replaced by their mean and both y words by their mean, so the top shrinks to its centre point and the four walls become triangles that meet there. When bit 2 of the frame counter's low byte ($8059) is clear, the wall pattern words at $80B6 and $80BA are exchanged first, so the two pairs of faces trade patterns every four frames. The walls are then drawn in the order y1, y2, x2, x1 ($82B0, $82D0, $8310, $82F0); there is no top face. Reached only by the jump at $89E2. One board record has this type.

Draws an object of type $E8 to $EF as a box with every face in the same half-tone. It sets all three pattern words, $80B6, $80B8 and $80BA, to $FFAA (pattern byte $AA with a row toggle of $FF, a one-pixel chequer), then draws the y1, y2, x2 and x1 walls and the top face last. Reached only by the jump at $8A0F, which follows the test (type AND $F8) = $E8. Thirty-six board records have these types.

Draws an object of type $E0: a box with all five faces (top, then the y1, y2, x2 and x1 walls) and, on the middle of its top, the 48 by 16 pixel picture that $BCF5 draws from the two 24-pixel halves at $CC0B and $CC6B. The picture's corner is the mean of the top copy's x1 and x2 less $18, in DE, and the mean of its y1 and y2 less 8, in HL. In play the picture shows three seven-segment digits. Reached only by the jump at $89DD. Six board records have this type.

Draws an object of type $FA, the type the list builder gives at $AB2F to the records it makes from the 16-byte entries of the table at $7F54. It makes four of them, the count held at $809F, and together they draw the worm's body. The record's pointer (+$0A) addresses one entry, and the section is a quadrilateral through four points held as (x, y) byte pairs: the pair at -$04, which belongs to the previous entry, this entry's pairs at +$0C and +$08, and the pair at -$08, again the previous entry's, with $40 taken from each y. They are written to $801B-$8029 and $A7D5 fills the shape. When entry byte +$06 is zero the fill is the pattern word $AAAA and nothing more is drawn. Otherwise the fill is $FF55 and a mottled disc is drawn over the middle of the section: its size is 10 times (128+B)/128, worked out by $811E with B taken from the curve at $6300 at an index of half of entry byte +$07, its corner is the mean of the four points less half the size, and $B7B6 draws it from the sized sprites listed at $BF59. Reached only by the jump at $89C4.

Draws an object of type $F2 as one sized sprite through $B7B6, with the base copy's x1 ($800B) in DE, its y1 ($800F) in HL and the low byte of its width, x2 - x1, in B. On the way it works out three means of base and top words and overwrites each at once, a leftover with no effect, and the RET at $8609 after the final jump is never reached. Reached only by the jump at $89C9. No record in the board data has type $F2 and the compare at $89C7 is the only instruction with $F2 as an immediate operand, but types are also stored from registers, so whether any object ever has this type is not established.

Draws an object of type $F7 as a 16 by 12 pixel sprite that turns. The picture is one of four at $CB4B, $CB7B, $CBAB and $CBDB, a rounded three-lobed shape in four positions, chosen by the low two bits of the frame counter at $8059, or of the counter negated when bit 0 of the list record's byte +$0C (its top height) is clear, so those objects turn the other way. The sprite's corner is the top copy's x1 and y1 ($8013, $8017) and $B7E3 draws it. Reached only by the jump at $89E7. The list builder lets a board record of type $F7 through only when its sixth byte is $0C ($AFE9); 58 board records are of that kind.

Draws an object of type $FB as a 16 by 16 pixel sprite with its corner at the top copy's x1 and y1. The byte at +1 of the entity record that the list record points to selects the picture: 9 or more draws nothing, 1 to 8 draws the sprite at $CA6F, a thin scatter of sparks, and 0 draws the one at $CAAF, a fuller burst. Reached only by the jump at $89F1.

Draws an object of type $E5 as a shadow on the board and a body above it. $81DB leaves the base copy of this type unscaled, so the base is the spot on the board beneath the object. While byte +$1B of the entity record is below $11, the 13-row sprite at $C8DF, a dithered cross, is drawn at the base copy's centre less 7 across and 6 down. The body is drawn over the top copy's centre. Its size is the low byte of the top copy's width, x2 - x1, or entity byte +$1C if that is smaller, and the value used is written back to +$1C: under $0D selects the 12-row sprite at $CA3F, under $10 the 15-row one at $CA03, under $14 the 18-row one at $C997 and anything larger the 22-row one at $C913, the last two 24 pixels wide. Its corner is the centre less half the row count in x and in y. All four sprites show a ball with four diagonal spikes. Reached only by the jump at $89EC.

Draws an object of type $E6 as a 16 by 15 pixel sprite whose address is the word at +$0F of the entity record, so the entity's own code chooses the picture. The sprite's corner is the top copy's centre less 8 in x and in y, and $B7E3 draws it. Reached only by the jump at $8A05.

Draws an object of type $F4: a box whose top is solid paper with four triangles of ink that grow and shrink. The walls come first (y1, y2, x2, x1, in the patterns $81DB set), then the top face with the pattern word $00FF. A size is taken from the frame counter at $8059: its low four bits, or 15 minus them when bit 4 is set, plus 5, so it runs from 5 up to 20 and back over 32 frames; it is kept in the low byte of $80B8. Four triangles are then filled with the pattern word $0000, one on each edge of the top with its apex that many pixels in toward the middle: on the y1 and y2 edges through $900C and on the x1 and x2 edges through $9590. Reached only by the jump at $89F6. Seven board records have this type.

Distance in pixels from the top copy's x1 to the stripe boundary that $8833 is working on. Set at $8862 to phase * width / 1024, where the phase is 16 times the low four bits of the frame counter and the width is the top copy's x2 - x1, and advanced by the step at $882E on each call of $891C ($8951). Read at $88BF, $88ED, $8906 and $8942.
Width of one full stripe on the top copy: a quarter of the low byte of the top copy's width. Written at $886A and read at $894C, by the striped block routine and its helper only.
The running stripe boundary for the base copy, measured from its x1: set at $8882 to phase * base width / 1024 and advanced by the step at $8830 at $8934. Read at $8893, $88AF, $88DD and $8926.
Width of one full stripe on the base copy: a quarter of the low byte of the base copy's width, x2 - x1. Written at $888A and read at $8930.
The top copy's width, x2 - x1, stored by $8833 at $8854. Only the low byte is read back, at $890A, to find how much of the top is left beyond the last stripe boundary.

Draws an object of type $E3: a box wrapped in five bands, alternately solid paper and solid ink, that travel from its x1 side to its x2 side. A band's pattern word is $00FF for paper or $0000 for ink. Bit 4 of the frame counter at $8059 decides which of them the first band gets, and the low four bits times 16 are the phase. For the top copy and for the base copy the first boundary lies at phase * width / 1024 from x1 and a full band is a quarter of the width; these four values are kept at $882D-$8830. The x1 wall is drawn first, in the first band's pattern or in $FFAA when the base offset is under 5. Then come the first, partial band ($8959), three full bands ($891C, which complements the pattern byte each time), and a last band that runs up to x2. The x2 wall is drawn in the last band's pattern, or in $FFAA when fewer than 6 pixels of the top lie beyond the last boundary. The phase wraps every 16 frames, exactly as bit 4 flips, so the bands advance a quarter of the width every 16 frames without a jump. Reached only by the jump at $8A00. Four board records have this type.

Moves on to the next band of the striped block and draws it. It complements the pattern byte at $80BE, sets the band's base limits to the base copy's x1 plus the offset at $882F and x1 plus that offset advanced by the step at $8830 (the new offset is stored), sets its top limits the same way from $882D and $882E, and falls into $8959. Called three times by $8833, at $88CA, $88CD and $88D0.

Draws one band of the striped block across three faces. The caller has put the band's x limits on the base copy in $801B and $801F and its limits on the top copy in $8023 and HL, which is stored to $8027 here. First the strip of the y1 wall is drawn through $900C, between the base copy's y1 edge and the top copy's. The two pairs of limits are then exchanged and the strip of the top face is drawn as a rectangle through $8E13 from the top copy's y1 to its y2, followed by the strip of the y2 wall through $900C, between the top copy's y2 edge and the base copy's. All three use the pattern at $80BE, and each wall strip appears only when $900C finds its first edge higher on screen than its second. Called from $88C7 and $8900 and entered by falling through from $891C.

Draws an object of type $E2, the commonest type in the board data with 102 records, as a box with a solid paper top and walls of sparse ink dots. It sets the top pattern word at $80B8 to $00FF and both wall pattern words, $80B6 and $80BA, to $AADD, then jumps to the face-code routine at $8A12, where type $E2 selects all five faces. Reached only by the jump at $89D8.

Chooses the drawing routine for a type with bits 7 and 6 both set ($C0-$FF), read from $804F. With bit 5 clear ($C0-$DF) it goes to the face-code box at $8A12. Otherwise it compares in this order: $FF returns at once with nothing drawn, $FA goes to $851C, $F2 to $85D2, $F3 to $840A, $F1 to $83DC, $E2 to $89A6, $E0 to $84E4, $E1 to $8482, $F7 to $860A, $E5 to $8667, $FB to $863F, $F4 to $874C, $F6 to $BB06, $E3 to $8833 and $E6 to $870F, and $F5 returns. Of the types left, $E8-$EF go to $84C8 and the other eight ($E4, $E7, $F0, $F8, $F9, $FC, $FD, $FE) fall into $8A12. Reached only by the jump at $827F.

Draws a box, leaving out the faces its type marks as not needed. Bits 4 to 2 of the type at $804F form a code: 0 draws the top and all four walls; 1 the four walls without the top; 2 the top and the y1, y2 and x2 walls; 3 the top and the y1, y2 and x1 walls; 4 the top and the y2, x1 and x2 walls; 5 the top and the y1, x1 and x2 walls; 6 the top and the two y walls; 7 the top and the two x walls. The top is $828F and the walls are $82B0 (y1), $82D0 (y2), $82F0 (x1) and $8310 (x2), each of which still draws nothing when its wall faces away from the view centre. Entered by the jump at $89B5 for type $E2, by the jump at $89BD for types $C0-$DF and by falling through from $8A0F; the unreached routine at $833A also calls it. The board data uses all eight codes.

A routine that nothing reaches: no instruction and no word in the image refers to $8A86, and the byte before it is the RET that ends $8A12. It clears $80BE, stores the means of the base and top copies' x1, x2 and y1 at $802B, $802D and $802F, and calls the empty routine at $8330. What it was for is not established.

Entry for types $80-$BF, wedges whose top slopes along x: one side wall has the full height and the top runs from that wall's upper edge down to the base at the opposite side. When (type AND $30) is $10 the high side is x1 and the routine goes on to $8AC9; for the other three values it is x2 and it jumps to $8B46. Reached only by the jump at $8284.

Draws a wedge that has its full height at x1 and slopes down to the base at x2. Unless type bit 3 is set, the x1 wall is drawn by $82F0. Unless (type AND 6) is 4, the triangular side under the y2 edge is drawn through $8FF5, with its apex at the top copy's (x1, y2) and its long edge along the base copy's y2; unless (type AND 6) is 6, the triangular side under the y1 edge is drawn the same way. Both use the pattern word at $80B6. Last comes the sloping face through $9579, in the pattern at $80B8, between the top copy's x1 edge and the base copy's x2 edge. The first triangle's apex is passed as the pair $8013 and $801F, and $801F equals the top copy's x1 only because $82F0 has just stored it there; with type bit 3 set it would be whatever an earlier shape left. Reached only by the jump at $8AC3. The board data holds only types $90, $92 and $94 for this routine, ten records, all with bit 3 clear.

Draws a wedge that has its full height at x2 and slopes down to the base at x1: the x2 wall through $8310 unless type bit 3 is set, the triangular side under the y2 edge unless (type AND 6) is 4 and the one under the y1 edge unless (type AND 6) is 6, both through $8FF5 in the pattern at $80B6 with their apex at the top copy's x2, and then the sloping face through $9579, in the pattern at $80B8, between the base copy's x1 edge and the top copy's x2 edge. Reached only by the jump at $8AC6, for a type whose bits 5 and 4 are anything but $10. Four board records come here (types $80, $82 and $84).

Entry for types $40-$7F, wedges whose top slopes along y. When (type AND $30) is $10 the high side is y1 and it goes to $8BD0; otherwise the high side is y2 and it goes to $8C2A. Unlike the x wedges, no other type bit is tested, so every face is attempted. Reached only by the jump at $8289.

Draws a wedge that has its full height at y1 and slopes down to the base at y2: the y1 wall through $82B0, the two triangular sides through $9579, under the x1 edge and under the x2 edge with their apex at the top copy's y1, and then the sloping face through $8FF5, in the pattern at $80B8, between the top copy's y1 edge and the base copy's y2 edge. The triangles are drawn in whatever $82B0 left at $80BE, which is the word from $80B6. The LD A,$F0 at the start has no effect, because $82B0 does not read A. Reached only by the jump at $8BCA. Seven board records come here (types $50, $52, $53, $56 and $58).

Draws a wedge that has its full height at y2 and slopes down to the base at y1: the y2 wall through $82D0, the two triangular sides through $9579 with their apex at the top copy's y2, drawn in the pattern from $80B6 that $82D0 left at $80BE, and then the sloping face through $8FF5, in the pattern at $80B8, between the base copy's y1 edge and the top copy's y2 edge. The LD A,$F0 at the start is not read by anything. Reached only by the jump at $8BCD. Thirteen board records come here (types $40, $41, $42 and $44).

Entry for types $00-$3F, boxes cut in half along a diagonal of their plan. Seen from above each is a right-angled triangle with two full walls at the right angle and a third, slanting wall along the cut. Bits 5 and 4 of the type say which corner keeps the right angle: $30 the corner (x1, y2) at $8C9B, $20 the corner (x2, y2) at $8CF9, $10 the corner (x1, y1) at $8D57 and $00 the corner (x2, y1) at $8DB5. Reached only by the jump at $828C.

Draws the half box whose right angle is at (x1, y2). The x1 wall ($82F0) and the y2 wall ($82D0) come first. The slanting wall is the four-sided shape between the top copy's diagonal, from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2), and the base copy's; its four corners go to $801B-$8029 for the four-point fill at $9819, in the pattern that the last wall call left at $80BE, the word from $80B6. The triangular top, with corners (x1, y1), (x1, y2) and (x2, y2) of the top copy, is drawn last through $8FF5 in the pattern at $80B8. The two LD A,$F0 instructions do nothing, since the wall routines do not read A. Reached only by the jump at $8C8B. Three board records come here (types $30, $31 and $33).

Draws the half box whose right angle is at (x2, y2): the x2 wall ($8310) and the y2 wall ($82D0), the slanting wall through $9819 between the diagonal from (x2, y1) to (x1, y2) on the base copy and the same diagonal on the top copy, in the pattern from $80B6, and then the triangular top through $8FF5 in the pattern at $80B8, with corners (x2, y1), (x1, y2) and (x2, y2) of the top copy. Reached only by the jump at $8C90. One board record, of type $20, comes here.

Draws the half box whose right angle is at (x1, y1): the x1 wall ($82F0) and the y1 wall ($82B0), the slanting wall through $9819 between the diagonal from (x2, y1) to (x1, y2) on the top copy and the same diagonal on the base copy, in the pattern from $80B6, and then the triangular top through $8FF5 in the pattern at $80B8, with corners (x1, y1), (x2, y1) and (x1, y2) of the top copy. Reached only by the jump at $8C95. One board record, of type $14, comes here.

Draws the half box whose right angle is at (x2, y1): the y1 wall ($82B0) and the x2 wall ($8310), the slanting wall through $9819 between the diagonal from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2) on the base copy and the same diagonal on the top copy, and then the triangular top through $8FF5 in the pattern at $80B8, with corners (x1, y1), (x2, y1) and (x2, y2) of the top copy. Because the x2 wall is the last one called here, the slanting wall takes the pattern from $80BA where the other three corners take $80B6. Reached only by the jump at $8C98. Two board records come here (types $01 and $06).

Draws an outlined, filled rectangle from the four words at $801B (x1), $801F (x2), $801D (y1) and $8025 (y2), in the pattern at $80BE. It sets $80B4 to $81, which asks the fill for cleared rows at the top and bottom, copies the words to $802B, $802D, $802F and $8031 and runs on into the clipping at $8E30. Nine references: the top face at $82AD, the stripe band at $8993, six calls in the type $F6 routine ($BB87, $BBAC, $BBC9, $BBD6, $BC04 and $BC1C) and $EB55.

Clips the rectangle whose corners are the signed words at $802B (x1), $802D (x2), $802F (y1) and $8031 (y2) to the frame buffer and fills it. The pattern byte at $80BE is put in A' first. The routine returns with nothing drawn if x1 is over 255, x2 is negative, y1 is over 127 or y2 is negative. Otherwise a negative x1 becomes 0, an x2 over 255 becomes 255, a negative y1 becomes 0 and a y2 over 127 becomes 127, and the fill at $8E67 is entered with x1 in B, x2 in D, y1 in C and y2 in E. A side that was clipped is therefore still outlined, along the edge of the buffer. Entered from $8E13 and called from two places in the polygon code, $925E and $95D6.

Fills the rectangle from column B to column D and row C to row E of the frame buffer; it returns at once when D is less than B or E is less than C. A cleared bit shows as paper and a set bit as ink, which are black and bright green once the new-game code at $758E has filled the play area's attributes with $44. On every row the pixels at columns B and D are cleared, which draws the left and right outline, and when bit 7 of $80B4 is set the whole first and last rows are cleared as well. Everything between is written a byte at a time with the complement of the pattern byte in A', so pattern $FF gives solid paper and $00 solid ink, and a pattern stays lined up with the byte columns of the screen. The routine takes keep and set masks for the two end bytes from the table at $8F00, indexed by x AND 7, works out the buffer address $F000 + 32 * row + column / 8, and stores the entry point of the row code in the operand of the JP at $8F87: $8F75 when both ends fall in one byte, otherwise $8F76 less two for each further byte column, which lands in the run of INC L and LD (HL),A pairs that ends at $8F74. With the row toggle at $80BF zero it draws the rows itself through $8F7E and $8F8A; with any other toggle it jumps to $8F9B, which exclusive-ORs the pattern with the toggle on alternate rows. Reached only by the jump at $8E64, from the instruction just before it.

One zero byte between the last instruction of the rectangle filler (the JP at $8EFC) and the mask tables, which start on the page boundary at $8F00. No instruction in the game names it, the word $8EFF occurs nowhere in the image, and it was neither read nor written in the recorded sessions. Purpose not established.

Eight masks, one for each pixel position within a byte, counted 0 to 7 from the left (bit 7): entry n holds the bits to the right of pixel n, $7F, $3F, $1F, $0F, $07, $03, $01, $00. The rectangle filler at $8E30 reads it twice, at $8E76 with the rectangle's right x and at $8E7F with its left x, forming the address from H = $8F (loaded at $8E74) and L = x AND 7, which is why the table starts a page and why it has eight entries. Of the five instructions in the game that load $8F as the high byte of a table address, this is the only one whose low byte can be 0 to 7. For the right end the entry itself is the set of bits to keep and its complement shifted left once the bits to fill; for the left end the entry is the set of bits to fill and its complement shifted left once the bits to keep. The shift leaves the pixel at x out of both sets, so the filler clears it.

Eight masks with one zero bit: entry n is $FF with the bit of pixel n cleared, $7F, $BF, $DF, $EF, $F7, $FB, $FD, $FE, so that ANDing a buffer byte with it clears that pixel. Every reader forms the address as $8F00 + ((x AND 7) OR 8), so there are eight entries. Five instructions read it: $9347 and $9364 in the trapezoid set-up, for the left and right edge pixels; $BA15, which clears a single pixel; and $CF05 and $CF10, which turn two entries into masks for the ends of a run of pixels.

Eight single-bit masks, $80 shifted right n times for pixel n: $80, $40, $20, $10, $08, $04, $02, $01. Nothing was found that reads them. Five instructions in the game load $8F as the high byte of a table address ($8E74, $9340, $9362, $BA13, $CEFB); each builds the low byte as x AND 7 or as (x AND 7) OR 8, which reaches $8F00-$8F0F and no further, no instruction names an address in $8F10-$8F17, and the recorded sessions did not read these bytes.

Twenty-eight zero bytes between the mask tables and the fill chain that starts at $8F34. No instruction names an address in $8F18-$8F33, the table readers cannot index this far (see $8F10), and the bytes were neither read nor written in the recorded sessions. Purpose not established.

The unrolled inner loop that fills the whole bytes of one row of the frame buffer: 32 pairs of INC L and LD (HL),A at $8F34-$8F73, a last INC L at $8F74 and RET C at $8F75. It is entered only through the JP at $8F87, whose operand is rewritten so that execution lands part of the way down: for a row whose left-end and right-end bytes are n columns apart the target is $8F76 - 2n, which runs n INC Ls and n - 1 stores, so the n - 1 bytes between the ends are set to A and HL finishes on the right-end byte. In a 32-byte row n is at most 31, so the lowest target is $8F38 and the two pairs at $8F34-$8F37 are never reached; with both ends in one byte the target is the RET C itself. With carry set the RET C returns to the caller of $8F87; with carry clear execution runs on into $8F76, which is how the plain rectangle loop at $8F7E uses the chain. Each byte filled costs 11 T-states (simulated: a rectangle one byte wider takes 11 more per row). $8F76-$8F7D is the end of the plain rectangle row: the fill byte goes back to A', the right-end byte becomes (old AND B') OR C', and DE is added to HL to reach the left end of the next row.

Row loop of the rectangle filler at $8E30 when there is one fill byte for every row, which is when ($80BF) is zero. On entry HL is the left-end byte of the first row, C the number of rows to draw plus one, DE is 32 less the number of byte columns between the two end bytes, and A' the fill byte, the complement of ($80BE). The alternate register set holds the end masks: D' the bits to keep in the left-end byte and E' the bits to write there, B' and C' the same for the right-end byte, the bits to write already ANDed with the fill byte. Each pass decrements C and returns at zero, writes the left-end byte as (old AND D') OR E', takes the fill byte into A, and goes through the JP at $8F87 with carry clear, so the chain fills the bytes between and runs on into $8F76 for the right-end byte and the step to the next row. Two references, both in $8E30: the CALL at $8EF4 for the rows between two border rows and the JP at $8EFC for a rectangle without them.

The JP that enters the chain at $8F34 at a computed point; its operand at $8F88-$8F89 is rewritten once for every rectangle and once for every trapezoid row whose ends are in different bytes. Two instructions write it. $8EAE in the rectangle filler stores both bytes: $8F75 when the row's two ends share a byte, otherwise $8F76 less twice the number of byte columns between them, $8F74 down to $8F38. $9412 in the trapezoid row stores only the low byte, $76 less twice that number, for 1 to 31 columns, and relies on the high byte still being $8F. Every value is the address of an INC L in the chain or of the RET C at $8F75 (simulated for all 32 widths from $8EAE and all 31 from $9412). As assembled the operand is $8F74. It is reached by falling in from $8F86 with carry clear and by three CALLs with carry set, from $8F91, $8FEF and $9418; A is the byte to store and HL the byte before the first one to fill.

Draws one row of cleared pixels from the rectangle's left x to its right x, then steps HL to the next row. The left-end byte keeps only the bits in D', the bytes between are set to zero by calling $8F87 with A = 0 and carry set, the right-end byte keeps only the bits in B', and DE is added to HL. This is the top line and the bottom line of a rectangle drawn with bit 7 of ($80B4) set, and the whole of such a rectangle when it is one row high. Six references, all from the rectangle filler: $8EEE, $8EF1 and $8EF7 on its plain path and $8FBA, $8FBD and $8FC3 on its dithered path.

The rectangle filler's path for a fill that alternates between two bytes row by row, entered by the JP NZ at $8ED2 when ($80BF) is not zero, with HL already the address of the first row's left-end byte. It chooses the first row's fill byte and leaves it in A': the complement of ($80BE) if bit 5 of the address's low byte is set, which is an odd row, otherwise that value XOR ($80BF). It then forms B - C, the number of rows less one, returning if it is negative, and does what the plain path does: with bit 7 of ($80B4) set a border row, the rows between through $8FDF and a second border row (one border row alone when the rectangle is one row high), otherwise all rows through $8FDF. In the bordered case the border row uses the first row but not its fill byte, so the fill that follows is one row out of phase with an unbordered rectangle and with the trapezoid filler: simulated with ($80BE) = $33 and ($80BF) = $FF, a bordered rectangle put $33 on odd rows and $CC on even rows, an unbordered one $CC on odd rows and $33 on even rows.

Second half of a dithered rectangle row, reached by the JP at $8FF2 once the bytes between the ends are filled. Writes the right-end byte as (old AND B') OR (fill byte AND C'), XORs the fill byte in A' with ($80BF) ready for the next row, adds DE to HL and falls into the loop head at $8FDF. H' and L' serve as scratch here, and H is borrowed for the XOR and put back.

Row loop of the dithered rectangle, with the same registers as $8F7E except that the bits to write in E' and C' have not been ANDed with a fill byte. Decrements C and returns at zero, writes the left-end byte as (old AND D') OR (fill byte AND E'), fills the bytes between with the fill byte by calling $8F87 with carry set, and jumps to $8FCB for the right end. Two references: the CALL at $8FC0 for the rows between two border rows and the JP at $8FC8 for a rectangle without them.

Register entry of the fill for a face whose top and bottom edges are horizontal. The caller passes the bottom edge in the active register set, HL = y, DE = left x, BC = right x, and the top edge in the alternate set, HL' = y, DE' = left x, BC' = right x. They are stored in ($8025), ($8023), ($8027) and ($801D), ($801B), ($801F), and execution falls into $900C. Twelve references: the JPs at $82CD and $82ED, each the last instruction of a face stub, and CALLs from $8AF9, $8B22, $8B76, $8B9F, $8C26, $8C80, $8CF5, $8D53, $8DB1 and $8E0F. The four at $8C26, $8CF5, $8D53 and $8E0F were not executed in the recorded sessions.

Fills the trapezoid described by six variables: top edge on row ($801D) from x = ($801B) to x = ($801F), bottom edge on row ($8025) from x = ($8023) to x = ($8027). It sets the mode byte ($80B4) to $81, which makes $90F9 draw the first and last rows as lines of cleared pixels, and returns without drawing unless the top row is above the bottom row, so a caller that passes the edges in the other vertical order draws nothing. The four x values are copied to ($802B), ($802D), ($802F) and ($8031) and it jumps to $90F9 with HL = the bottom row and DE = the top row. Five references besides the fall-through from $8FF5: CALLs from $87A1, $87CF, $8968 and $89A2 and the JP at $D2BE. The two at $87A1 and $87CF were not executed in the recorded sessions.

Decides which end of a trapezoid the fill at $90F9 can start from, looking only at the high bytes of the four x values: ($802D) and ($8031), the right edge at the start and end rows, then ($802B) and ($802F), the left edge. A high byte of zero means the x is inside the buffer's 256 pixels. It returns A = $80 when an edge starts inside and ends outside (start from the start row), $81 when an edge starts outside and ends inside (start from the end row), as it also does for a right edge that starts negative and ends at 256 or more, and $82 when neither edge settles it. The right edge is tested first and its answer stands; the left edge is consulted only when the right edge is inside at both ends or starts at 256 or more and ends outside. In two cases it returns a coordinate's high byte in A instead, which matches none of the three values and makes the callers draw nothing: both right x values negative ($904D), and a left x that starts at 256 or more and ends outside ($9077). Three calls, from $9114, $912D and $917E. All 81 combinations of negative, inside and 256-or-more were simulated against this reading.

Finds the x at which an edge crosses a given row. The active register set holds three y values, HL = the row wanted, BC = the y of the edge's first end, DE = the y of its second end; the alternate set holds the x values, HL' at the first end and DE' at the second. If HL - BC or DE - BC is negative, or DE - BC is zero, it switches sets and returns the first end's x unchanged. Otherwise it leaves the low byte of HL - BC in A' and DE - BC in BC, switches sets and falls into $909E, which returns HL = x1 + (x2 - x1) * (row - y1) / (y2 - y1). Twelve calls: six from the quad splitter at $993E ($9974, $99B0, $99E2, $9A08, $9A46, $9A78), three from $9BBD, $9C31 and $9C97, and three from $E26F, $E2D6 and $E344. $90F7, the early exit, is EXX and RET.

Linear interpolation: returns HL + (DE - HL) * A' / BC', where BC' is BC of the alternate register set. It takes the absolute difference of HL and DE, multiplies it by A' in eight shift-and-add steps ($90B0-$90BB), divides the 16-bit product by BC' with a restoring division ($90C1-$90E4) that first shifts the divisor up to the top of the word, and adds the quotient to the original HL or subtracts it, by the sign saved at $90A2. The quotient is rounded toward zero and is one byte: simulated on 1,500 random inputs the result was always HL plus or minus min(255, ((|DE - HL| * A') mod 65536) div BC'), so a step of more than 255 comes back as 255. Ten calls besides the fall-through from $908B: $9150, $915F, $91A1, $91B0, $91D2 and $91E1 where the trapezoid is clipped to the buffer's rows, and $96CF, $96F1, $9782 and $97A4 in the upright quad.

Fills a trapezoid with horizontal top and bottom into the frame buffer at $F000, clipped to its 256 by 128 pixels. Rows count from 0 at $F000 to 127, and above and below in these comments mean smaller and larger row numbers. HL = the y of the end row and DE = the y of the start row, which must be the smaller; ($802B) and ($802D) are the left and right x on the start row and ($802F) and ($8031) on the end row, all signed 16-bit. It first puts the row step back to +32 by storing $0020 in the operand of the LD BC at $9561. It returns if the end row is above the buffer or the start row below it. With both rows inside it asks $9042 where to start: $80 or $82 goes to $9219 to walk down from the start row, $81 goes to $91F0 to walk up from the end row, anything else returns. A start row above the buffer is handled at $9127 and an end row below it at $916E. Each row drawn has the pixels between its two edges set to the fill pattern and the two edge pixels cleared, so the sloping sides come out as lines of cleared pixels; sideways clipping happens as the edges are walked. Fifteen references, all between $903F and $993A: the JPs at $903F and $963D and thirteen CALLs from the two quad fillers.

Trapezoid whose start row is above the buffer. DE, doubled at $910B to test it, is put back, and C, the first row to draw, becomes 0. When $9042 answers $81 or $82 the fill walks up from the end row through $91F0 and stops at row 0, with nothing to compute. When it answers $80 the walk has to begin at row 0, so the two x values there are interpolated by $909E as x_start + (x_end - x_start) * (-y_start) / (y_end - y_start) and stored back in ($802B) and ($802D), DE becomes 0 and control returns to $9114 to classify again. Any other answer returns. $912B, two instructions in, is also where the JP at $91ED arrives.

Trapezoid whose end row is below the buffer (128 or more). HL, doubled at $9102 to test it, is put back and B, the last row to draw, becomes 127. A start row that is negative as well goes to $91BF, and one that is itself 128 or more returns. When $9042 answers $80 or $82 the fill walks down from the start row through $9219 and stops at row 127. When it answers $81 the walk has to begin at the bottom, so the code from $918E interpolates the two x values with the factor (128 - y_start) / (y_end - y_start), which is their position on row 128, stores them in ($802F) and ($8031) as the values for row 127, sets HL to 127 and returns to $9114.

Trapezoid whose start row is above the buffer and whose end row is below it. The code repeats $918E-$91BC and ends with JP $912B, so the bottom ends are interpolated first and the top-clip code finishes the job. Unlike $9127 it does not undo the doubling of DE done at $9174-$9176, so the height it divides by is y_end - 2 * y_start, the factor is 128 - 2 * y_start, and the doubled DE later also reaches $9270 as part of the row count the slopes are computed from. Simulated with a trapezoid from y = -20 to y = 147, the sides came out several pixels from their true positions on row 0. Reached only by the JP C at $9178, and not executed in the recorded sessions.

Sets the fill to run upward from the end row. It exchanges ($802B) with ($802F) and ($802D) with ($8031), so the start values are those of the bottom row, stores $FFE0 (-32) in the operand of the LD BC at $9561 as the row step, takes the first row from L, and joins $921B. Three references: the JP Z at $911E when $9042 answered $81, and the JP Zs at $9132 and $9137 when the start row is above the buffer and it answered $81 or $82.

Common end of the entry code. The first row to draw, E on this path and L on the path from $91F0, is saved in ($80B3), and y_start - y_end is formed in HL. If that is zero the trapezoid is a single row: the smaller of the two left x values and the larger of the two right x values are taken and a line of cleared pixels is drawn between them by the rectangle filler at $8E30, with ($80B4) set to $81 for the call and put back after it. The row is stored for $8E30 as a word whose high byte is whatever is left in H, the high byte of the larger right x, so a one-row trapezoid whose right x is 256 or more draws nothing (simulated). If the difference is positive the routine returns. Otherwise, at $9268, A' is given B - C, the number of rows to draw less one, and $9270 is called. Four references to $9219, from $9119, $9123, $9183 and $9188.

Prepares the row loop and runs it. On entry HL = y_start - y_end, that is minus the number of row steps n between the two ends, A' = the number of rows to draw less one, and ($80B3) = the first row. For the left edge it forms dx = ($802F) - ($802B) and picks the loop body by writing the displacement of the JR at $94C8: 0 when dx is zero, $06 or $2C when it is negative, $55 or $70 when it is positive, the second of each pair when |dx| is n or more, an edge that moves a pixel a row or more. IX gets the error term, -n / 2 for the slower edges and |dx| / 2 for the faster. The right edge is treated the same way from ($8031) - ($802D), with the JR at $942D (0, $06, $23, $4B, $6F) and IY. The low bytes of |dx| + 1 go to ($8051) and ($8050) as pixel counts for the faster bodies, so the counts are wrong for an edge 256 or more pixels wide. The register set that is the alternate one during the loop is left holding BC = |dx| of the left edge, DE = |dx| of the right edge and HL = -n. Then the masks and the address: a start x whose high byte is not zero is replaced by column 0 with mask $7F on the left, or column 31 with mask $FE on the right, and that edge is made vertical by storing 0 in its JR; otherwise D and E get the one-zero-bit masks from $8F08. B is the right byte column less the left one and HL is $F000 + 32 * row + left column. With ($80B4) not zero the first row is drawn with $FF in A', which clears everything between the edges, the rows between with the pattern, and the last row with $FF again, stopping as soon as $93E1 returns carry clear; with ($80B4) zero every row gets the pattern. The pattern put in A' is ($80BE) on odd rows and ($80BE) XOR ($80BF) on even rows, by bit 5 of L. One call, from $926C.

Draws ($8052) rows of a trapezoid. For each row HL is the left-end byte, B the number of byte columns from it to the right-end byte, D and E the masks whose single zero bit marks the left and right edge pixels, and A' the pattern. The pixels strictly between the two edge pixels are set to the complement of the pattern: in one byte when B is 0 ($93E8), otherwise the part of the left-end byte to the right of the edge pixel, the bytes between through the chain at $8F34 after the low byte of the JP operand at $8F88 has been set to $76 - 2 * B, and the part of the right-end byte to the left of the edge pixel. The JR at $942D then runs the right edge's body with HL on the right-end byte, $94C5 moves HL back and runs the left edge's body, and $9560 steps to the next row. It returns with carry set when the rows are done and with carry clear when a body finds its edge leaving the buffer on the far side. A negative B is not handled: the RET M at $93E5 comes after the two PUSH BC and so takes the pushed BC as its return address (simulated: with the left edge three byte columns to the right of the right edge, PC went to $FD1E, inside the frame buffer). Of 668,199 random shapes with their edges the right way round and no sloping edge spanning 256 pixels or more across, none got there; shapes with wider edges can, through the one-byte pixel counts and the one-byte quotient of $909E. A full-width row with vertical edges takes 816 T-states (simulated). Four references besides the fall-through from $93DE: $939D, $93BC, $93C8 and $9574.

The JR whose displacement selects the loop body for the right edge. $931C writes it once for each trapezoid, from the edge's direction and slope; $9350 writes 0 when the edge starts outside the buffer and $9499 writes 0 when it runs into the buffer's last column. The five values and where they land: 0 at $942F (vertical), $06 at $9435 (moving left by less than a pixel a row), $23 at $9452 (moving left by a pixel a row or more), $4B at $947A (moving right by less than a pixel a row), $6F at $949E (moving right by a pixel a row or more). Each is the first instruction of a body; all five were reached in simulation, against each of the five left-edge cases. As assembled the byte is $6F.

Right edge body for an edge that stays in one pixel column: clears the edge pixel in the right-end byte with the mask in E and goes to $94C5. It serves a right edge whose two x values are equal, one whose start x is outside the buffer, and one that has run into the last column.

Right edge body for an edge moving left by less than one pixel a row. It clears the edge pixel, then adds the right edge's |dx| to the error term in IY; when that carries it adds -n and rotates the mask in E one pixel to the left. When the zero bit wraps round the byte, L and the span B step one byte left, and if the byte just left was column 0 the edge has crossed the whole buffer and the routine returns with carry clear, which ends the fill.

Right edge body for an edge moving left by one pixel a row or more. With the count from ($8050) in C it clears the edge pixel and moves the mask one pixel left, adding -n to IY each time, until that addition no longer carries; then it adds |dx| back to IY, stores the byte, saves the count and goes to $94C5. The pixels cleared along the way are the edge's line on this row. It stops early, through $94C0, when the count reaches zero, and it returns with carry clear if the step left takes it out of column 0.

Right edge body for an edge moving right by less than one pixel a row: the arithmetic of $9435 with the mask rotated right. When the zero bit wraps into the next byte, L and B step one byte right. If that takes L past column 31 the code at $9494 undoes the step, puts the zero bit back on the last pixel of the row and stores 0 at $942E, so that from the next row on the edge is a vertical line down the buffer's right-hand column.

Right edge body for an edge moving right by one pixel a row or more: the mirror of $9452, using the same count in ($8050). Stepping past column 31 goes to $9494, which pins the edge to the right-hand column as described at $947A. It ends at $94C0, which stores the byte being worked on and saves the count, and which $9452 also uses when its count runs out.

Moves HL from the row's right-end byte back to its left-end byte by subtracting the span B from L, then the JR at $94C8 selects the loop body for the left edge. Its displacement at $94C9 is written by $92C1 once for each trapezoid; $9330 writes 0 when the edge starts outside the buffer and $94F1 writes 0 when it runs into the buffer's first column. The five values and where they land: 0 at $94CA (vertical), $06 at $94D0 (moving left by less than a pixel a row), $2C at $94F6 (moving left by a pixel a row or more), $55 at $951F (moving right by less than a pixel a row), $70 at $953A (moving right by a pixel a row or more). As assembled the byte is $70. Nine jumps from the right-edge bodies arrive at $94C5, and $94C0 falls into it.

Left edge body for an edge that stays in one pixel column: clears the edge pixel in the left-end byte with the mask in D and goes to $9560. It serves a left edge whose two x values are equal, one whose start x is outside the buffer, and one that has run into the first column.

Left edge body for an edge moving left by less than one pixel a row. It clears the edge pixel and adds the left edge's |dx| to the error term in IX; when that carries it adds -n and rotates the mask in D one pixel to the left. When the zero bit wraps round the byte, L steps one byte left and the span B grows by one. If the byte just left was column 0 the code at $94EC undoes the step, puts the zero bit back on the first pixel of the row and stores 0 at $94C9, so that from the next row on the edge is a vertical line down the buffer's left-hand column.

Left edge body for an edge moving left by one pixel a row or more. With the count from ($8051) in C it clears the edge pixel and moves the mask one pixel left, adding -n to IX each time, until that addition no longer carries; then it adds |dx| back, stores the byte, saves the count and goes to $9560. Stepping left out of column 0 goes to $94EC, which pins the edge to the left-hand column as described at $94D0. When the count reaches zero it leaves through $955B.

Left edge body for an edge moving right by less than one pixel a row: the arithmetic of $94D0 with the mask rotated right. When the zero bit wraps into the next byte, L steps one byte right and B shrinks by one; if that takes L past column 31 the left edge has left the buffer on the right and the routine returns with carry clear, which ends the fill.

Left edge body for an edge moving right by one pixel a row or more: the mirror of $94F6, using the same count in ($8051), except that stepping past column 31 returns with carry clear instead of pinning the edge. It ends at $955B, which stores the byte being worked on and saves the count before falling into $9560, and which $94F6 also uses when its count runs out.

Steps a trapezoid to its next row. Adds the operand of the LD BC at $9561 to HL: $0020, a row down, as stored by $90FC at every entry to $90F9, or $FFE0, a row up, as stored by $9210 when the fill starts from the end row. Both stores are 16-bit and cover exactly the two operand bytes, $9562 and $9563. It then XORs the pattern in A' with ($80BF), decrements the row count in ($8052) and jumps back to $93E1, or returns with carry set when the count reaches zero. Nine jumps from the left-edge bodies arrive here, and $955B falls in.

Register entry of the fill for a face whose left and right edges are vertical. The active register set carries the right side, HL = x, DE = top y, BC = bottom y, stored in ($801F), ($8021) and ($8029); the alternate set carries the left side in the same order, stored in ($801B), ($801D) and ($8025). Execution falls into $9590. Eight references: the JPs at $830D and $832D, each the last instruction of a face stub, and CALLs from $8B42, $8BBF, $8BEC, $8C06, $8C46 and $8C60. The two at $8BEC and $8C06 were not executed in the recorded sessions.

Fills a quadrilateral with vertical left and right sides: the left side at x = ($801B) from row ($801D) down to row ($8025), the right side at x = ($801F) from row ($8021) down to row ($8029). It sets ($80B4) to 0 and returns unless the left x is less than the right x. Where the two sides overlap in y it fills a rectangle with the rectangle filler at $8E30, from one row below the lower of the two top corners to one row above the higher of the two bottom corners; when those limits are the wrong way round $8E30 draws nothing. The sloping top and bottom are added as triangles by $90F9, whose edge bodies draw the slopes as lines of cleared pixels. The code that follows the rectangle here deals with a left top corner higher than the right one: if the right side's top is above the left side's bottom, a triangle from the point (left x, row ($801D)) widening to the full width on row ($8021), then on to $966B; if it is not, the sides do not overlap and $96B3 takes over. A right top corner level with or above the left one goes to $9640. $9610 deals with two top corners on one row before the rectangle is drawn: the rectangle then starts one row below them, unless the right side has no height, which goes to $961D. Two CALLs, from $87FB and $8829, neither executed in the recorded sessions, besides the fall-through from $9579.

The upright quad when both top corners and the right side's bottom corner are on one row, which leaves a triangle with a flat top from the left x to the right x and its point at (left x, row ($8025)). ($80B4) is set to $81, so the top row is drawn as a line of cleared pixels, and the triangle is passed to $90F9 with a JP; ($80B4) stays at $81 afterwards. Reached only by the JR Z at $9616, and not executed in the recorded sessions.

Top of the upright quad when the right side's top corner is level with or above the left side's. If the left top is level with or below the right side's bottom corner, the sides do not overlap in y and $9766 takes over. Otherwise it fills the triangle from the point (right x, row ($8021)) widening leftward to the full width on row ($801D), and falls into $966B. When the two top corners are on one row the triangle is a single row, which $90F9 draws as a line of cleared pixels: the flat top edge. The SBC HL,DE at $964D and the ADD HL,DE at $9667 cancel out and their flags are not used. Reached only by the JP P at $95E3.

Bottom of the upright quad. If the right side's bottom corner is above the left side's, it fills the triangle from the full width on row ($8029) narrowing to the point (left x, row ($8025)). Otherwise it fills the triangle from the full width on row ($8025) narrowing to the point (right x, row ($8029)); with the two bottom corners on one row that is a single line of cleared pixels, the flat bottom edge. Each path ends with its own RET, back to the caller of $9590. Reached by the JR at $960E and by falling in from $9668.

Upright quad whose left side lies wholly above its right side, row ($8021) being level with or below row ($8025), so that there is no rectangle and both sloping edges cross the middle. Two calls to $909E find the x at which the top edge reaches the row of the left side's bottom corner, stored in ($8023), and the x at which the bottom edge reaches the row of the right side's top corner, stored in ($8027). Three calls to $90F9 then fill the triangle between the left side and the top edge (rows ($801D) to ($8025)), the band between the two sloping edges (rows ($8025) to ($8021)) and the triangle between the bottom edge and the right side (rows ($8021) to ($8029)). Reached only by the JP P at $95EF.

Mirror of $96B3 for a right side lying wholly above the left side, row ($801D) being level with or below row ($8029). ($8023) receives the x at which the top edge reaches the row of the right side's bottom corner and ($8027) the x at which the bottom edge reaches the row of the left side's top corner; the three pieces run from row ($8021) to ($8029), from ($8029) to ($801D) and from ($801D) to ($8025). Reached only by the JP P at $9648.

Fills a convex quadrilateral given as four corners, V0 = (($801B), ($801D)), V1 = (($801F), ($8021)), V2 = (($8023), ($8025)) and V3 = (($8027), ($8029)), x then y, whose outline runs V0, V1, V3, V2. It wants the higher of V0 and V1 in the V1 slot: if V0 is the higher it exchanges V0 with V1 and V2 with V3 in the variables themselves, calls $993E, and exchanges the left and right x values that come back; otherwise it calls $993E directly. $9886 then draws. The quad appears when its highest corner is V0 or V1 and the outline in that order runs clockwise, taking x to the right and rows downward, and otherwise not, except that a sliver a pixel or two wide can pass wound either way. Of 200,000 random convex quads tested, the 61,805 that met both conditions were all drawn, and of the other 138,195 only twelve such slivers were. Six references: CALLs from $8CD5, $8D33, $8D91, $8DEF and $BA83 and the JP at $A8BE, of which only $8D91 and $A8BE were executed in the recorded sessions.

Draws the quad from what $993E left: four rows from top to bottom in ($8033), ($8035), ($8037) and ($8039); the top corner's x in ($803B); the left and right x on the second row in ($803D) and ($803F), on the third in ($8041) and ($8043); and the bottom corner's x in ($8045). It returns without drawing if the four rows are not in ascending order or if on either middle row the left x is greater than the right x, which is the test that rejects a quad wound the other way. The band between the two middle rows is filled first with ($80B4) = $81, so with a line of cleared pixels on its first and last rows. Then, with ($80B4) = 0, come the triangle from the top corner down to the second row and the triangle from the third row down to the bottom corner. Each triangle draws its last or first row in pattern over the band's line, so a line survives only where a triangle has no height, and then $90F9 draws it as a single cleared row. Reached by the JPs at $9829 and $9883.

Splits a quad into three horizontal bands for $9886. It takes the corner in the V1 slot, (($801F), ($8021)), as the highest, V0 as the next corner down the left side, V3 as the next down the right side and V2 as the corner opposite V1. The top row ($8033) and its x ($803B) are V1's. The two middle rows are those of the two middle corners; on each it stores that corner's x on its own side and, through $908B, the x at which the edge on the other side crosses the row. The bottom row ($8039) and its x ($8045) are the lowest corner's. Three comparisons pick one of four orderings: ($801D) with ($8029) at $9952, then ($801D) with ($8025) at $9982 or ($8029) with ($8025) at $9A16. The code from $9957 covers V3 level with or above V0 and V0 the lowest: second row V3's, with the x of edge V1-V0 on the left and V3's on the right; third row V2's, with the x of edge V1-V0 on the left and V2's on the right; bottom corner V0. Two calls, from $9826 and $9864.

Case of $993E with V3 level with or above V0 and V2 the lowest corner. The third row is V0's, with V0's x on the left and, on the right, the x at which edge V3-V2 crosses that row; the bottom corner is V2. Reached by the JP M at $9984.

Case of $993E with V0 above V3. The second row is V0's, with V0's x on the left and, on the right, the x at which edge V1-V3 crosses that row. If V2 is level with or above V3, the code from $9A1B makes the third row V2's, with V2's x on the left and the x of edge V1-V3 on the right, and the bottom corner V3. Reached by the JP M at $9954.

Case of $993E with V0 above V3 and V3 above V2. The third row is V3's, with V3's x on the right and, on the left, the x at which edge V0-V2 crosses that row; the bottom corner is V2. Reached by the JP M at $9A18.

A signed 16-bit amount remembered for the record at IX in the loop at $A405, which walks ($809F) records of 16 bytes from $7F54. $A499 stores here a quarter of the record's first word (IX+0 and IX+1, shifted right twice with the sign kept), and the code after it takes that amount off the word and adds it to the word at IX+$10, the first word of the next record. $A6B6 adds it to ($80A1) to form a position whose high byte goes to ($8033). $A714 reads it again and, when it is not zero, adds it back to the record's word, takes it off the word at IX+$10, adds it to ($80A1), and $A743 sets it to zero. Those four instructions are all that name it. What the records are in the game is not established here.

The same for the record's second word: $A4C3 stores a quarter of the word at IX+2, which is then taken off that word and added to the word at IX+$12. $A6C2 adds it to ($80A3) to form a position whose high byte goes to ($8034); $A76B reads it and, when it is not zero, puts it back on IX+2, takes it off IX+$12 and adds it to ($80A3), and $A79A sets it to zero. Four instructions name it: $A4C3, $A6C2, $A76B and $A79A.

The same for the record's third word, with a different fraction: $A4F4 stores a quarter of the word at IX+4 when that word is negative and an eighth of it when it is not ($A4E5-$A4F2), and the amount is then taken off that word and added to the word at IX+$14. $A67E reads it and adds it to ($80A5); unless the high byte of the sum equals ($8036) the code keeps the sum, puts the amount back on IX+4, takes it off IX+$14, and $A6B0 sets it to zero. Three instructions name it: $A4F4, $A67E and $A6B0.

Four zero bytes between the three words above and the routine at $9A89. No instruction names an address in $9A85-$9A88, and they were neither read nor written in the recorded sessions. The word $9A87 does occur once in the image, at $F171, inside the picture data that occupies the frame buffer's addresses when the game loads. Purpose not established.

Finds what lies under or against one point of the worm. The point is given as signed 8-bit offsets in ($8033) for X and ($8034) for Y, measured from the head's whole-number position when the display list was built, and a height in ($8035). The routine sign-extends the two offsets into ($8041) and ($8042), then walks the display list from the head pointer at ($EB7E), following the link word at the start of each record until it is zero. Records of type $FF and $FA (byte +$0E; $AB2F gives the worm's own records $FA) are skipped, and so is any record whose box (+$02 low X, +$06 high X, +$04 low Y, +$08 high Y, all 16-bit) does not hold the point with one unit to spare on every side. For the rest $9B83 returns the object's surface height in ($803D), its underside in ($803E) and a slope word in ($803F), or carry when the point is outside the object's shape. A surface below the running floor ($8036), which starts as the point's own height, is only remembered: the highest such surface goes to ($803B) with its record in ($8037) and its slope in ($8039), the later record winning a tie. A surface at or above the floor counts as touched unless its underside is more than 10 above the floor (the sum is held at $FF if it overflows), which lets the worm pass beneath; a touch sets ($803B) to $FF, raises ($8036) to the surface, copies the slope word, and stores the record pointer when the point's own height plus 10 reaches the underside. On return ($803B) is $FF if the point touches something, otherwise the height of the highest surface below it, zero when there is none; a point at height 0 starts with $FF, so the board itself counts as touched. Because ($8036) rises as records are processed, the result can depend on their order in the list. Called from $9DEB for the head and from $A56A for each body joint, the only two callers.

Tests the query point against one display-list record (IX) for $9A89 and reports the object's height there. It clears the slope word ($803F) and branches on the top two bits of the type byte (+$0E): $C0 goes to $9BD5, $80 to $9BFF, $40 to $9C66. The remaining class, types $00 to $3F, is handled here and has a triangular outline, the box cut along a diagonal. $908B interpolates the X of the diagonal at the point's Y: the diagonal runs from the box's low X at low Y to its high X at high Y when bits 5 and 4 of the type are equal, and from high X at low Y to low X at high Y when they differ. With bit 4 set the solid side is X at or below the diagonal, with bit 4 clear X at or above it. A point on the open side returns with carry set, a miss; otherwise the code joins the flat-top case at $9BDA. One caller, $9B20.

The flat-top case of $9B83. Class $C0 (types $C0 to $FF) arrives at $9BD5, and the triangular class joins at $9BDA once the point is known to be on its solid side. A record of type $F1, the type the firing code at $7725 gives a sparky, is looked at more closely: the word at +$0A points to the pool record it was built from, and if byte +$10 of that record is not zero the routine returns with carry set, so the sparky is not there for the worm to touch. Otherwise ($803D) takes the record's top (+$0C), ($803E) its underside (+$0D), and carry is clear. A class other than $C0 leaves at $9BD7 for $9BFF.

Class $80 of $9B83 (types $80 to $BF): a wedge whose height changes along X. $908B interpolates between the record's two heights (+$0C and +$0D) as the point's X goes from the box's low X to its high X. When bits 5 and 4 of the type differ the height falls from +$0C at low X to +$0D at high X; when they are equal it rises, and bit 0 of ($8040) is set to record that. With bit 5 clear the interpolated height is the surface, stored in ($803D), and +$0D is the underside in ($803E): a ramp. $9CCC then builds the slope word in ($803F): the low byte is 256 times the smaller of the ramp's X extent (the low byte of +$06 minus that of +$02) and its height (+$0C minus +$0D) divided by the larger, and the high byte carries bit 0 for rising with the coordinate, bit 1 clear for the X axis, and bit 7 when the height is the larger of the two. With bit 5 set the roles are exchanged: the surface is the flat top +$0C and the interpolated height is the underside, an overhang, and no ratio is computed, so the low byte of the slope word stays zero. Carry is clear on every return. A class of $40 leaves at $9C01 for $9C66.

Class $40 of $9B83 (types $40 to $7F): the wedge of $9BFF turned to run along Y. Bit 1 of ($8040) is set first to mark the axis, the interpolation runs over the point's Y between the box's low Y (+$04) and high Y (+$08), and the extent passed to $9CCC is the low byte of +$08 minus that of +$04. Bits 5 and 4 of the type keep their meanings: equal bits make the height rise with Y and set bit 0 of ($8040), and bit 5 set makes the interpolated height the underside beneath a flat top. Returns at $9CB2 or $9CCB with carry clear.

Divides the smaller of B and C by the larger and returns the quotient as an 8-bit fraction: L is 256 times the smaller over the larger, rounded down, found by eight steps of shift and subtract. Equal inputs, two zeros included, give $FF. H returns the caller's A with bit 7 set when C was the smaller, so the caller can tell which way round the ratio was taken. A', DE and BC are used as working registers and no memory is touched. Four callers: $9C5E and $9CC4, which pass a ramp's extent in C and its height in B to build the slope word, and $E304 and $E372.

The first routine the frame loop at $7638 calls each frame, from $765C, its only caller. It moves the worm's head and then, without returning in between, drags the body after it: the normal exit is the RET at $A7D4, and a bounce or a stop leaves early at $9F4B or $9F55.
