($8000), which marks a wall hit within the frame, is cleared, and at $9CF5 (entered again from $9F34 after a deflection) $A926 is called with the heading ($8001) in E, the whole part of the speed ($8003) in D and the slope word of the surface under the head ($8005) in HL. Headings count 256 to the turn: $00 moves toward +X, $40 toward -Y, $80 toward -X and $C0 toward +Y. $A926 leaves velocity components in ($803D), ($803F) and ($803B), and the frame's steps are half of each: ($7FF8) in X, ($7FFA) in Y, and for Z half of the slope component less 256 times the fall counter ($8004), in ($7FFC). All are signed 16-bit values in 256ths of a unit; on the flat at a whole speed of 10 and a heading of $00 the X step is $04FB, just under 5 units. A fall counter of 5 or more sets bit 0 of the status byte ($8058), which makes the frame loop discard that frame's controls. The counter then rises by 2 unless the high byte of the Z step plus 9 is negative; with no slope component that holds it at 20, a fall of 10 units a frame. If the counter is below 3 after this, which means the head was supported at the end of the last frame, the slope changes the speed: the size of the slope component is divided by the speed plus 256 in eight shift-and-subtract steps, the quotient is doubled, and it is taken from the 16-bit speed ($8002) when the component points up and added when it points down. A result whose high byte is 12 or more is replaced by $0E02, or by $0002 if bit 7 is set. The SBC at $9D8A subtracts the constant 0 and changes nothing, so on level ground the speed is left alone.

Works out where the step would put the head and asks $9A89 what is there. The query offsets ($8033) and ($8034) are the high bytes of the X and Y steps plus the carry from adding each step's low byte to the fraction of the position ($7FF4, $7FF6), which makes them the whole units the head moves this frame. The new height is ($7FFE) plus the Z step, kept in ($80A1) with its high byte as the query height ($8035); a downward step that would pass below zero is cut to end at zero, and ($7FFC) is rewritten to match. B is loaded with the whole part of the new height for $9EB0. If $9A89 reports nothing touched (($803B) is not $FF) the head is in the air: bit 0 of the whole speed ($8003) is set, so an airborne worm is never at speed 0, the new height is stored in ($7FFE), and control goes to $9F74 to make the move with the fall counter left running. Otherwise the code continues at $9E0A.

The head's new position touches something. The fall counter ($8004) is cleared and IX is loaded with the display-list record chosen by $9A89; when the high byte of that pointer is zero there is no record and control goes straight to $9EB0. Otherwise the record's type (+$0E) decides. $F1, a sparky that can be picked up (see $9BDA): ($8056), the period of the tone the buffer clear at $EAA9 plays this frame, is set to $10; the heading ($8001) is turned by a random amount from -15 to +16, the low five bits of ($E471) less 15; bits 0 and 1 of the whole speed ($8003) are set; the sparky count ($805D) goes up by one; and the sparky's 30-byte pool record, whose address is at +$0A, is deleted by copying the pool's last record over it, after the count byte ($7C71) is reduced and the end pointer ($7C72) moved back 30 bytes. The list record's type becomes $FF so that nothing else meets it this frame. $F6: ($8058) and ($805B) are both set to $C0; a negative ($8058) is the dying state used at $A43B, and bit 7 of ($805B) later sends the end-of-game code at $783C to the sequence at $78C9. $E5: only the list record's type is set to $FF. $F3, a bug: the count in the first body record ($7F5A) goes up by one, sound script $E4E1 is requested through $E4F7, and the bug's pool record is deleted in the same way. Every case continues at $9EB0.

Decides whether the head can mount what it has met. B holds the whole part of the head's new height from $9DF1, though after a deletion at $9E5D or $9EA7 the LDIR has left it zero and the rise is measured from height 0. If the floor ($8036) is less than 11 above B the head steps onto it at $9F59. Anything higher is a wall; that includes a sparky the head has just eaten, since the firing code at $775B makes one 18 units tall. With no record for the surface the worm is stopped at $9F4C, and so it is when ($8000) shows that this frame has already been deflected once. Otherwise ($8000) and ($8055), the period of the tone played while the frame is copied to the screen at $E9E8, are set to $0C, and the side of the wall is read from the signs of the object's box, whose coordinates are relative to the head before the move: high Y negative (the object lies wholly toward -Y), then low Y not negative, low X not negative, high X negative, tested in that order. If none holds the head is inside the box's outline and the worm is stopped. Each side has a window of 32 heading values centred on the direction straight into the wall: $30 to $4F, $B0 to $CF, $F0 to $0F and $70 to $8F. Inside the window the worm bounces at $9F37. Outside it the heading is replaced by one that runs along the wall, turned three steps away from it: $FD or $83 for an object toward -Y and $7D or $03 for one toward +Y, chosen by bit 6 of the old heading, and $43 or $BD for one toward +X and $3D or $C3 for one toward -X, chosen by bit 7. The new heading is stored at $9F31 and the frame's move is worked out again from $9CF5, this time with ($8000) set.

The head has run straight at a wall: the heading ($8001) is turned half a circle with XOR $80, the 16-bit speed ($8002) is divided by four, and the routine returns to the frame loop without moving the head or the body this frame. Reached from the four window tests at $9EF4, $9F05, $9F16 and $9F27.

Stops the worm dead: the fall counter ($8004) and the 16-bit speed ($8002) are zeroed and the routine returns to the frame loop without moving anything. Three jumps lead here: $9EBD (a wall with no object record), $9EC8 (a second wall in the same frame) and $9EED (the head inside an object's outline).

Three bytes, $C3 $C0 $A3, which would decode as JP $A3C0, the start of the board-edge test further down. They follow the RET at $9F55, no instruction names $9F56, and the address occurs nowhere in the image as a word, so they are never executed. Why they were left here is not established.

Makes the head's move once it is known to be possible. Entered at $9F59 when the head rests on a surface or steps up to one: the change in whole height goes to ($7FFD), the whole part of the height ($7FFF) becomes the floor ($8036), the low byte of the Z step is cleared, and the slope word of the surface ($8039) is kept in ($8005) for the next frame's velocity. Entered at $9F74 from $9E07 when the head is in the air, which skips all of that. Then the X step ($7FF8) is taken from the first body record's X offset ($7F54), so that the first joint stays where it was, and added to the 16-bit X position ($7FF4). The high byte of the position is the place within a board cell, 256 units across, so a carry in the direction of travel means the head has entered the next cell: toward +X the code falls into $9F92, toward -X it goes to $A035, and with no crossing to $A1B8. The SBC at $9F7B has no AND A before it. Coming from $9F59 the carry is clear, but coming from $9E07 it is still set from the CP $FF at $9DF5, so in every airborne frame the offset loses one extra 256th of a unit.

The head has crossed into the next board cell toward +X, so the window of cell pointers at $6432 moves one column. The window is five rows of five words, row for Y and column for X, with the head's cell in the middle at $644A. The first word of each row is saved in the five words at $AECE, the table is moved down two bytes with LDIR, and each row's last word is refilled from the cell now in column 3: a cell begins with four link words, and the word at +0 is its neighbour toward +X. A null pointer is replaced by $A8C1, which holds a zero word, so its neighbour is null too. $A0EB then completes column 4 and $A313 rows 0 and 4. From $9FEC every 30-byte pool record is visited, from the last ($7C72 less 30) back to the first at $7C74, to correct its cell reference: bytes +2 and +3 are the record's column and row in the window, or, when +3 is 5 or more, the address of a cell outside it. An address is looked up with $A192 and becomes a column and row again if its cell is now in the window; a column is reduced by one, and a record that leaves through column 0 is given the saved address of the cell it was in. The constants added to IX are $FFE2, minus 30, and $838C, minus $7C74, whose carry tells whether the record is still at or above the start of the pool; $7C74 is then added back. The walk ends with a jump to $A1B8.

The mirror of $9F92 for a crossing toward -X. The last word of each row is saved at $AECE, the table is moved up two bytes with LDDR, and each row's first word is refilled from the cell now in column 1 through its link word at +4, the neighbour toward -X. The base $A8BD stands in for a null pointer because $A8BD plus 4 is the zero word at $A8C1. $A0EB completes column 0 and $A313 rows 0 and 4. The pool walk from $A09A adds one to each record's column, and a record whose column reaches 5 is given the saved address of the cell it was in. The walk ends with a jump to $A1B8.

Completes one column of the cell window from the cells already in it. IY points at the column's word in row 0 ($6432 for column 0, $643A for column 4). Going down, each non-null cell's link word at +6, its neighbour toward +Y, is written to the row below; then, coming back up from row 4, each non-null cell's link word at +2, its neighbour toward -Y, is written to the row above. A null entry leaves the next one as it was. Called six times, all from the four window scrolls: $9FDB, $A089, $A21C, $A223, $A2BC and $A2C3.

Searches the 25 words of the cell window at $6432 for the cell address in HL. If it is there the routine returns its column in L and its row in H, both 0 to 4; if not it returns with HL unchanged and A at 5. The pool walks use it to turn the address a record carries into window coordinates once its cell has scrolled into view; a record whose cell is still outside keeps the address. Six callers: $A00E, $A0BC, $A248 and $A2E8 in the window scrolls, and $D767 and $DA65.

The Y part of the head's move, reached from $9F8C when no cell edge was crossed in X and from the two X scrolls when their pool walks finish. The Y step ($7FFA) is taken from the first body record's Y offset ($7F56) and added to the 16-bit Y position ($7FF6). With no cell crossing control goes to $A3B3, and for a crossing toward +Y to $A275; a crossing toward -Y falls into $A1D7.

The head has crossed into the next cell toward -Y. The window's last row is saved at $AECE (ten bytes), rows 0 to 3 are moved down one row with LDDR, and each word of row 0 is refilled from the cell now below it in row 1 through its link word at +2, the neighbour toward -Y; $A8BF plus 2 is the zero word at $A8C1, for a null. $A313 completes row 0 and $A0EB columns 0 and 4. The pool walk from $A226 adds one to each record's row (+3), and a record whose row reaches 5 is given the saved address from $AECE indexed by its column. The walk ends with a jump to $A3B3.

The crossing toward +Y. Row 0 is saved at $AECE, rows 1 to 4 are moved up one row with LDIR, and each word of row 4 is refilled from the cell now above it in row 3 through its link word at +6, the neighbour toward +Y; $A8BB plus 6 is the zero word at $A8C1, for a null. $A313 completes row 4 and $A0EB columns 0 and 4. The pool walk from $A2C6 takes one from each record's row, and a record whose row passes below 0 is given the saved address indexed by its column. The walk ends with a jump to $A3B3. The operands $A8BB, $A8BD and $A8BF used by the scrolls are addresses inside the last two instructions of $A7D5; they serve only as bases for this arithmetic and nothing is read from them.

Completes one row of the cell window, the counterpart of $A0EB. IY points at the row's first word ($6432 for row 0, $645A for row 4). Going along the row, each non-null cell's link word at +0, its neighbour toward +X, is written to the next column; then, coming back from column 4, each non-null cell's link word at +4, its neighbour toward -X, is written to the column before. A null entry leaves the next one as it was. Called six times, all from the four window scrolls: $9FE2, $9FE9, $A090, $A097, $A215 and $A2B5.

The Z step ($7FFC) is taken from the first body record's Z offset ($7F58), the last of the three subtractions that leave the first joint in place while the head moves. Reached from $A1D1 when no cell edge was crossed in Y and from the ends of the two Y scrolls at $A234 and $A2D4.

Tests whether the head is still on the board: the high byte of the window's centre word, at $644B, is zero when the cell the head has entered does not exist. In that case the heading ($8001) is turned half a circle, bit 1 of the status byte ($8058) is set so that the frame loop discards this frame's controls, one sparky is taken from ($805D), and ($8056) is set to 9. The loop at $A3DB stores 0 in place of any result of $F0 or more, which catches the borrow from an empty count. The move itself is not undone, so the head is left inside the missing cell.

Sets up the pass over the body. IX points at the first of the 16-byte body records at $7F54, the loop counter ($80A0) is loaded from ($809F), which holds 4 and which no instruction naming it writes, and the running position of the joint being placed is started from the head: ($80A1) and ($80A3) take the frame's X and Y steps, so they are measured from where the head was, and ($80A5) takes the head's height ($7FFE).

One pass of the body loop, for the record at IX. A record holds the signed 16-bit offset of a joint from the one in front of it (+0 X, +2 Y, +4 Z, in 256ths of a unit), a bug count at +6 and the whole part of the joint's height at +7. The link's length is taken as the sum of the three absolute offsets. While that sum is under 11 units the link is slack and nothing is pulled. Otherwise a quarter of each offset is moved out of this record and into the next (+$10, +$12, +$14), which draws the joint a quarter of the way toward the one in front and leaves its follower where it was; for Z the share is a quarter when the joint is below its leader and an eighth when it is above. The shares are kept at $9A7F, $9A81 and $9A83 so that the wall code at $A670 can return them. If the X and Y offsets alone add up to 45 units or more the high bytes of all three offsets are zeroed first, which collapses the link. From $A50E the offsets are added to the running position to give the joint's place: the high bytes become the query point ($8033), ($8034) and ($8035), the height is also written to +7, and a Z offset that would put the joint below zero is zeroed instead. A joint 20 units or more above its leader sets bit 1 of the status byte ($8058), which like bit 0 makes the frame loop discard the frame's controls. When bit 7 of ($8058) is set the worm is dying: each pass takes one from the whole speed ($8003) until it is zero, a link 2 units or longer has the high bytes of its X and Y offsets moved by +1 or -1 according to bit 1 of ($E46F) and of ($E470), a shorter link has its bug count cleared, and the pull is always applied, so the body shakes and draws together. The fourth record's shares collect in the six bytes at $7F94, past the last record.

Finds the ground for the joint just placed, and is entered again each time a pick-up or the wall code has changed things. $9A89 is asked about the query point. If nothing is touched the joint drops toward the highest surface below it, by at most 5 units a frame: at $A581 the change is added to the high byte of this record's Z offset and to the running height ($80A6), taken from the next record's Z offset, and the loop moves on at $A7C5. If something is touched and it has a display-list record, IY is pointed at the record and its type (+$0E) is compared with $F7, $F5, $F3 and $F1 in turn, the four cases that follow. Any other type, and a touch with no record, is treated as plain ground at $A670.

A body joint touches an object of type $F7, a spindle; the display list only carries the $F7 records whose byte +5 is $0C (see $AFE9). Byte +1 of the board record the object came from is set to $FF, which keeps it out of the display list until the new-game code at $75BE restores it. ($8055) and ($8056) are set to 8, five sparkies are added to ($805D), the spindle count ($805B) goes up by one, and its new value is added to the 16-bit score at ($8060), so each spindle is worth one point more than the last. The list record's type becomes $FF and the joint is settled again from $A568. The head has no such case at $9E19: only a body joint collects a spindle.

A body joint touches an object of type $F5, the de-bugger. If this record's bug count (+6) is not zero it is cleared and sound script $E4E1 is requested through $E4F7. Either way the object is then treated as ground at $A670. Each record is cleaned as its own joint reaches the object, and the head's contact with it has no effect on the counts. A type other than $F5 goes on to $A5F6.

A body joint touches an object of type $F3, a bug. The bug count of this record (+6) goes up by one, sound script $E4E1 is requested, and the bug's 30-byte pool record is deleted as at $9E8E: the count byte ($7C71) is reduced, the end pointer ($7C72) moved back 30 bytes and the pool's last record copied over the bug's with LDIR. The list record's type becomes $FF and the joint is settled again from $A568. These counts are what $77A0 examines each frame: when all four records hold at least one bug it sets ($8058) to $FF and the worm dies. A type other than $F3 goes on to $A626.

A body joint touches a sparky that can be picked up (type $F1): the same reward as for the head at $9E21, except that ($8056) is set to $11. The heading ($8001) is turned by -15 to +16 from ($E471), bits 0 and 1 of the whole speed ($8003) are set, ($805D) goes up by one, the pool record is deleted, the list record's type becomes $FF, and the joint is settled again from $A568. Any other type leaves the test at $A628 for $A670.

The joint is touching the board or an object that is not picked up. If the floor ($8036) is less than 23 above the joint, the joint is raised to it at $A581, which also covers a joint already resting there. A greater rise is a wall, and the pull that brought the joint there is taken back. First the Z share at $9A83 is considered: if returning it would put the joint level with the floor, the joint is raised to the floor and the pass ends; otherwise the share is returned to this record and taken from the next. Then the place the joint had before the pull is compared with the object's box. When its Y lies strictly between the box's low and high Y (+$04, +$08) the joint's whole Y offset is passed to the next record, which lines the joint up in Y with the one in front, and its X share is returned; otherwise the whole X offset is passed on and the Y share returned. The query point is reset from the running position and the joint is settled again at $A568. If there is no object record, or the share to be returned is already zero, the code at $A7B2 instead cancels the high byte of the Z offset, which brings the joint to its leader's height.

Eleven bytes that would decode as LD A,($80A6); LD E,A; LD A,($8036); SUB E; JP $A581: the opening of $A670 without its comparison with 23, which would raise a joint to the floor whatever the height. They follow the unconditional JP at $A7B7 and no instruction names them, so they are never executed. Why they remain is not established.

The end of one pass of the body loop. IX moves on 16 bytes to the next record, the counter at ($80A0) is reduced, and the loop repeats from $A405 until it reaches zero. The RET at $A7D4 is the normal end of the routine that began at $9CF1 and returns to the frame loop.

Puts the four corners of a quadrilateral into the order the filler at $9819 expects, then jumps to it. The corners are four pairs of 16-bit X and Y at $801B, $801F, $8023 and $8027, taken as being in order round the outline. The routine finds the corner with the smallest X plus Y, the first one winning a tie, rotates the list so that this corner comes first, and then exchanges the last two, which leaves the smallest, the corner after it, the corner before it and the opposite corner. A carries the working index: bits 3 and 2 end as the number of the smallest corner, bit 3 causing an exchange of corners 0 with 2 and 1 with 3, and bit 2 a rotation by one place. Two callers, $8575 and $8580.

A zero word that stands for the neighbour pointers of a missing cell, followed by one byte that nothing uses. When the 5 by 5 grid of cell pointers at $6432 is shifted and the cell it has to step from is null, the shift code substitutes an address chosen so that adding the neighbour's offset in a cell header lands here: $9FC7 loads $A8C1 for offset 0, $A200 loads $A8BF for offset 2, $A071 loads $A8BD for offset 4 and $A29E loads $A8BB for offset 6. All four then read $A8C1 and $A8C2, so a missing cell has a null neighbour in every direction. The addresses $A8BB, $A8BD and $A8BF lie inside the instructions before this word and are never read themselves. The third byte, $A8C3, holds $C9; the four loads above are the only references to these bytes and none reaches it.

Returns the size of the sine of the angle in A, where 256 steps make a full turn. The low six bits of the angle index the 64-byte quarter wave at $63C0-$63FF, counted back from 63 when bit 6 of the angle is set, so the result in A rises from 0 to $FF and falls again over each half turn: $00 gives 0, $3F and $40 give $FF, $7F and $80 give 0. The sign is left for the caller in the alternate flags: the routine shifts the angle left and then executes EX AF,AF', so on return A' holds the angle and the carry in F' is the angle's bit 7, set for $80-$FF where the sine is negative. Callers multiply the size first, then execute EX AF,AF' and negate the product on carry. HL returns the table address that was read, and whatever AF' held on entry is lost. Sixteen call sites: $A92A and $A963 (the worm's movement), $B416, $B443, $B496, $B4B7, $B50C, $B530, $B561 and $B583 (creature drawing), $BDF1, $D2C5, $D2E4, $D303, $DF07 and $DF2A.

Unsigned multiply giving the full 16-bit product: HL = E x A. These two instructions move E into D and clear E, so that DE holds E x 256, and fall into the eight shift-and-add steps at $A8DB, which add E x 128, E x 64 and so on down to E x 1 for each set bit of A from bit 7 down. A returns 0 and DE returns the original E. AF' is not touched, which lets a caller keep the sign left there by the sine lookup at $A8C4 across the multiply. Eleven call sites: $B41D, $B44A, $B49D, $B4BE, $B512, $B536, $B567, $B589, $BDF7, $DF0D and $DF30.

Multiplies a 16-bit value by an 8-bit fraction: HL = DE x A / 256. It is eight unrolled steps, each halving DE and adding it to HL when the next bit of A, taken from bit 7 down, is set. Every halving drops the bit shifted out, so the result can be up to 7 below the exact quotient: DE = $FFFF and A = $FF give $FEF8 where the exact figure is $FEFF. A returns 0. Called directly from $AC69 and $AC7F, where a step of the worm's body is scaled into a half width, and entered from $A8D8 with DE = E x 256, which makes the result the whole product E x A.

Turns the worm's heading and speed into its movement for the frame. In: E = heading (256 to a turn; $00 moves right and $40 moves up the screen), D = speed, HL = the slope word for the surface under the worm, C = a value handed on to the slope routine. It takes the sine of heading + $40 through $A8C4 and multiplies its size by the speed, then does the same with the heading itself, and stores speed x cosine in ($803D) and minus speed x sine in ($803F) as signed 16-bit numbers: at speed 10 a heading of $00 gives 2550 and 0, and $40 gives 0 and -2550. Bit 1 of the slope word's high byte chooses which of the two the slope applies to: when it is clear the x product goes through $A9A2 before it is signed, and when it is set the y product goes through $A99A. The arithmetic is done in the alternate register set. On return L and H hold the high bytes of the x and y results. The one caller, $9D02, passes the heading ($8001), the speed ($8003), the slope word ($8005) and C = 0, and halves the two results into ($7FF8) and ($7FFA).

Entry to the slope routine at $A9A2 for the y part of the worm's movement: it inverts bit 0 of B, the direction bit of the slope flags, and falls through. The y result is stored with its sign reversed by the caller ($A986-$A992), and turning the bit over makes it mean the same on both axes: with bit 0 clear the climb comes out negative when the worm moves toward larger x or toward larger y. Called from $A982 only, when bit 1 of the slope flags is set.

Applies the slope of the surface to one part of the worm's movement. It runs in the alternate register set with HL = the part's size (speed x sine size), B = slope flags, C = gradient, A = the value the caller of $A926 passed in C (0 in the game) and A' = the angle the sine was taken of. With a gradient of 0 it stores A x 256 in ($803B), copies A to the main B and returns with HL unchanged. Otherwise it forms the travel along the ground and the climb: with flag bit 7 clear the travel is the part itself and the climb is part x gradient / 256, and with bit 7 set the two are exchanged, for a surface that rises faster than it runs. The travel is then multiplied by the byte at $6380 + gradient / 4 and divided by 256; that 64-byte table falls from $FF to $B6 and is within 1 of 255 / sqrt(1 + (gradient / 256) squared), so the worm keeps its speed along the slope. The climb keeps only its high byte before it is multiplied by the same table byte. The travel returns in HL and ($8033); the climb goes to ($803B) with its high byte copied to the main B, and it is negative when flag bit 0 equals the sign bit of the angle in A'. ($8035), ($8037) and ($8039) are work words, the last two always 0 when A is 0. Called from $A94A for the x part and entered from $A99A for the y part.

Builds the frame's display list: a linked list of 15-byte records, one for each thing to be drawn, kept in drawing order. A record holds a link to the next record (+0), its left, upper, right and lower edges as signed words measured from the worm (+2, +4, +6, +8), the address of what it was made from (+$0A), its top and bottom heights (+$0C, +$0D) and its type (+$0E). The routine begins by storing 0 in the head pointer at $EB7E, which empties the list; the LD HL,$EB8D before that is overwritten at once and does nothing, and the two zero bytes written next go through HL = 0 to $0000 and $0001, which are ROM, so they change nothing either. Records are filled from $EB9C upward, with ($8047) pointing at the next free one, and nothing checks how far they reach. The first four are the worm's body, made by the loop at $AB29, which runs four times, the count read from ($809F), over the 16-byte entries at $7F54. Each entry holds a step in x, y and height from the joint before it. The steps are added into running totals in ($80A1), ($80A3) and ($80A5), the last starting from the worm's height ($7FFE). Each record gets the span between the old and the new whole-number position on each axis, widened by 3 either way when the two are fewer than 7 apart, a bottom height equal to the joint's height, a top height 10 above it, the entry's address and type $FA. The loop also writes the joint's two edge points into the last eight bytes of the entry, each point twice: the step is scaled by a byte from the table at $E48C, chosen by the high byte of the sum of the sizes of its x and y parts (30 at most), turned a quarter turn either way, added to the joint and magnified by (128 + height) / 128 through $8116. ($8067) is decremented for each joint, and the joint at which it reaches 0 has the worm's speed ($8003) added to its table index, which narrows it; the frame loop sets ($8067) to 1-4 from the frame counter at $7659, so the narrow joint moves along the body from frame to frame. The four records are filled here and inserted last, at $AED8; the code that follows lists the board and then the objects. Called from $7632 (new game), $7662 (the frame loop) and $78D6 (the loop at $78C9 in the end-of-game sequence).

The second part of the display-list build, entered by falling out of the worm loop. It saves the address of the next free record in ($8047), zeroes ($8068), the count of board records and objects listed in the frame, and calls $AEF9 nine times, once for each cell of the 3 by 3 block around the worm. The cell addresses come from the middle of the 5 by 5 grid of cell pointers at $6432, in the order the worm's own cell ($644A), up ($6440), left ($6448), right ($644C), down ($6454), then the corners up-left ($643E), up-right ($6442), down-left ($6452) and down-right ($6456). Each call passes the cell's offset from the worm's cell in B for x and C for y, as $FF, 0 or 1, and in DE one of the nine six-byte slots at $8069-$809E, which are laid out row by row so that the worm's own cell has the fifth, $8081.

The third part of the display-list build: the walk over the object pool. Objects are 30-byte records from $7C74 up to the address in ($7C72), and the loop at $AE45 takes them from the last to the first. Objects of type $F0 or $E3 are skipped, and an object whose grid row at +3 is 5 or more goes straight to the test at $AEB9. For the others the grid column (+2) and row (+3), each less 2, become the cell offsets in ($8049) and ($804A), a seven-byte record in the board's format is assembled at $AECE from the object's top height (+$0D), bottom height (+$0B), x (+5), width (+8), y (+7), depth (+9) and type (+0), the object's address is put at +$0A of the free list record, and $AF73 is called to list it if it is in view. ($804E) is zeroed before the call and is non-zero afterwards only if $AF73 got as far as the insert at $B008. At $AEB9 an object that was not listed and whose type is $FB has its byte +1 reduced by one, stopping at 1. When the walk passes below $7C74 it jumps to $AED8.

Ten bytes of scratch shared by two pieces of code. The display-list builder assembles a seven-byte record in the board's format here for each object in the pool ($AE77-$AE95): top height from the object's +$0D, bottom height from +$0B, x from +5, width from +8, y from +7, depth from +9 and type from +0, and gives its address to $AF73. The code that shifts the 5 by 5 grid of cell pointers uses all ten bytes to hold the five pointers of the row or column that is leaving the grid (stored at $9F95-$9FAD, $A038-$A050, $A1DA and $A278) and reads them back two bytes at a time at $A025, $A0DB, $A265 and $A303.

The end of the display-list build, reached by the jump at $AE4F once the object pool is exhausted. It inserts the worm's four records, at $EB9C, $EBAB, $EBBA and $EBC9, into the list through $B008 in that order and returns to the builder's caller. The LD IX,$EB8D at the start is overwritten by the next instruction and does nothing. The worm goes in last, and $B008 steps over records of type $FA without comparing them, so each segment is placed against the board and the objects only; segments that end up at the same place in the list lie in reverse order there, with the segment at the front of the worm drawn last.

Notes where one of the nine cells around the worm lies and lists what is in it. In: HL = the cell's address, or 0 for no cell, B and C = the cell's offset from the worm's cell in x and y (-1, 0 or 1), DE = the cell's six-byte slot in the table at $8069. The offsets are saved in ($8049) and ($804A). Three words go into the slot: x offset x 256 - ($7FF5) + $80 and y offset x 256 - ($7FF7) + $40, which place the cell's corner on the screen given the worm's position inside its own cell, and the cell's address. A null cell ends there. Otherwise the loop at $AF37 walks the cell's records, which start 8 bytes into the cell, after its four neighbour pointers, are 7 bytes each and end at a zero byte; each one is passed to $AF49 with HL = its address. The slots are read back by the floor routine at $EB2B. Called nine times, from $ADDB, $ADE7, $ADF3, $ADFF, $AE0B, $AE17, $AE23, $AE2F and $AE3B.

Called for each board record with HL = its address; before the record is listed it looks at the record just before it. If that record's type, the byte at HL - 1, is $F7 and its depth byte at HL - 2 is not $0C, then the two bytes at HL - 3 and HL - 2 are the address of a routine, which is written into the operand of the CALL at $AF63 and called with HL pointing at that earlier record. So a record of type $F7 whose depth is not $0C is a handler that runs once a frame, when the walk reaches the record after it, whether or not either record is in view; a handler placed last in its cell would never run, and none is. The tape image has 23 handler records, using $BD6F (2), $BD90 (7), $BDD1 (13) and $BED1 (1). For the first record of a cell the byte tested is the last byte of the cell's header, the high byte of a cell address, which is never $F7.

The CALL whose operand is rewritten at $AF5F with the address taken from a handler record; in the tape image it reads CALL $BD6F. The handler is entered with HL = the address of its own record, DE = its own address and BC = 7, and with the cell's offset from the worm's cell still in ($8049) and ($804A). After it returns, HL is restored and stepped forward to the record the walk had reached, and that address is stored at +$0A of the next free list record, ($8047), before control falls into $AF73. The same closing steps are reached from $AF4D and $AF54 when there is no handler to call.

Fills the free list record at IX from a seven-byte record at HL and inserts it if it can be in view. The seven bytes are top height, bottom height, x, width, y, depth and type, and ($8049) and ($804A) give the cell the record belongs to as an offset from the worm's cell. Top and bottom are copied to +$0C and +$0D, and a bottom of $FF ends the routine there, which is how a record is switched off: $A5B3 stores $FF in the bottom byte of a type $F7 record that the collision code has found. The left edge is cell offset x 256 + x - ($7FF5), stored at +2, and the right edge adds the width, stored at +6; the upper and lower edges are made the same way from y, ($7FF7) and the depth, stored at +4 and +8. These are 16-bit positions relative to the worm, which sits at the centre of the 256 by 128 picture, and the routine returns early, leaving the record out of the list, as soon as it finds the left edge at 128 or more, the right edge below -128, the upper edge at 64 or more, or the lower edge below -64. A record of type $F7 is listed only when its depth is $0C; the others are handler records. A record that passes gets its type at +$0E, the count in ($8068) goes up by one, $B008 inserts the record, and ($8047) moves on by 15 bytes. Entered by falling in from $AF63 for board records, and called from $AEAD for objects with HL = $AECE.

Inserts the record at IX into the display list. It walks the list from the head pointer at $EB7E, keeping in ($804D) the record after which the new one will go, which at first is the head itself. Records of type $FA, the worm's segments, are passed over. Every other record is compared with the new one by $B045: a zero result moves on and changes nothing, carry makes that record the insertion point and moves on, and neither flag ends the walk, as does a link whose high byte is 0. The new record is then linked in after the insertion point: that record's link is copied into the new record's first two bytes and replaced by the new record's address. A record therefore goes straight after the last record it has to be drawn after, among those met before the first one it has to be drawn before, and at the front if there is none. The list is in drawing order, first drawn first. The high byte of ($804D), at $804E, is also read by the object walk at $AEB2 to learn whether $AF73 got as far as this routine. Five call sites: $AFFB for board records and objects, and $AEE0, $AEE7, $AEEE and $AEF5 for the worm.

Decides the drawing order of two records, IX the one being inserted and IY one already in the list. It returns Z when there is no order between them, carry without Z when IX has to be drawn after IY, and neither flag when IX has to be drawn before IY. The height ranges are looked at first: if IY's top height (+$0C) is below IX's bottom height (+$0D), or IX's top is below IY's bottom, the two are apart in height. Records whose heights overlap or touch go straight to $B0A5 and its answer is returned as it stands. Records apart in height whose outlines overlap on both axes are settled by height at $B2C8. Records apart in height whose outlines do not overlap are also put to $B0A5, as a call, but only an answer of after is kept: an answer of before is turned into no order by the XOR A at $B0A3. The outline tests are signed 16-bit subtractions of the edges at +2, +4, +6 and +8. Called from $B024 only.

Orders two boxes by where they lie around the centre of the picture, which is the origin of the records' coordinates and the point the view looks straight down on. Perspective pushes the top of a box outward from that point, so of two boxes on the same side the one nearer the centre can hide part of the other and has to be drawn later. The routine first picks a side: if either record's right edge (+6) is negative, both left edges (+2) must be negative or the answer is no order, and otherwise the pair is treated as right of centre. Then, if both upper edges (+4) are negative the pair is treated as above centre; otherwise both lower edges (+8) must be zero or more or the answer is no order, and the pair is treated as below centre. Within the quadrant, if the two x ranges do not overlap, the box nearer the centre in x is drawn later, unless the other box lies wholly nearer the centre in y, when there is no order. If the x ranges overlap and the y ranges do not, the box nearer the centre in y is drawn later. If both overlap, the heights decide at $B2C8. Flags are returned as in $B045. One return differs from its three counterparts: at $B243, for the upper left quadrant, the INC A that forces NZ is missing, so when the x ranges overlap and the listed record's upper edge equals the new record's lower edge the answer is no order instead of before. Reached from $B053 by a jump and from $B09E by a call.

Orders two records whose outlines overlap, by height, according to the type of the listed record IY. For a type whose top two bits are 00 or 11 the carry is set when IY's bottom height (+$0D) is below IX's bottom height, so the record with the higher base is drawn later. The other two classes, $40-$7F and $80-$BF, are the ones the surface finder at $9BFF and $9C66 treats as slopes, and for them bits 5 and 4 of the type choose: below $20, the carry is set when IY's bottom is below IX's top height (+$0C); from $20 up, when IX's bottom is not below IY's top. The closing DEC E leaves the carry alone and sets Z only when the listed record's type is $01, so that one type always answers no order; one board record, at $6D6F, has it. No record in the board data has a slope type with bits 5 and 4 at $20 or more, and only such a type leads to the five instructions at $B2DB. Reached by JP M from $B09B, $B130, $B1B2, $B240 and $B2C1.

Draws the frame from the display list. It follows the links from the head at $EB7E, keeping the address of the record in hand in ($804B), until it meets a link whose high byte is 0. For each record it copies the four edges into the drawing variables, left (+2) to ($802B), right (+6) to ($802D), upper (+4) to ($802F) and lower (+8) to ($8031), loads C with the top height (+$0C), B with the bottom height (+$0D) and A with the type (+$0E), and calls $81DB, which scales the box for each of the two heights and draws the shape the type selects. Records are drawn in list order, so later ones paint over earlier ones. Before the walk it stores $0040 in ($80C6) and $FFC0 in ($80C8); these two stores are the only instructions that refer to either word. Four call sites: $7668 in the frame loop, and $791D, $78E7 and $7907 in the end-of-game sequence (the frame step at $7914 and the loops at $78C9 and $78EF).

One step of a multiply-and-add number generator: HL = HL x 1509 + 41, modulo 65536, built from shifts and adds. BC returns the old HL and DE returns $0029. The sequence visits all 65,536 values before it repeats. Its two call sites, $EB5A and $EB64, are both in the floor routine at $EB2B, which seeds it with a cell's address, takes 7 plus the low three bits of the first result as a count, and for each further result plots one dot at x = low byte, y = high byte inside the cell. A cell therefore shows the same 7 to 14 dots every frame, fixed to the board.

Draws a record of type $F3, a creature with six legs. The type's handler at $840A jumps here, from $844B or $847F, after copying the object's fields. In: ($801B) and ($801F) = the box's left and right edges on screen, ($801D) = its upper edge, ($8023) = the creature's heading, ($8024), ($8025) and ($8026) = six leg positions, one per nibble, ($8021) = the object's width byte. It works out the width on screen w = right - left, puts the centre, left + w / 2 and upper + w / 2, in ($802B) and ($802D), and w x 1.5 in ($8030). If the width byte is 7 it jumps to the three-part form at $B4E0. Otherwise it draws six legs, each with $B491 then $B5AF, at heading + $68, $77 and $8B plus a low nibble and at heading + $18, $09 and $F5 minus a high nibble, with bit 7 of C set for the first three. It finishes with two round blobs through $B7B6: a head w / 2 across whose centre is w / 2 from the creature's centre along the heading, and a body three quarters of w across with its corner at left + w / 8, upper + w / 8. The first instructions store $14 in ($8056), the tone divider that $EAA9 reads while it clears the frame buffer. In the frame loop that byte is zeroed at $767F before $EAA9 runs again, and the frame step at $7914 sets it itself, so the value stored here reaches $EAA9 only in the loops at $78C9 and $78EF.

Finds where one leg ends. In: A = the leg's angle relative to the creature's heading. It adds the heading ($8023), takes the sine through $A8C4, multiplies it by ($8030) with $A8D8 and halves the high byte of the product, which comes to at most three quarters of the creature's width, gives it the sine's sign and adds the centre x ($802B). The same steps with the angle less $40 give the y offset, which is added to the centre y ($802D). Returns DE = x, HL = y, C = the angle halved ($00-$7F) and B = the width ($802F). Called six times, from $B3AC, $B3C3, $B3D0, $B3E7, $B3F4 and $B40B.

The form drawn for a type $F3 creature whose width byte is 7, reached from $B3A2: three small sprites plotted with $B7E3. The middle one, five rows, goes 3 pixels left of and above the centre and alternates between the data at $CB23, when bit 0 of the frame counter ($8059) is clear, and at $CB37. A seven-row sprite from $CB07 goes 3 left of and 4 above the centre, less 5 x the cosine and sine of the heading, and a six-row sprite from $CAEF goes 3 left of and 3 above the centre, plus the same; each product is taken through $A8C4 and $A8D8 and comes to 4 pixels at most. It stores $11 in ($8056), with the same short life as the store at $B36C. $DE5D-$DE86, in the handling of type $FB objects, create an object of type $F3 with this width.

Draws one leg as a strip one byte wide. In: DE = x and HL = y of the leg's end from $B491, C = the leg's angle halved, with bit 7 set by the caller for three of the six legs. Bits 5 to 2 of C pick one of the 16 four-byte entries of the table at $C667, counted back from 15 when bit 7 is clear. An entry holds an x offset, a y offset, the strip's place in the data that follows the table at $C6A7, counted in rows, and its height, 2 to 8 rows. The x offset is negated when bit 6 of C is set, and the strip is then drawn mirrored through $B702. The y offset is negated when bits 6 and 7 of C differ, and the strip is then drawn from its last row upward: the row step stored in ($B7B4) is $001F going down and $FFDF going up. Rows that fall outside the 128 rows of the frame buffer are clipped by cutting the row count and skipping strip data. A row of strip data is two bytes; the first is ORed into the buffer and the second is then exclusive-ORed. A strip at a multiple of 8 pixels is written one byte a row by the loop at $B6CE. Any other is split across two buffer bytes with the shift tables in pages $5B-$61 by the loop at $B6DF, whose two stores, at $B6EF and $B6FD, are switched between LD (HL),A and NOP so that a strip crossing the left or right edge writes only the byte that is in view. When the strip starts 1 to 7 pixels left of the buffer, $B6B3-$B6C3 take $20 from L twice, with no borrow into H, where once with a borrow was needed: the half in view is drawn one row too high, or seven rows too low when L was below $40. Called six times, from $B3B1, $B3C6, $B3D5, $B3EA, $B3F9 and $B40E.

The store of the left-hand buffer byte in the two-byte loop of the leg strip routine. Its opcode is written before each strip: $77, LD (HL),A, by $B698 and $B6A3, or $00, NOP, by $B6B8 when the strip starts left of the buffer and this byte would fall outside it. The instructions that follow step to the next buffer byte and build the right-hand half of the row from the shift table.

The store of the right-hand buffer byte in the same loop, written the same way: $77 by $B69B and $B6BD, or $00 by $B6A7 when the strip starts at pixel 248 or beyond and this byte would wrap onto the next row. After it come the step to the next row, the loop back to $B6DF and the return.

The start of the mirrored leg strip, reached from $B689 when bit 6 of C is set. In: DE = x, HL = the buffer address for that position, B = rows. A negative x returns at once. An x of 256 or more goes on to $B725. An x of 8 or more sets both stores of the mirrored loop, at $B778 and $B792, to LD (HL),A and jumps to $B738. An x below 8 reaches $B717, which is AND A then RET, so a mirrored strip that starts within 8 pixels of the left edge is not drawn at all.

Five instructions that nothing reaches: XOR A, LD ($B778),A, LD A,$77, LD ($B792),A, JP $B738. They follow the RET at $B718, and no jump, call or stored word in the image names $B719. They are the left-edge case of the mirrored plot that starts at $B702: for a column of 0 to 7 they would switch off the first screen write at $B778, keep the second at $B792 and go on to $B738, the counterpart of what $B6A1 does for the unmirrored shape at the right edge. The test at $B70A branches to the AND A and RET at $B717 instead, so a mirrored shape whose column is 0 to 7 is not drawn at all.

Part of the 8-pixel shape plotter entered at $B5AF, reached only from $B705: the shape is being drawn mirrored (bit 6 of its flags in C) and the high byte of its column, in D, is not zero. It returns unless that high byte is 1, adds $20 to L because the buffer address in HL was formed from the low byte of the column alone and is 32 bytes short, and returns again unless the low byte is under 8, so only columns 256 to 263 go on. For those it stores $77 at $B778 and $00 at $B792: of the two bytes each row spans, the left one, which lands in column 31 of the buffer, is written and the right one, which would land in the next row, is not. It then falls into $B738.

The mirrored half of the 8-pixel shape plotter entered at $B5AF, which draws the legs of the six-legged bugs. On entry HL is the frame-buffer address ($F000 plus 32 bytes a row) of the byte holding the shape's column, E the low byte of that column, B the number of rows and the alternate HL the data, two bytes a row: a mask and a pattern. HL steps back one byte first, so the eight pixels drawn are the ones that end just left of the column, and every data byte is passed through the bit-reversal table at $6200, which flips the shape left to right. Each buffer byte becomes (byte OR mask) XOR pattern, and after each row the word at $B7B4 is added to HL. When the column is a multiple of 8 the loop at $B748 writes one byte a row. Otherwise the loop at $B760 splits the reversed mask and pattern over two bytes with the shift tables in pages $5B to $61 (page $5A plus column AND 7; an odd index gives the part shifted right, an even index the part carried into the next byte) and writes them with the instructions at $B778 and $B792, whose opcodes other code replaces: $B70E and $B731 store $77 (LD (HL),A, write the byte) at $B778, $B711 stores $77 at $B792 and $B735 stores $00 there (NOP, leave the buffer byte alone). Between the two bytes the address is stepped with INC L, which does not carry into H: when the first byte is column 31 of a row whose number is 7 more than a multiple of 8, which can only come from $B725, the rows after it are written 256 bytes lower than they should be. Entered by the jump at $B714 and by falling in from $B735.

Draws a spark picture of the size in B. HL is the row and DE the column of the top left corner, both signed 16-bit. A size under 21 is used as it is; a larger one draws the 20-row picture after adding (B - 21) / 2, rounded down, to both HL and DE, which keeps the picture near the middle of the larger square. The size, doubled, indexes the address table at $BF27, the alternate A is cleared, which sets its zero flag for 16-pixel rows, and the code joins $B7D0, which switches to 24-pixel rows for sizes 17 and over and plots through $B7E3. The LD A,B at $B7A1 has no effect, A being loaded again at $B7AC. One reference: the jump at $8407 that ends the drawer of type-$F1 objects, which passes the mean width of the object's projected base and top as the size.

The row step of the 8-pixel shape plotter entered at $B5AF: loaded into DE at $B6C5 and $B73A and added to the frame-buffer address after each row. $B635 stores $001F for a shape drawn top row first and $B661 stores $FFDF for one drawn bottom row first; with the one byte the loops step inside a row these come to 32 and minus 32, one buffer row down or up. The two bytes are written separately, the low at $B637 and $B663 and the high at $B63B and $B668. Six references in all and zero on the tape.

Draws a speckled disc picture of the size in B, with the same registers and the same rule as $B797 (a size over 20 draws the 20-row picture moved by (B - 21) / 2 in both directions) but with the address table at $BF59. From $B7D0 the code is shared with $B797: the size doubled indexes the table, the picture address goes to the alternate HL, and B picks the row width, 16 pixels up to size 16 and 24 pixels from 17 up, before the plot at $B7E3. Four references: calls at $85CE (in the type-$FA drawer) and at $B473 and $B48D (the two body discs of the bug drawn at $B36A), and the jump at $8606 that ends the type-$F2 drawer.

Entry to the masked shape plotter for data 24 pixels wide: it sets the alternate A to $FF, which leaves the alternate zero flag clear, and falls into $B7E3, which then reads six bytes a row. Called five times: from $BC88, $BCBC and $BCD4 for the floppy disk's hub and the two halves of its label, and from $BCFE and $BD0E for the two halves of the counter display. The sized entries $B797 and $B7B6 run into it for sizes 17 and over.

Plots a masked picture into the frame buffer at $F000 (256 by 128 pixels, 32 bytes a row). HL is the row and DE the column of its top left corner, both signed 16-bit; B is the number of rows; the alternate HL points at the data; the zero flag in the alternate AF gives the width, set for 16 pixels (four bytes a row) and clear for 24 pixels (six bytes a row). A data row is pairs of a mask byte and a pattern byte from left to right, and each buffer byte becomes (byte OR mask) XOR pattern: mask 1 with pattern 0 sets a pixel, both 1 clears it, pattern 1 alone inverts it and both 0 leaves it. Rows above the top of the buffer are skipped in the data and rows below row 127 are dropped. The routine returns without drawing when no row is left, when the row is below -256 or above 127, when the column is below -256 or above 255, or when a negative column puts the whole width left of the buffer. For a column that is a multiple of 8 the loops at $B89D (three bytes a row) and $B98B (two) write whole bytes; otherwise each mask and pattern byte is split over two buffer bytes with the shift tables in pages $5B to $61 (page $5A plus column AND 7) and the loops at $B8C3 and $B9A8 write four and three bytes a row. Clipping at the left and right edges is done by replacing the opcodes of the write instructions. $B82D-$B836 store $77 (LD (HL),A, write the byte) at $B8D5, $B8F7, $B918 and $B92A, and $B931-$B937 do the same at $B9BA, $B9DB and $B9ED. Then $00 (NOP, leave the buffer byte alone) is stored for each byte that would fall outside the 32 columns: at the right edge at $B92A, then $B918, then $B8F7 ($B84C, $B852, $B858) or at $B9ED, then $B9DB ($B94D, $B953), and at the left edge at $B8D5, then $B8F7, then $B918 ($B873, $B879, $B87F) or at $B9BA, then $B9DB ($B96E, $B974). The whole-byte loops use copies: $B8A4, $B8AD and $B8B6 take the opcodes at $B8D5, $B8F7 and $B918 ($B888-$B897), and $B992 and $B99B take those at $B9BA and $B9DB ($B97C-$B985). Nine calls reach this entry ($863B, $8663, $86A5, $870B, $8748, $B504, $B559, $B5AB, $BCA4) and the branch at $B7DE.

Clears one pixel of the frame buffer. HL is the row and DE the column. It returns at once unless D is zero, H is zero and bit 7 of L is clear, which together are the test for a point inside the 256 by 128 buffer. It then forms $F000 + row * 32 + column / 8 and ANDs that byte with the mask at $8F08 + (column AND 7), one of the eight bytes $7F, $BF, $DF, $EF, $F7, $FB, $FD, $FE. Five callers: $EB76, in a loop that scatters 7 to 14 cleared pixels over the square of each cell on the screen, and $BC28, $BC34, $BC40 and $BC4C, which take one pixel out of each corner of the floppy disk.

Draws a run of filled quadrilaterals from the script at BC. Each one is handed to $9819, which fills the shape whose corners are the four points at $801B/$801D (call it A), $801F/$8021 (B), $8023/$8025 (the pen) and $8027/$8029 (D), with the pattern word at $80BE. A zero byte ends the script. An even first byte starts a five-byte command: bytes 0 and 1 move the pen down and right by four times their low seven bits read as a signed number (bit 7 is ignored), and three corner bytes then give D, A and B as offsets from the pen. An odd first byte starts a two-byte command that carries the strip on: the pen takes the old A, D takes the old B, and the two bytes give the new A and B. In a corner byte the high nibble is the x offset and the low nibble the y offset, and in each nibble bits 1-3 are the size in steps of 8 pixels, 0 to 56, and bit 0 makes it negative. $9819 exchanges A with B and the pen with D when A is higher on the screen than B, and the next command starts from the points as it left them. Called from $BB62 with the script at $BAAE and jumped to from $BCF2 with the one at $BAF9; the third reference is its own loop at $BA87.

Returns in HL the pen row at $8025 plus the y offset in the low nibble of the script byte at (BC): bits 1-3 times 8, negated when bit 0 is set. BC is not moved. The decoding from $BA8E on is shared with $BA9F. Called three times by $BA19, from $BA41, $BA68 and $BA75.

Returns in HL the pen column at $8023 plus the x offset in the high nibble of the script byte at (BC): it shifts the byte right four places and jumps into $BA8E to decode it as $BA8A does. Called three times by $BA19, from $BA47, $BA6E and $BA7B.

Progress of the animation that closes a completed game, in which a hand comes down the screen and carries the floppy disk off. $7614 sets it to zero when a game starts, and while it is zero $BB06 draws the disk with no hand. The loop at $78EF adds 1 a frame while bit 7 is clear and subtracts 3 a frame once bit 7 is set, and leaves when the sum reaches $80 or the difference falls below it. $BB06 uses the low seven bits as the row of the pen for the hand script, sets bit 7 ($BB25) once that row is past the top edge of the disk, and from then on draws the disk 13 rows above the pen row, so it rises with the hand. Seven references: written at $7614, $7901 and $BB25, read at $78EF, $BB0C, $BB30 and $BCD7.

The script $BA19 draws the hand from: 54 bytes, eight five-byte commands and seven two-byte ones, and the zero that ends it at $BAE4. They make 15 quadrilaterals: four fingers of three pieces each, pointing down, and three pieces above them for the palm and forearm. With the pen started at column 127 the shape spans columns 71 to 199 and runs from 88 rows above the starting pen row to 40 below it. Read only through the pointer loaded at $BB5F. The 20 zero bytes from $BAE5 to $BAF8 are read by nothing.

A second script for $BA19, 12 bytes and the zero at $BB05: a five-byte command, a two-byte one and another five-byte one. $BB06 draws it last, after the disk, where the script at $BAAE is drawn before it. Of its three quadrilaterals $9819 fills only the first, a slanted one 32 pixels across, columns 103 to 135, from 48 rows to 16 rows above the starting pen row; that puts its lowest row 3 above the top row of the lifted disk, over the lower pieces of the hand. The other two hand $9819 corners in an order it turns down, and it returns without drawing them. Read only through the pointer loaded at $BCEF.

Draws a board item of type $F6, the floppy disk whose touch ends the game: the type dispatch jumps here from $89FB, the only reference. It works from the item's projected top face, left and right columns at $8013 and $8015 and top and bottom rows at $8017 and $8019. Five rectangles go through the fill at $8E13: the body in pattern word $00FF as three pieces that leave two pixels off each corner, a band of pattern $FF55 from 5 columns inside the left edge to 5 inside the right and from row top+1 to top+7, and a label block of pattern $0000 over the same columns from top+9 to top+28. $B9F2 then clears the pixel one step in from each corner. Four pictures follow, placed from the centre of the face (cx, cy) and not scaled: the 17-row hub at (cx-8, cy-4), taken from $C75F or $C7C5 as bit 0 of the frame counter at $8059 is 0 or 1; the 21-row slot from $C82B at (cx-4, cy+18); and the 8-row label halves, $C87F at (cx-24, top+16) and $C8AF at (cx, top+16). When the byte at $BAAD is not zero the routine also draws the hand. It puts the pen for $BA19 at column 127 and the row in the low seven bits of $BAAD, sets bit 7 of $BAAD once that row is past the disk's top row, moves the disk up 13 rows (bit 7 clear) or to 13 rows above the pen row (bit 7 set), draws the script at $BAAE in pattern $AAAA before the disk, fills from the disk's left column to 2 past its right and from 2 rows above it to row 128 with pattern $0000, and draws the script at $BAF9 after the disk. The NOP at $BC7A does nothing.

Plots the 48 by 16 pixel counter display that $BD12 keeps built at $CC0B: the left half from $CC0B at row HL and column DE, then the right half from $CC6B at the same row and column DE + 24, each as 16 rows of 24-pixel data through $B7E0. Its one caller, $8518, ends the drawer of type-$E0 items and passes the centre of the item's top face less 24 columns and 8 rows, which puts the three digits in the middle of the block's top. The second half is plotted with the two register sets changed over (the address is loaded before an EXX and the position after it), so the routine returns with the set that was the alternate one on entry selected.

Rebuilds the picture of the three-digit counter in the 192 bytes at $CC0B. A is the hundreds digit, B the tens and C the units. It fills $CC0B-$CCCA with $FF, which as mask and pattern pairs for the plotter means every pixel cleared, then runs $BD3E three times to XOR the lit segments of each digit into the pattern bytes, which leaves those pixels set: the hundreds digit and then the tens digit from the stream at $CCD5 with base $CC0B, the stream pointer running on from the first digit into the second, and the units digit from the stream at $CD6B with base $CC6D. Two callers: $75E5 with all three digits zero when a game starts, and $DEE3 after the counter at $BD6C-$BD6E has been stepped.

Draws one seven-segment digit into a picture buffer. A is the digit: the byte at $CCCB + A is its mask, one bit a segment from bit 7 down. The alternate HL points into a segment stream and the main DE holds the buffer's base address. For each of the seven segments it reads a count and then, when the segment's mask bit is set, steps over that many two-byte entries, or, when the bit is clear, takes each entry as an offset and a byte and XORs the byte into the buffer at base plus offset. The alternate HL is left just past the seventh segment, which is how $BD12 reads two digits from one stream. Called from $BD27 and $BD32 and entered a third time by falling in from $BD3B.

Units digit, 0 to 9, of a three-digit counter that the type-$E0 blocks show on their tops. The word stores at $75D8 and $75DC, which overlap, zero it and the two bytes after it when a game starts. $DEB8 adds one and on reaching ten carries into $BD6D; $DED9 stores the result, and the word load at $DEDC reads it back as the C that $BD12 draws as the right-hand digit. $DEB8 is reached only from $DBDA, in the code that moves type-$F0 and type-$F1 objects. Four references.

Tens digit of the counter at $BD6C: stepped at $DEC0 when the units wrap, stored at $DED5, and loaded with the units by the word load at $DEDC as the B that $BD12 draws in the middle. Three references by address, $75DC, $DEC0 and $DED5.

Hundreds digit of the counter at $BD6C: stepped at $DEC8 when the tens wrap, going from 9 back to 0 at $DED0, stored at $DED1 and passed to $BD12 in A at $DEE0 as the left-hand digit. The only thing that zeroes it at the start of a game is the high byte of the word store at $75DC. Three references by address, $DEC8, $DED1 and $DEE0.

Record handler that raises a board item. Like the four after it, it is called through the patched CALL at $AF63 while a cell's items are listed for drawing, once for each handler record, with HL at the record: four parameter bytes, the handler's own address at +4/+5 and the tag $F7 at +6, followed from +7 by the seven bytes of the item it drives (height of the top at +7, height of the base at +8, x at +9, x size at +$0A, y at +$0B, y size at +$0C, type at +$0D). This one adds parameter 0 to the top height, holding at $FF if the sum overflows. While the result is below parameter 1 it is stored; once it reaches parameter 1 the top is set to parameter 1 and $BD90 is written into +4/+5, so the item starts down on the next call. Two records on the tape carry it, at $6AB8 (up 5 a call to $DB) and $6D61 (up 3 a call to $A0), and $BD90 puts it back each time one of those items reaches its floor.

Record handler that lowers a board item: it subtracts parameter 2 from the item's top height at +7, holding at 0 if the difference goes negative, and stores the result while it is not below parameter 3. Otherwise the top is set to parameter 3 and the handler at +4/+5 is replaced. For an item whose type at +$0D is $F4 the new handler is $BE07, and parameter 0 is set to 5 plus the low five bits of the random byte at $E471, the number of calls that item then waits at the bottom. For any other item it is $BD6F, which sends it up again. Seven records on the tape carry it, each one placed just before one of the board's seven type-$F4 items in its cell's list; $BD6F and $BE07 install it when an item reaches the top.

Record handler that moves an item's top height (+7) along a sine wave of the frame counter at $8059. Parameter 0 sets the speed: when positive the counter's low byte is shifted left that many times, when negative the 16-bit counter is shifted right that many times and its low byte taken, when zero the low byte is used as it is. Parameter 1 is added as the phase, $A8C4 looks the angle up in the quarter-wave table at $63C0, $A8D8 multiplies the result by parameter 2, and the high byte of the product, negated in the second half of the cycle, is added to parameter 3. The top therefore swings just under parameter 2 either side of parameter 3. Thirteen records carry it. Twelve have speed 2, swing $32 and centre $50 and differ in phase: each drives one of a row of adjoining blocks in the cells at $6B46, $6BAA and $6BF2, with the phase rising by 10 from block to block in the first two, so each row ripples once every 64 frames. The other, at $6D9B, has 3, 0, $60 and $90.

Record handler that $BD90 installs for a type-$F4 item when it reaches its floor; no record on the tape starts with it. It counts parameter 0 down by one a call and returns until that reaches zero; after that parameter 0 is kept at 1 and each call adds parameter 2 to the item's top height (+7) until it reaches parameter 1. On every call at the top it tries to release a bug: when the allowance at $8066 is not zero and the count at $7C71 is below $0C it adds one to $7C71, takes one from $8066 and writes a 30-byte record at the address in $7C72, the end of the object pool that starts at $7C74. The record's type is $F3: $840A draws that type through $B36A as two discs and six legs, and $9E7C takes it out of the pool and adds one to the byte at $7F5A when the worm touches it. Bytes +2 and +3 are the offset of the cell being listed plus 2 ($8049, $804A); +5 and +7 are the middle of the item in x and y less 5, with zero in +4 and +6; +8 and +9, the size, are $0A, or $0E once the high byte of the frame counter has reached $11 and the low byte is a multiple of 8; +$0B is the item's top height and +$0D that plus $12, with zero in +$0A and +$0C; +$0E to +$11 are the random bytes at $E46F, $E46F, $E470 and $E471; +$12 to +$15 are 5, $0F, $28 and 1; +$16 is 7 or $27 by bit 5 of $E471; +$18 is 2. Bytes +1, +$17 and +$19 to +$1D are left as they were. $7C72 then moves on by 30 and the handler becomes $BD90, so the item sinks, waits and rises to release another. If nothing can be released the item stays at the top and tries again on the next call.

Record handler carried by one record, at $6FFA, in the cell that also holds the floppy disk (the type-$F6 item at $6FF3). It drives the three items after the record. The third, a type-$E0 block, has its top height (+$15) set on every call: $20 while the count of spindles at $805B is below $32 (50), $50 from then on. The first slides along y. Parameter 1 is a pause, counted down by one a call and held at $63 while the byte at $D42B is not zero. When it reaches zero, parameter 2 becomes a new target, $40 plus five bits of the random byte at $E470. On the calls after that the item's y (+$0B) moves a quarter of the remaining distance towards the target, its y size (+$0C) is set to $C0 less the new y, which keeps its far edge at $C0, and the y of the second item (+$12) is set to $0B less than the first's. When the quarter step comes to zero a new pause of 1 to 16 calls is taken from the random byte at $E471. Parameters 0 and 3 are not read.

Twenty-five addresses of spark pictures, indexed by size: $B797 doubles a size of at most 20 and reads the word here. Entry n is a picture n rows high, 16 pixels wide (four bytes a row) up to 16 rows and 24 pixels wide (six bytes a row) from 17 to 20. Entries 0 and 1 are both $BFBD. Entry 15 is the 16-row picture without its empty first row, and entry 18 the 19-row picture without its empty first row. Entries 21 to 24 repeat $C279, the 20-row picture, and cannot be read, because the size is cut to 20 before the lookup. One reference, the load at $B7AE.

Twenty-five addresses of speckled disc pictures, indexed by size as $BF27 is and read by $B7B6. Entries 0 and 1 are both $C2F1. Entry 15 is the 16-row picture without its first row; entries 17 and 18 are the same address, the 18-row picture being the 17-row one with a row more below; entry 19 is the 20-row picture without its first row. Entries 21 to 24 hold $C5B3, the address of the first explosion picture, and cannot be read. One reference, the load at $B7CD.

A third table of 25 picture addresses that nothing reads: no instruction names $BF8B, the word does not occur anywhere in the image, and the two lookups reach no further than 40 bytes past $BF27 and $BF59. Entries 0 to 17 are those of $BF27. Entries 18 to 20 are $C4D5, $C541 and $C53B, the disc pictures that $BF59 has in the same places, and entries 21 to 24 are $C5B3.

The spark pictures the table at $BF27 points to, as rows of mask and pattern pairs for $B7E3: a solid middle with short broken rays all round it, one picture for each size from 1 to 20 pixels. The pictures of 1 to 14 rows follow one another from here, n rows of four bytes each, as far as $C160; this symbol covers them up to $BFFF, where the 6-row picture is seven bytes in, and $C000 carries on.

The spark pictures of $BFBD continued: the last 17 bytes of the 6-row picture, then the pictures of 7 to 14 rows at four bytes a row ($C011, $C02D, $C04D, $C071, $C099, $C0C5, $C0F5, $C129), the 16-row picture at $C161 (the 15-row entry points one row into it, at $C165), and at six bytes a row the 17-row picture at $C1A1, the 19-row one at $C207 (the 18-row entry points at $C20D) and the 20-row one at $C279, which ends at $C2F0. All are reached only through the table at $BF27.

The disc pictures the table at $BF59 points to: a round blob with a speckled surface for each size from 1 to 20 pixels, as rows of mask and pattern pairs. The pictures of 1 to 14 rows run from $C2F1 at n rows of four bytes each; the 16-row picture is at $C495 and the 15-row entry points one row into it; at six bytes a row the 17-row and 18-row pictures both start at $C4D5 and the 20-row one at $C53B, with the 19-row entry one row into it at $C541. The last row of the 18-row picture is also the first row of the 20-row one. The block is 706 bytes and ends at $C5B2. Plotted only through $B7B6.

First of three explosion pictures, each 15 rows of four bytes (16 pixels wide): a small ragged burst. The drawer of type-$E6 objects at $870F plots 15 rows from the address held at +$0F/+$10 of the object's record. This address is put there when an object turns into an explosion ($D871, $DE2A), and is stored in the pointer at $790F by the end-of-game sequence at $7868 and $787A. Four instructions load it; the same value also fills the unread entries 21 to 24 of the tables at $BF59 and $BF8B.

Second explosion picture, 15 rows of four bytes: the burst grown to the full 16 pixels, with a small hole in the middle. Loaded at $DE0C when a type-$E6 object's countdown at +$0E reads 2, and at $7871 and $7880 by the end-of-game sequence. Three references.

Third explosion picture, 15 rows of four bytes: a ragged ring with an open middle. Loaded at $DE13 when a type-$E6 object's countdown at +$0E reads 1, the last call before the object is removed, and at $7886 by the end-of-game sequence. Two references.

Sixteen four-byte records, one for each of sixteen directions of a leg stroke, from straight up round by the left to almost straight down, read by the 8-pixel shape plotter at $B5AF. The index is bits 2-5 of the direction byte in C, counted from the far end of the table when bit 7 of C is clear. Byte 0 is a signed x offset added to the column, negated when bit 6 of C is set, which also draws the picture mirrored. Byte 1 is a signed y offset added to the row, negated, with the picture drawn bottom row first, when bits 6 and 7 of C differ. Byte 2 is the number of the picture's first row in the row table at $C6A7 and byte 3 its row count, 2 to 8. One reference, the load at $B5B5.

The pictures of the sixteen leg strokes: 92 rows of two bytes, a mask and a pattern, 8 pixels wide. Each record at $C667 gives its picture's first row and row count, and the sixteen lie end to end with 8, 8, 7, 7, 7, 5, 4, 3, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 8 rows, a short dotted line that turns from upright through level and back to upright. The address itself is never loaded: $B5E4 adds twice the row number plus $40 to $C667.

The hub of the floppy disk, first of two versions: 17 rows of six bytes (24 pixels, 17 of them used), a ring with a square hole in the middle and marks between the two. $BB06 plots this one when bit 0 of the frame counter is 0 and the one at $C7C5 when it is 1, so the marks change place every frame. One reference, the load at $BC7D.
Second version of the floppy disk's hub, 17 rows of six bytes: the same ring and hole as $C75F with the marks in the other positions. Loaded at $BC82 when bit 0 of the frame counter is 1.

The head slot of the floppy disk: 21 rows of four bytes, an upright oval 9 pixels wide with every pixel set. $BB06 plots it below the hub through $B7E3 in the 16-pixel form. One reference, the load at $BC9C.

Left half of the lettering on the floppy disk's label: 8 rows of six bytes (24 pixels). It clears the pixels of the letters D, U and R and sets a bar three pixels wide down its left edge. Plotted by $BB06 24 columns left of the centre of the disk. One reference, the load at $BCCE.

Right half of the label lettering, 8 rows of six bytes: the letters E, L and L cleared and a bar three pixels wide set near the right edge. With $C87F it spells DURELL across 48 pixels. One reference, the load at $BCB6.

A shadow for the type-$E5 object: 13 rows of four bytes, the outline of a ball with four diagonal spikes drawn as a checkerboard of cleared pixels. The type-$E5 drawer at $8667 plots it first, at the centre of the object's projected base less 7 columns and 6 rows, when the byte at +$1B of the object's record is below $11. One reference, the load at $867C.

Largest of four pictures of the type-$E5 object, a ball with four diagonal spikes and a small square in its middle: 22 rows of six bytes (24 pixels wide). The drawer at $8667 chooses by the width of the object's projected top face, never more than the byte at +$1C of its record, which it lowers to that width; this picture serves widths of 20 and over. It is centred on the face. One reference, the load at $86F7.
The spiked ball at 18 rows of six bytes (24 pixels wide), for a top face 16 to 19 pixels wide. Loaded at $86EE, where the alternate A is also made non-zero to select the 24-pixel form of the plotter.
The spiked ball at 15 rows of four bytes (16 pixels wide), for a top face 13 to 15 pixels wide. One reference, the load at $86E2.
The spiked ball at 12 rows of four bytes, the smallest of the four, for a top face under 13 pixels wide. One reference, the load at $86D9.

First of the two pictures of a type-$FB object: 16 rows of four bytes, a loose scatter of single cleared pixels. The drawer at $863F plots nothing while the byte at +1 of the object's record is 9 or more, this picture while it is 8 down to 1, and the one at $CAAF when it is 0. One reference, the load at $864E.

Second picture of a type-$FB object, 16 rows of four bytes: more cleared pixels than $CA6F, gathered into a rough ring round the middle. Loaded at $8654 when the byte at +1 of the object's record is 0.

A ring 6 pixels across with a mark inside, 6 rows of four bytes. It is one end of the three-part shape that $B4E0 draws in place of legs and discs for a type-$F3 object whose size byte is 7: plotted at $B5AB, up to 4 pixels from the centre in the direction given by the byte at +$0E of the object's record, then 3 columns left and 3 rows up. One reference, the load at $B5A5.

A ring 7 pixels across, 7 rows of four bytes: the other end of the three-part shape drawn at $B4E0, plotted at $B559 up to 4 pixels from the centre the opposite way from $CAEF, then 3 columns left and 4 rows up. One reference, the load at $B553.

The middle of the three-part shape drawn at $B4E0, 5 rows of four bytes: a blob 5 pixels across with four set pixels, plotted at $B504 at the centre less 3 in both directions on frames where bit 0 of the frame counter is 0. One reference, the load at $B4EF.

The other version of the middle, 5 rows of four bytes: a full 5 by 5 square with eight set pixels round its edge, used on frames where bit 0 of the frame counter is 1. One reference, the load at $B4E5.

Four pictures of a spindle, each 12 rows of four bytes ($30 bytes): a rounded three-cornered shape seen at four angles. The drawer of type-$F7 items at $860A adds $30 times a two-bit number to $CB4B. That number is the low two bits of the frame counter when bit 0 of the item's top height is set and the low two bits of the negated counter when it is clear, so the picture advances a step every frame and spindles at odd and even heights step in opposite orders. One reference, the load at $862B.

Left half of the built picture of the three-digit counter: 16 rows of six bytes as mask and pattern pairs, holding the hundreds digit and the left part of the tens digit. It is working memory, zero on the tape. $BD12 fills the 192 bytes from here with $FF and XORs the lit segments into pattern bytes, and $BCF5 plots the result. Four instructions load this address ($BCF8, $BD13, $BD20, $BD2E) and $BD16 loads $CC0C as the destination of the fill.

Right half of the counter picture, 16 rows of six bytes: the rest of the tens digit and the units digit. $BD12 reaches it with offsets of $60 and more from $CC0B for the tens digit and with base $CC6D, one byte pair in, for the units digit ($BD37). $BCF5 plots it from the load at $BD01, 24 columns right of the left half.

Ten bytes, one for each digit 0 to 9, read by $BD3E at $CCCB plus the digit. Bits 7 down to 1 stand for the seven segments in the order top, upper left, upper right, middle, lower left, lower right, bottom. A set bit leaves the segment dark and a clear bit draws it: 0 is $10 (only the middle dark), 1 is $DA (only the two right-hand segments drawn) and 8 is $00. Bit 0 is not used. One reference, the load at $BD42.

Segment data for the hundreds and tens digits of the counter picture, 150 bytes that two calls of $BD3E read through once. For each of a digit's seven segments there is a count and then that many pairs of a buffer offset and a byte to XOR in; both digits have groups of 4, 6, 5, 4, 5, 6 and 4 pairs. Every offset is odd, so each falls on a pattern byte of a six-byte row. The second digit's offsets run from $0B to $B5 and so cross from the left buffer at $CC0B into the right one. The pairs of the middle segments, at $CCF7 and $CD42, are stepped over without being read while the digit is 0, 1 or 7. One reference, the load at $BD24.

Segment data for the units digit, 75 bytes in the form of $CCD5: seven groups of 4, 6, 5, 4, 5, 6 and 4 pairs. The offsets are the ones the hundreds digit uses, applied from base $CC6D instead of $CC0B, and the XOR bytes are shifted to the digit's place within its bytes. One reference, the load at $BD3B.

Ten 8-byte shapes of the digits 0 to 9, a byte for each pixel row, the digit as clear bits on a set background. The routine at $7B63 and $7B6B copies the eight bytes at $CDB6 + 8 * n straight to the screen, n being the low nibble of A when entered at $7B63 and the high nibble at $7B6B. Its 16 call sites, between $78A7 and $7B2A, all follow the decimal conversion at $7B2E, so n is 0 to 9 and nothing past $CE05 is read. One reference, the load at $7B71.

The value of the worm's cell pointer at $644A when $CE0A last painted its map of the 25 cells around the worm.
