Each frame $CE0A compares the two, once the word at $CE08 has been found unchanged, and returns without painting if they match; $CE25 stores the new pointer when they differ. Zero on the tape. Two references, $CE1A and $CE25.

The word at $805B as it stood when $CE0A last ran: its low byte is the number of spindles collected and its high byte, $805C, the number last printed in the panel. $CE0A subtracts the new value from the old, stores the new one at $CE14 on every frame, and paints its map of the cells around the worm again when they differ. Zero on the tape. Two references, $CE0A and $CE14.

Decides, once per pass of the frame loop, whether the insert map at the bottom left of the panel has to be redrawn. It compares the word at $805B (the spindle count at $805B and the panel's displayed copy of it at $805C) with the copy it keeps at $CE08, and the pointer at $644A (the centre entry of the five by five table of square pointers at $6432, the square the worm is in) with its copy at $CE06. It stores the new values and runs on into the redraw at $CE29 when either differs, otherwise it returns. The panel code at $7AA2, which runs straight after this routine, then copies $805B to $805C, so the word has changed again by the next pass and a change of the spindle count redraws the map on two passes running. Called from the frame loop at $768E, its one caller.

Redraws the whole insert map: the 25 board squares around the worm, 16 pixels to a square. It walks the table of square pointers at $6432 backwards from its last entry at $6462, five rows of five, keeping the map position of the current square in $8027 (x, $50 down to $10 in steps of $10) and $8028 (y, $B8 down to $78) and the table pointer in $8029, and calls $CE73 for each entry. After the fifth entry of a row, when that square (table column 0) exists, it takes the pointer at offset 4 of the square's header, the link to the neighbour beyond the left edge, and draws that square too with x = 0, so that a record wide enough to reach into the window still shows. It returns when y drops below $78. Reached from $CE18 when something changed, and called from $D36D when the halt screen ends.

Draws one square of the insert map. HL is the square's address, or zero where the board has none. For zero it paints the block black through $CFF5 with A = 0 and returns. Otherwise it paints the block with attribute $20 (black ink on green paper) and steps through the square's 7-byte records, which start 8 bytes in and end at a zero byte, looking at the type byte at offset 6 of each. Type $E2 is plotted with no attribute of its own, so it shows black on the green; types $E8-$EF are plotted with attribute $26 (yellow ink); a type $F7 record whose offset 5 is $0C and whose offset 1 is not $FF is plotted with $27 (white ink); every other record is skipped. The $F7 records with offset 5 = $0C are the spindles: the new-game code at $75A8 picks out the same records to reset their offset 1, and the worm's collision code at $A5AC sets it to $FF when it adds one to the spindle count at $805B, so the white dots are the spindles still to collect. Called from $CE52 and $CE6D.

Pixel mask for the first (leftmost) display byte of the rectangle being plotted on the insert map. When the rectangle fits in one byte this is the whole mask. Written at $CF2A, $CF34 or $CF41 and ORed into the display at $CFA3.

Pixel mask for the second display byte of the rectangle being plotted on the insert map: the right-hand mask when it spans two bytes, $FF when it spans three, zero when it fits in one. Written together with $CEBB by the word stores at $CF2A and $CF34, or cleared at $CF45. ORed into the display at $CFA7, and tested at $CFD2 to decide whether a second attribute cell is coloured.

Pixel mask for the third display byte of the rectangle being plotted on the insert map: the right-hand mask when it spans three bytes, otherwise zero. Written at $CF2E, $CF39 or $CF48, ORed into the display at $CFAB and tested at $CFE1 to decide whether a third attribute cell is coloured. The two bytes after it, $CEBE and $CEBF, hold zero and no instruction refers to them.

Plots one board record as a filled rectangle on the insert map. IX is the record, B the attribute for its cells (0 for none), and $8027 and $8028 hold the map position of its square. The left edge is the square's x plus the record's x (offset 2) divided by 16, the right edge the square's x plus x plus width (offset 3) divided by 16, and the same for y from offsets 4 and 5. A record wholly outside x $18-$57 or y $88-$B7 is skipped and the rest is clipped to that window, 64 by 48 pixels. The masks for the first and last byte are made from the single-bit table at $8F08 and stored at $CEBB-$CEBD. The rows are then ORed into the bottom third of the display at byte column x/8 - 2, which puts map x $18 at screen pixel 8, and every attribute cell the rectangle touches is given the record's attribute if it still holds $20, so the first coloured record in a cell keeps it. It ends by jumping back to the record loop at $CE87. Reached from the three type tests at $CE98, $CEA1 and $CEB8. The eight bytes at $CFE7 colour a third cell in a row; that takes a coloured record at least 128 units wide, and the widest record of types $E8-$EF on the board is $78.

Paints the 16 by 16 pixel block of one map square with the attribute in A: the four character cells at column x/8 - 2, row y/8 and the ones to their right and below, where x is $8027 and y is $8028, each through $D027. It returns at once when x/8 is zero, which is the case for the extra square $CE29 draws left of the window. Called from $CE79 with A = 0 (no square) and from $CE82 with A = $20.

Turns one character cell of the insert map into a blank cell of attribute C. DE is the cell's attribute address. The cell is left alone unless it lies in columns 1-8 of rows 17-22, the window of the map: D must be $5A, the low five bits of E 1 to 8, and the top three bits of E neither 0 nor 7. Inside the window it writes C to the attribute and zeroes the cell's eight pixel bytes at $50xx-$57xx. Called three times from $CFF5, which also falls into it for its fourth cell.

Rotation angle of the halt screen's ball, 256 to a turn. $D049 is added to it on every pass at $D136. It is $01 in the loaded image and, like the rest of the ball's state, is not reset when the halt screen is entered, so each halt carries on from the last.

Angle of the gore edge that $D2C2 is asked to compute. Set to the rotation in $D046 with its top two bits forced on ($D13F), then advanced by $20, an eighth of a turn, for each of the eight gores of the ball ($D177).
Counts the gores of the ball in one pass: set to 8 at $D14D and decremented at $D16C; the pass ends when it goes below zero.

Amount added to the ball's rotation $D046 on every pass: $0A in the loaded image, set to $F6 (-10) when the ball bounces off the right-hand limit ($D104) and back to $0A when it bounces off the left ($D11C).

Horizontal position of the ball's centre in frame-buffer pixels. $D04D is added on every pass and the result is held between $32 and $C7 ($D0F2-$D12C). $C4 in the loaded image. The gore edges at $D051-$D054 are offsets from it.

Frame-buffer row of the top of the ball. $D04C is added on every pass ($D0C4). $0A in the loaded image; from that state it runs 10, 10, 11, 13, 16, 20, 25, 31, 38, 46, 55 and back again, a bounce every 19 passes.

Vertical speed of the ball in rows per pass. One is added on every pass ($D0C0), so it falls faster and faster. When the top row reaches $37 or more the speed is negated and one is subtracted ($D0E1), which the next pass's added one cancels, so the bounce loses nothing. Zero in the loaded image.
Horizontal speed of the ball in pixels per pass: 5 in the loaded image, negated at each side limit ($D10A, $D122). The byte after it, $D04E, holds zero and no instruction refers to it.

The previous gore edge's x at the radius-17 latitude of the ball (the copy of $D051 made at $D15F before the next edge is computed). Together with $D051 it gives the two ends of the strip edges nearest the poles.
The previous gore edge's x at the ball's equator, radius 34 (the copy of $D052 made at $D15F). Compared with $D052 at $D17D to decide whether the gore between the two edges faces the viewer.
The x of the current gore edge at the radius-17 latitude: $D04A plus or minus 17 times the sine of the angle in $D047, written by $D2C2.
The x of the current gore edge at the equator: $D04A plus or minus 34 times the sine of the angle in $D047, written by $D2C2.
The previous gore edge's x at the radius-29 latitude (the copy of $D054 made at $D165).

The x of the current gore edge at the radius-29 latitude: $D04A plus or minus 29 times the sine of the angle in $D047, written by $D2C2. The two bytes after it, $D055 and $D056, hold zero and no instruction refers to them.

Three constants, 5, 13 and 16 ($D057, $D058, $D059): the heights in rows of the strips a gore of the ball is drawn in. Each gore is six strips of 5, 13, 16, 16, 13 and 5 rows, 68 rows in all. Read at $D1C9-$D28A, never written.

Zero at the start of each pass ($D0B6) and non-zero once the ball's shadow has been drawn, which happens before the first gore that faces the viewer. While the shadow is drawn it also keeps the fill pattern byte $80BF ($D1A1, restored at $D22D). The three bytes after it, $D05B-$D05D, hold zero and no instruction refers to them.

The halt screen: the manual's "H halts play and runs a bouncing ball routine". Called from the frame loop at $779A, its one caller, once the halt key (bit 4 of the control byte $8057) has been pressed and released. This first part sets the scene. It fills the attributes of rows 0-16 ($5800-$5A1F) with $55 (bright, cyan ink on red paper) and puts $6D (cyan on cyan) in the first two and last two cells of row 16. It draws a strip of 8-pixel tiles into row 16, the top row of the panel: seven tiles from the table at $D3EA in columns 14, 12 ... 2 and the tile at $D422 in columns 15, 13 ... 3, through $D371. It then builds columns 16-29 of that row as the mirror image of columns 2-15, taking each byte through the bit-reversal table at $6200 and shifting the whole row one pixel left with a set bit entering at the right. Last it zeroes the high bytes of the six trapezoid parameters ($801C, $801E, $8020, $8024, $8026, $8028) and runs on into the pass loop at $D0B5. The ball's own state at $D046-$D05A is not reset.

One pass of the halt screen, repeated until a key is down. It moves the ball: the fall speed $D04C grows by one and is added to the top row $D04B, and once the top row is $37 or more the speed is reversed and $8055 is set to 6 for the speaker; the x speed $D04D is added to $D04A, and at $C7 on the right or $32 on the left the ball is put on the limit, the x speed negated, the spin $D049 set to -10 or +10 and $8055 set to 5. It then calls $D37D to redraw the backdrop in the frame buffer, adds the spin to the rotation $D046, computes the first gore edge for that angle with its top two bits set ($D2C2), clears the fill pattern at $80BE/$80BF, sets the gore count to 8 and runs on into $D150. The seven instructions at $D0CC bounce the ball off row 7 at the top; from the loaded state the bounce on the floor loses nothing and the top row is never less than 10, so that test never succeeds.

Draws the ball, a sphere of eight gores, as a loop over the gores. For each it complements the fill byte $80BF and stores that AND $AA in $80BE, keeps the last edge ($D051, $D052, $D054 to $D04F, $D050, $D053), counts $D048 down and leaves for $D336 after the eighth, then advances the angle $D047 by $20 and computes the new edge with $D2C2. A gore is drawn only if it faces the viewer, which is when the new equator point $D052 is left of the previous one $D050. Before the first such gore ($D05A still zero) it draws the shadow at $D18F: with the fill bytes set to $FF and $00, six strips through $D2A0 that follow the previous edge moved one pixel right and are 13 pixels wide, the top and bottom strips widened as far as the mirror image of that edge about the ball's centre. The gore itself, from $D238, is six strips through $D293 of 5, 13, 16, 16, 13 and 5 rows from the top row $D04B: a point at the centre $D04A, then the previous and new edges at radius 17, 29, 34, 29 and 17, then the centre again. $D293 flips the fill for every strip, and with the flip per gore that gives the ball its chequered surface.

Flips the fill pattern and draws one strip of a gore. A is the strip's height in rows, D and E the x of its two lower corners. It complements $80BF, stores that AND $AA in $80BE, so the pair alternates between $00/$00 and $AA/$FF, and runs on into $D2A0. Called six times, from $D252 to $D28D, once for each strip of a gore.

Draws one strip of the ball or its shadow as a trapezoid stacked under the last one. The previous lower edge becomes the upper edge ($8023 to $801B, $8027 to $801F, the row $8025 to $801D), the row $8025 is moved down by C, and D and E become the new lower corners in $8023 and $8027. It then jumps to the trapezoid filler at $900C, which draws into the frame buffer with the pattern in $80BE/$80BF only when the lower row is below the upper one. Called six times for the shadow, from $D1CD to $D227, and entered six times per gore from $D293.
One byte, $C9, a RET that nothing reaches: the routine before it leaves through its JP to $900C and no instruction refers to this address.

Computes where one gore edge of the ball lies at three latitudes. For the angle in $D047 it takes the sine from $A8C4 (a magnitude of 0-255 with the sign returned in the alternate carry flag), multiplies it by 17, 34 and 29 with $D320, keeps the high byte of each product, negates it for angles of $80 and above, and adds it to the ball's centre x $D04A, giving $D051, $D052 and $D054. The largest offsets are 16, 33 and 28 pixels. Called from $D142 for the first edge of a pass and from $D17A for each of the eight that follow.

Returns HL = A times DE, the low 16 bits, by shifting A right and DE left and adding DE for every set bit; A = 0 returns 0 at once. A is left zero and DE shifted. Called three times from $D2C2 and from $885A and $887A in the drawing routine at $8833, five callers in all.

Ends a pass of the halt screen. It calls $E9E8, which copies the frame buffer to the display and drives the speaker from the value in $8055, then zeroes $8055 and reads all eight keyboard half-rows at once (IN from port $FE with the high byte zero). With no key down it jumps back to $D0B5 for another pass, so any key at all ends the halt. That includes the halt key itself, which the frame loop at $7789 then finds still down and answers with another halt once it is released. On a key it puts the game's screen back: attributes of rows 0-15 to $44 (bright green ink on black), the attributes of row 16 copied from row 23, and the pixels of row 16 rebuilt as the bottom row of the panel turned upside down (31 bytes of each of the eight lines, $57E0 to $5000 and so on). It then calls $CE29 to redraw the insert map and returns to the frame loop. Row 16 is the panel's top border and row 23 its bottom one. Rebuilding the one from the other only works where they are mirror images; in the panel as it stands during play they differ in columns 10 to 12, so those cells of the top border come back changed.

Copies the eight bytes at HL into one character cell of row 16: the eight display lines $50xx-$57xx at column E. It leaves HL after the tile and E one column to the left. Called from $D07D and $D081 while the halt screen builds its strip.

Fills the whole frame buffer, $F000-$FFFF, with the halt screen's backdrop by pushing words with the stack pointer started at $0000, so it writes from $FFFF downwards: 4,096 bytes, 128 rows of 32. The result is 16 blank rows of $FF at the top and below them seven bands of 16 rows. Each band starts with a dotted line across ($FE in byte column 2, then 26 bytes of $AA in columns 3-28), and of the 15 rows under it every second one carries $FE in the even byte columns 2-28: a dotted grid of 13 by 7 cells of 16 pixels, with no line under the last band. The caller's stack pointer is kept in $E9E6 meanwhile. Called from $D12F on every pass, where the game's own passes clear the buffer with $EAA9.

Seven 8-byte tiles, 56 bytes, for the strip the halt screen draws along row 16. The loop at $D079 takes them in order for columns 14, 12, 10, 8, 6, 4 and 2; its column counter starts at 15 and it stops when the column reaches 1, which is how the count of seven is fixed. Each tile is eight display lines, top first. Read only through $D371.
One 8-byte tile, $AA $FF $AA $FF $AA $FF $FF $AA, drawn by the loop at $D079 in each odd column from 15 down to 3 of row 16, between the tiles of $D3EA.
Passes left before the next member of the train being emitted is written. Reloaded from $D42B at $D63A each time a member is written and counted down at $D624-$D628.

Zero when no train is being emitted. Set to $13 (19) at $D618 when one starts and cleared at $D68E after its last member; while it is non-zero it is the value $D42A is reloaded with, so members follow each other 19 passes apart. Tested at $D52D, and read by the board handler at $BEE3. Nothing clears it when a new game starts: its only writers are the two named here.
Address of the board square that holds the record the train starts from (a word). Stored at $D58C and copied into bytes 2 and 3 of every member's record at $D63D.
The x at which each member of the train is created, within the square at $D42C. Worked out at $D5B8, $D5C5 or $D5D7 from the start record and copied into byte 5 of each member at $D646.
The y at which each member of the train is created. Worked out at $D5AB, $D5E4 or $D5F1 from the start record and copied into byte 7 of each member at $D64C.
Byte 0 of the start record, its top height, kept at $D59A. Each member is created standing on it: this value goes into byte $0B (bottom) and this plus 10 into byte $0D (top) at $D65A-$D662.

Heading the train sets off on: $00, $40, $80 or $C0, chosen at $D5BB-$D5F4 from the low two bits of the start record's type and stored at $D5FB. Copied into byte $0E of each member, and with $80 added into byte $13, at $D669-$D671.

Members of the current train still to be written: set at $D60B to the number of followers plus one for the leader, 2 to 5, and counted down at $D685-$D689; at zero $D42B is cleared. Like $D42B it is not reset when a game starts. The four bytes after it, $D433-$D436, hold zero and no instruction refers to them.

Passes to wait before another type $FB record may be created. $0A in the loaded image; counted down at $D449 on passes when nothing is in view, and set back to $0A at $D45F each time a record is created.

Called once per pass from the frame loop at $765F, its one caller: makes new objects in three steps, each of which first steps the random generator at $E472, and then runs every object through $D691. This first step creates the points bugs come up from. If the display code counted nothing at all in view on its last build ($8068 = 0; $AFF4 adds one for each board record or object it accepts), the delay $D437 has run out and the pool counter $7C71 is below 13, it adds 2 to the counter, sets the delay to 10 and writes a record at the pool's end pointer $7C72: type $FB, byte 1 = $14, table position 2,2 (the worm's square), x and y from the worm's position bytes $7FF5 and $7FF7, size $10 by $10, bottom height 0 and top 1; the end pointer moves on 30 bytes. The handler at $DE41 counts byte 1 down and at zero writes a type $F3 bug beside the point, which is what the second count is for.

Second step of $D438: creates a type $E5 object. It needs the pool counter $7C71 below 9, and either the counter at 1, which means the pool is empty, or the random byte $E46F equal to $4E. The record goes at the end pointer: a table position next to the worm's (bits 0, 1 and 3 of the random byte $E470 pick one of the eight positions around 2,2), x and y $80 (the middle of the square), size 10 by 10, bottom height $CF and top $D9, bytes $0E-$11 from the random bytes $E46F, $E46F, $E470 and $E471, byte $12 = 5, byte $13 = $0F and byte $1C = $63. If the table has no square at that position ($DF9F returns a zero high byte) the record is abandoned where it stands; otherwise the end pointer moves on 30 bytes and the counter goes up by one. An empty pool therefore gets one of these at once, unless the square picked is missing. The type is handled at $DC69.

Third step of $D438: the trains that run along the tracks. With a train already being emitted ($D42B non-zero) it goes to $D624. Otherwise a new one starts only on a pass where the low six bits of the random byte $E470 are $19 and the pool counter $7C71 is below 11. It takes a number from 1 to 8 out of bits 1-3 of $E46F and scans the 25 squares of the table at $6432 in table order, counting the records whose type is $E8-$EB; the record that brings the count to that number is the start and control goes to $D586. With fewer such records in the 25 squares no train starts. Either way the pass ends in the walk at $D691.

Sets up a train at the record found by $D52A (IX the table entry of its square, HL just past the record, A its type). It keeps the square's address in $D42C and the record's top height in $D430, then takes the side the train leaves by, and its heading, from the low two bits of the type: $E8 the right edge (x + width) heading $00; $EA ten units left of the record (x - 10) heading $80; $E9 ten units before it in y (y - 10) heading $C0; $EB its far edge in y (y + depth) heading $40; on the other axis the start is centred (start + half the size - 5). Bits 5 and 6 of the random byte $E471 give the number of followers, 1 to 4: that number goes into byte $16 of the leader's record, one more goes into $D432 and onto the pool counter $7C71, $13 into $D42B and 1 into byte $18. The leader itself, type $F0, is written through $D634. The board's 129 squares hold five records of type $E8, five of $E9, four of $EA and one of $EB.

Counts the gap $D42A down and, when it reaches zero, writes the next follower of the train at the pool's end pointer: type $F1 (the leader comes in at $D634 with type $F0 already in A). The record gets the square's address from $D42C in bytes 2-3, x and y from $D42E and $D42F, size 10 by 10, bottom height from $D430 and top 10 above it, the heading $D431 in byte $0E and the opposite heading in byte $13, byte $14 = 4, byte $0F = $FF, the state that sends a type $F1 record to the rider code at $DB0F, and byte $10 = 0. The gap is reloaded from $D42B, the end pointer moves on 30 bytes, and when $D432 reaches zero $D42B is cleared. The pool counter is not touched here: it was raised for the whole train at $D613. Because $D42B and $D432 survive the start of a new game while the counter is reset to 1 ($7624), followers left over from a train cut short by the end of a game are written into the next game uncounted, and each one later removed takes the counter one too low: with two left over and nothing else in the pool it goes from 1 to 0 to $FF.

Runs every object in the pool once per pass: loads the end pointer $7C72 and falls into the loop at $D694, which works down from the last record to the first. Reached at the end of $D438 by five jumps ($D53B, $D543, $D583, $D62B, $D68C) and by falling out of $D68E.

The loop of the object walk. HL is the record just handled, or the end pointer on entry from $D691. If it is not above $7C74, the first record, the walk is over and it returns to the frame loop. Otherwise it steps down 30 bytes and dispatches on the type byte there: $F3 to $D6C9, $F1 to $D9ED, $F0 to $DB0C, $E3 to $DAF1, $E5 to $DC69, $E6 to $DDF8 and $FB to $DE41; a record of any other type is removed through $DEE6. Every handler ends by jumping back here with its record in HL: 19 jumps in all. $DEE6 removes a record by copying the pool's last record over it, so walking downwards means the record moved in has already had its turn.

Handler for a type $F3 record: the bug that crawls over the board, chases the worm and, on touching it, is taken out of the pool and counted onto a segment of the worm by the worm's own code at $9E7C and $A5F6. IY is set to the record. A negative speed byte ($12) marks a bug that a sparky has hit: $FF becomes $FE and the bug waits a pass, anything lower turns it into a burst at $DE22. Otherwise bytes $13 and $12 are made non-zero, $DF04 works out the step from the heading (byte $0E) and speed and the position it leads to, and $DFB8 tests that position against the board and the other objects. No square there ($8028 = 0) and the bug is blocked ($D8BC). A collision ($803B = $FF) goes to $D845. Otherwise $803B is the height of the surface underneath: if the bug's bottom is less than 6 above it, the bug moves and settles on it ($D735). A deeper drop depends on the mode in byte $15: mode 0 steps off and falls 6 a pass only if that surface is not below the worm's height $7FFF, mode 1 always steps off, and modes 2 and 3 treat the drop as a block.

Makes the bug's move. Entered at $D735 with the drop in C, which is negated, or at $D738 with a signed height change in A (from $D8B9 and from $DC66, where a rider turns into a bug). The change is added to the bottom and top heights (bytes $0B and $0D), the three limb bytes are stepped by $D97D and $D996, the tested position is stored in bytes 4-7 from $8029, $801B, $802A and $801D, and the square it lies in ($8027) is looked up by $A192, which gives its column and row in the table at $6432, or leaves the address as it is when the square is not among the 25; the result goes into bytes 2-3. A bug whose square is outside the table (byte 3 is 5 or more) counts byte $17 down; at zero one is added to the reserve of bugs at $8066 and the record is removed. Inside the table byte $17 is reloaded with $28, so a bug is given up 40 passes after leaving it. Then the mode decides: with bit 0 of byte $15 clear the bug chases ($D7E4); with it set it wanders. Wandering counts the timer in byte $16 down; once it is zero, a bug inside the table and less than $200 from the worm by $D941 changes to mode 2 with the timer at $14. Each pass the heading turns by the rate in byte $13; a random byte from $E472 equal to $C6 flips bit 1 of the mode; and the low five bits of the random byte are added to byte $14, each carry out of it reversing the turn rate.

The chasing half of the bug's behaviour, taken when bit 0 of the mode byte $15 is clear. Outside the table it only sets bit 0 of byte 1 of the record, which no instruction was found to read for this type, and the timer in byte $16 to $14. Inside, $D941 measures the distance to the worm. With the timer at zero and the distance $300 or more it does the same as outside. With the timer at zero and the worm nearer, bit 1 of the mode is set from the heights: if the worm's height $7FFF is below the bug's bottom the bit is cleared, which lets the bug come down off things, and the timer becomes $20; otherwise the bit is set and the timer stays at zero. With the timer running it is counted down. Then it steers: the signs of the two differences left by $D941 select one of the diagonals $20, $60, $A0 or $E0, the one that points away from the worm, and the heading (byte $0E) is moved by the size of the turn rate (byte $13) away from that, so it homes on the opposite diagonal, towards the worm. A bug with larger x and y than the worm settles on heading $A0, one with smaller x and larger y on $E0, smaller x and y on $20, larger x and smaller y on $60, and then swings one step either side of it.

The bug's move met something ($803B = $FF). If it is a sparky, a type $F1 object ($8035 = $F1, its record in $8037), 20 ($0014) is added to the score at $8060, the one place this part of the code scores. A large bug (size byte 8 = $0E) only shrinks to size $0A, while the sparky becomes a burst (type $E6, byte $0E = 4, picture $C5B3) and the sound at $E4E8 is started through $E4F7. Any other bug gets $FF in its speed byte, which makes it a burst two passes later, and the sparky is removed: the pool counter and end pointer step back and the pool's last record is copied over the sparky's. The copy goes wrong when the bug is itself the last record and the sparky lies below it: the bug's record is the one moved, the $FF lands in the abandoned copy, and the bug is handled a second time and lives on, with the sparky gone and the 20 points given. For anything else met, and after the large bug's case, the top of the obstacle ($8036) decides: level with the bug's bottom, it moves on ($D746), which is also what happens on every move of a bug at height zero, where $DFB8 reports a collision with nothing; a bug of size 7 is blocked by any step; other bugs climb a step of less than $14 ($D738) and are blocked by more.

The bug cannot go where it was heading. With the step zeroed it tests its present position again ($DF44, $DFB8). If nothing holds it up there it sinks toward the surface underneath by up to 6 through $D735, without moving. Otherwise it turns on the spot. In a wandering mode (bit 0 of byte $15 set) the heading turns by the rate in byte $13 and the limb bytes are stepped by $D97D if the rate is negative, $D996 if not. In a chasing mode a heading that is not a multiple of $40 is rounded to the nearest one and byte $18 set to 9; one that already is turns a further $40 and byte $18 is counted down, and when it reaches zero bit 1 of the mode is cleared, the timer in byte $16 set to $13 and byte $18 back to 9. The exit at $D900, which six jumps share, hands the record back to the walk at $D694.

Returns in HL how far the object at IY is from the worm: the sum of the absolute differences in x and in y, with 256 units to a board square. The object's position is its table column and x (bytes 2 and 5) and its table row and y (bytes 3 and 7); the worm's is column and row 2 with x from $7FF5 and y from $7FF7. The signed differences, object minus worm, are left in $803D (x) and $803F (y), where $D81C reads their high bytes. Only meaningful for an object inside the table; both callers, $D7A3 and $D7F6, check byte 3 first.

Adds $20 to each of bytes $0F, $10 and $11 of the record at IY. In a type $F3 record these three bytes are what the drawing code copies out at $842F and reads at $B3A5-$B40E, a nibble at a time, to pose the bug. Called from $D746 on every move and from $D935 when a blocked bug turns with a negative rate.

Subtracts 2 from each of bytes $0F, $10 and $11 of the record at IY, the same three bytes $D97D adds $20 to, so a move changes each by $1E. Called from $D749 on every move and from $D93B when a blocked bug turns with a positive rate.

State 0 of a type $F1 record, the mine a burper leaves: the fire code at $7771 gives a shot state 0 and $A0 in byte $0E when bit 6 of the control byte is set. Byte $0E is counted down one a pass. Until it reaches zero the mine takes the ordinary move at $DA18 with a speed of 0, so all it does is sink to the surface under it. At zero the state becomes $FD, and from $D9B2, where later passes enter directly, it rises: 7 is added to its bottom and top heights each pass and the new position is tested with $DF44 and $DFB8. Any collision turns it into a burst at $DE22, and so does a height that passes $FF, where both heights are set to $FA first. The wait is 160 passes, and a rise from height 0 that meets nothing ends in the burst on its 34th pass. The type $E5 handler at $DDF1 also sets state $FD, for a waiting mine it finds under an $E5 object.

Handler for a type $F1 record, a sparky: the fire code at $7722 writes one for each shot, taking one off the count at $805D, and $D62E writes one for each follower of a train. While the timer in byte $10 is running it is counted down; a shot starts it at $37, and the worm's collision test at $9BDD passes over a sparky until it is zero. A state of 4 in byte $0F, which is how a blaster is fired, becomes 7 the first time the record is handled. The state then selects: 0 the waiting mine at $D9A9; $FF the rider code at $DB0F; $FE the fizzle at $DA9D; $FD the rise at $D9B2; anything else is used as the speed (byte $12), so a blaster travels at 7. $DF04 and $DFB8 work out and test the move. With no square there the record is removed ($DEE6). With no collision the sparky sinks toward the surface underneath by at most 6 and moves ($DA3C). A collision goes to $DA74.

Shared end of a move. From $DA3C the signed height change in A is added to the object's bottom and top heights (bytes $0B and $0D). From $DA4A the tested position is stored: $8029, $801B, $802A and $801D into bytes 4-7, and what $A192 returns for the square in $8027, its table position or its address, into bytes 2-3; then the walk goes on at $D694. $DA3C is fallen into from the sparky's own drop at $DA3A and jumped to from $DA88, $DAEE, $DB86 and $DB9F; $DA4A, with no change of height, is jumped to from $D9DF, $DA83 and the type $E5 handler at $DDF5.

The sparky's move met a board record ($803B = $FF). Objects of types $F1 and $F0 are not tested against other objects ($E10C), so it can only be the board. A record of type $E2, a track, sends the sparky to $DAC7. Otherwise the step up to the obstacle's top ($8036 less the sparky's bottom) decides: none and it moves on, less than $0C and it climbs it, $0C or more and it has hit a wall: it is removed at once if its x or y byte is zero, else its state becomes $FE and the fizzle below begins on the same pass.

State $FE of a sparky, one that has hit a wall. Each pass takes 2 from each size byte (8 and 9) and adds 1 to y and to x (bytes 7 and 5), so it shrinks about its centre. It is removed when a size reaches zero, which from size 10 is the fifth pass, or if y or x wraps to zero.

A sparky whose move met a type $E2 record becomes a rider: state $FF, heading rounded to the nearest multiple of $40, byte $13 the opposite heading, byte $15 = 3, byte $14 = 6 and byte $16 = 0. It is lifted to the record's top ($8036) through $DA3C and from the next pass is run by $DB0F.

Handler for a type $E3 record: what the leader of a train (type $F0) is turned into at $DC21 when it reaches a record of type $EC, $EE or $EF, where it waits to count its followers in. The handler only runs two timers: byte $17 is counted down every pass, and each time it reaches zero byte $18 is counted down. When byte $18 goes below zero the number left in byte $16, the followers that have not arrived ($DBF0 takes one off for each that does), is added to the reserve of bugs at $8066 and the record is removed. With $14 in byte $17 and 1 in byte $18, the values in the leaders of the template at $7951, that happens 276 passes after the leader arrives.

Handler for a type $F0 record, the leader of a train, and, entered at $DB0F, for a type $F1 record in state $FF: a follower, or a sparky that has joined a track. Riders move at speed 7 along the board records of type $E2. After the move is worked out and tested ($DF04, $DFB8) the timer in byte $14 is counted down; on the pass it reaches zero byte $13 is set to the reverse of the heading and byte $15 to 3, and if the record met or underneath ($8035, $8037) is of type $E2 and less than $1E across the direction of travel, the tested position is centred on it ($801B or $801D = its start + half its width - 5) and the test is made again. Then, from $DB6D: with no square there, or with a surface underneath that is not type $E2, or with a collision with anything other than type $E2 or types $E8-$EF, the rider turns ($DBA2). With a type $E2 record underneath or met it takes that record's height and moves ($DA3C). A collision with a record of type $E8-$EF leaves for $DBC6, where the journey ends.

The rider cannot go on. It sets the timer in byte $14 to 6 and adds $40 to the heading (byte $0E), a quarter turn, without moving on this pass. If the new heading is the reverse one kept in byte $13 it takes one from byte $15 and turns again, so it does not double back; when byte $15 goes below zero, which from the 3 that $DB27 gives it is the fourth time the turning comes round to the reverse heading, the rider becomes a burst at $DE22. Any other heading is tried on the next pass, and the exit at $DBC0 hands the record back to the walk.
Three bytes, $FD $34 $13, which decode as INC (IY+$13). Nothing reaches them: the instruction before is an unconditional JP, the code after begins at $DBC0, and no jump or call names $DBBD.

The exit of the handler at $DB0C, which type-$F0 records share with type-$F1 records whose +$0F is $FF. It is reached from $DBB1 once the heading in +$0E has been turned by $40 and does not match the byte in +$13: it copies IY, the record being handled, into HL and jumps to $D694, which goes on to the record 30 bytes below in the object list. One reference, the JP NZ at $DBB1.

Reached from $DB91 in the handler at $DB0C when the probe at $DFB8 reports a hit ($803B = $FF) on something whose type byte in $8035 is $E8 to $EF. A type-$F0 record ($DC12) is removed through $DEE6 if that type is $E8-$EB or $ED; for $EC, $EE or $EF it becomes type $E3 and settles on the board record at ($8037): +$0B = the record's first byte, its top, +$0D = that plus $0B, +$05 and +$08 = its x and width, +$07 and +$09 = its y and depth, and the walk continues at $D694. A type-$F1 record goes to $DC4C for $E8-$EB, to the counter at $DEB8 for $ED, and for $EC, $EE or $EF becomes type $F3 and runs the probe again, which now tests other objects too. If that leaves $E3 in $8035, the record at ($8037) is taken to be a type-$E3 object, with no check that it is not one of the board's four type-$E3 records: its +$16 is decremented and this record is removed, and when +$16 reaches zero the $E3 record is removed first, by copying the last record of the list over it. When the record being handled is itself the last in the list, that copy puts it in the $E3 record's place, where it lives on as type $F3, and the removal that follows drops the record before it instead. If the second probe leaves anything else in $8035 the record goes to $DC4C, which makes it type $F3 with +$12 = 4, +$13 = 6, +$15 = 2 and +$16 = 2 and jumps to $D738 with A = ($8036) minus its own +$0B, the height it has to rise to stand on what it hit. The board on the tape holds 15 records of types $E8-$EB, 17 of $EC, 4 of $ED and none of $EE or $EF.

Handler for type-$E5 records, entered from the dispatch at $D6B6 with HL = the record. A record whose +$03 is 5 or more, meaning its square has left the 5-by-5 window at $6432, is removed. Otherwise it steers at the point the view is centred on, ($7FF5, $7FF7) in window square (2, 2): for x it takes $0200 + ($7FF5) minus its own position (+$02 as the high byte, +$05 as the low), adds four times that difference to the velocity in +$14/+$15 and keeps the whole part (+$15) within -4 to 4; the same for y with ($7FF7), +$03, +$07 and +$17/+$18. The velocities go to $8033-$8038 for $DF44 and their sign bytes to +$16 and +$19. When both differences are between -20 and 19 it writes 2 to $8056, sets the attribute bytes at $5A6A, $5A6B, $5AAA and $5AAB to $47 (four of the sixteen panel cells that $7A56-$7A94 recolour in every frame), and lowers +$0B and +$0D by 5; if either passes below zero it has landed: +$0B = 1, +$0D = $0B, and it becomes type $F3 with +$18 = 2 and +$15 = 1. Then come $DF44 and the probe at $DFB8. With no square at the new place ($8028 = 0) the whole parts of both velocities are negated and the step is dropped. With no hit, the height beneath it ($803B) is stored in +$1B, which the drawing code reads at $8674; if the thing beneath is a type-$F1 record whose +$0F is 0, that record's +$0F is set to $FD, which is what makes a waiting burper rise (the manual's 'rise to a Sputnik overhead'); and $DA4A stores the new position. On a hit with a type-$F1 record, that record is removed by copying the last record of the list over it, 35 is added to the word at $8060 and this record becomes the burst at $DE22; when this record is itself the last in the list the copy keeps it alive in the other's place and the burst is written just past the end of the list. A hit on another $E5 bounces it as above. A hit on anything else lifts it onto the thing and makes it type $F3 if the thing's top is 0 to 14 above the flyer's own base; otherwise it bounces.

Handler for type-$E6 records, the short burst that a destroyed object turns into, entered from $D6BB with HL = the record. +$0E is its life. A value of 5 or more sends the record to $DE22 to be set up from the start. Otherwise +$0E is decremented and the record is removed through $DEE6 when that takes it below zero. While the value before the decrement was 4 or 3 the shape pointer in +$0F/+$10 is left alone; at 2 it becomes $C5EF and at 1 $C62B. From the 4 that $DE22 stores this gives four passes, showing $C5B3 twice, then $C5EF, then $C62B, and removal on the fifth. The three shapes are 60 bytes apart and are drawn by the code at $870F.

Turns the record in IY into a burst: type $E6, +$0E = 4, shape pointer +$0F/+$10 = $C5B3, and 8 in both $8055 and $8056, so that the next buffer clear and the next buffer copy each click the speaker every eighth pixel row, 16 times (a sound script that is playing replaces the 8 in $8055 at that copy). It ends at $D694 with HL = the record. Six references: $D6D6, $D9DC, $D9EA, $DBBA, $DD76 and, for a type-$E6 record whose +$0E is 5 or more, $DE00.

Handler for type-$FB records, entered from $D6C0 with HL = the record. $D462 makes one at the position the view is centred on, with +$01 = $14, and +$01 is its countdown. If bit 7 of +$01 is set the record is removed through $DEE6; if +$01 is 0 nothing happens. Otherwise +$01 is decremented and $8055 set to $21, three clicks in that frame's buffer copy, and on the pass that brings it to 0 a type-$F3 record is written at the end of the list ($7C72): the marker's square (+$02/+$03), its x and y (+$05, +$07) plus 4, each replaced by $FE if the sum passes 255, a size of 7 by 7 (+$08, +$09), +$0B = 1, +$0D = 6, heading +$0E = the low byte of the frame counter at $8059, +$12 = 3, +$13 = 5, +$14 = $13, +$15 = 2, +$16 = $13 and +$18 = 1. The other bytes of the new record keep whatever the memory held. The end pointer moves on by 30; the count at $7C71 is not changed here, because $D458 added 2 when it made the marker.

Reached from $DBDA when a type-$F1 record whose +$0F is $FF meets a board record of type $ED. It adds one to the three decimal digits at $BD6C (units), $BD6D (tens) and $BD6E (hundreds), carrying at 10 and wrapping from 999 to 000, calls $BD12 with A = the hundreds, B = the tens and C = the units, and falls into $DEE6, which removes the record. The same three bytes are zeroed and passed to $BD12 when a game starts, at $75D8-$75E5.

Removes the record in IY from the object list: it decrements the count at $7C71, moves the end pointer at $7C72 back by 30, copies the 30 bytes of what was the last record over the one being removed, and jumps to $D694 with HL = IY, so the walk carries on with the record below. The order of the list is not kept. When IY is itself the last record the copy is onto itself. 19 references, all jumps from the object handlers between $D6C6 and $DE48.

Turns the heading in +$0E (256 to a full turn) and the speed in +$12 of the record in IY into a velocity. The y part is speed * sin(heading) and the x part speed * sin(heading + $40), each a table sine from $A8C4 multiplied at $A8D8 and negated when the angle is in the second half of the turn, giving a signed number with a fraction byte. x goes to $8033 (fraction), $8034 (whole) and $8037 (sign extension), y to $8035, $8036 and $8038. It then falls into $DF44. A speed of 4 gives x = 3.98, y = 0 at heading 0 and x = 0, y = 3.98 at heading $40, the table's largest sine being 255/256. Called from $D6F4, $DA1B and $DB13.

Works out where the record in IY would be after one step, without changing the record. The new x is +$05 with its fraction +$04 plus the velocity in $8033, $8034 and $8037, kept as a 16-bit number in $801B with the fraction in $8029, and $801F is that plus the width +$08. The new y comes the same way from +$07, +$06 and $8035, $8036 and $8038 into $801D and $802A, with $8025 = y plus the depth +$09. A high byte other than 0 means the box has crossed the edge of its 256-unit square. It also copies the base and top heights +$0B and +$0D to $8023 and $8024, and the square reference +$02/+$03 to $8021. Entered by falling in from $DF04, and called from $D8C8, $D9D2 and $DD38 with the velocity already in place.

Resolves a square reference in HL into the address of a board square. When H is less than 5, L and H are a column and a row of the 5-by-5 window of square addresses at $6432 (25 words; the middle one, $644A, is the square the view is centred in) and HL returns the word at $6432 + 2 * (5 * H + L), which is 0 where the board has no square. When H is 5 or more HL is taken to be an address already and is returned unchanged. L is not range-checked. Called from $D4D6, $DFE2 and $E149.

Tests the box that $DF44 set up against the board and, for most record types, against the other objects. This first half clears the four square pointers $80A9-$80AF and the results $8035-$803C, stores the box's height ($8024 = top minus base), puts the base height in $8036 as the running floor, and resolves the object's square through $DF9F into $8027. From the high bytes of the box's right and far edges ($8020 and $8026) it picks the 2-by-2 block of squares the box can touch and fills $80A9 (lower x, lower y), $80AB (higher x, lower y), $80AD (lower x, higher y) and $80AF (higher x, higher y) from the object's square and the four link words that begin every square: +0 is the neighbour towards higher x, +2 lower y, +4 lower x and +6 higher y. BC, each half 0 or 1, is where $80AF lies relative to the object's square. It continues at $E0D2. Seven callers: $D6F7, $D8CB, $D9D5, $DA1E, $DB16, $DBE1 and $DD3B.

Fills $80A9, the square at lower x and lower y of the probe's 2-by-2 block: the lower-x link (+4) of the square in $80AB if that pointer is not zero, otherwise the lower-y link (+2) of the square in $80AD; if both are zero $80A9 is left as it is. Called from $E014, $E029 and $E041.

Fills $80AB, the square at higher x and lower y of the probe's block: the higher-x link (+0) of the square in $80A9 if there is one, otherwise the lower-y link (+2) of the square in $80AF. Called from $E017 and $E03B.

Fills $80AD, the square at lower x and higher y of the probe's block: the lower-x link (+4) of the square in $80AF if there is one, otherwise the higher-y link (+6) of the square in $80A9. Called from $DFFE, $E02F and $E03E.

Fills $80AF, the square at higher x and higher y of the probe's block: the higher-x link (+0) of the square in $80AD if there is one, otherwise the higher-y link (+6) of the square in $80AB. Called from $E001 and $E02C.

Second half of the probe at $DFB8, reached by a jump from each of its four cases with BC = the position of the square in $80AF, which it keeps in $80B1/$80B2. If the box's base is at height 0 it starts with $803B = $FF: a hit on the floor, with type 0. It calls $E1CF for each of the four squares, passing that square's position in BC. Unless the record in IY is type $F1 or $F0 it then goes through every object record from the end of the list down to $7C74, leaves out IY itself, resolves each one's square through $DF9F and, where that is one of the four squares, tests it with $E3D9. Last, at $E199, it sets $8027 to the square holding the box's new origin: the object's own when the high bytes of $801B and $801D are both 0, otherwise whichever of the four pointers those high bytes select, which is 0 where the board has no square. Results: $803B = $FF for a hit, with $8036 = the top of the thing hit, $8035 = its type, $8037 = its address and $8039 = its slope word; otherwise $803B = the top of the highest thing beneath the box, 0 if there is none, with $8035 and $8037 naming it.

Tests the probe's box against every record of one board square. HL = the square (it returns at once for 0) and BC = the square's position relative to the object's own, stored in $8049 (x) and $804A (y). Records are 7 bytes long from the square's +8 up to a zero first byte: top height, bottom height, x, width, y, depth, type. A record whose rectangle does not overlap the box, or whose type is $F7, is passed over. The top two bits of the type give the shape. $C0 is a level block. $80 is a ramp along x and $40 a ramp along y: bytes 0 and 1 are the heights at its two ends, $908B interpolates the surface height at the box, and $9CCC turns rise and run into a slope word for $803F (256 * the smaller over the larger, with flags in the high byte). $00 is a block cut along a diagonal, which counts only if $908B puts the box's edge on the solid side. Then, at $E378: a surface lower than the running floor in $8036 is remembered in $803B if it is the highest so far beneath the box; otherwise, unless the box's top (the floor plus $8024, held at $FF) is below the record's bottom, it is a hit: $803B = $FF and the floor in $8036 rises to the surface. In either case $8037 = the record, $8039 = the slope word and $8035 = its type. On the tape the board has 459 records in 129 squares: 418 of the $C0 kind (81 of them type $F7), 14 of $80, 20 of $40 and 7 of $00. No ramp among them has bit 5 of its type set, the case that the branches at $E2E0 and $E34E handle. Called four times, from $E0E7, $E0F2, $E0FD and $E109.

Tests the probe's box against one other object record, in IX; BC = the position of that object's square relative to the moving object's, stored in $8049/$804A. It returns if the two rectangles (+$05, +$08, +$07 and +$09 of IX against $801B, $801F, $801D and $8025) do not overlap. If the other object's top (+$0D) is below the running floor in $8036 it becomes the thing beneath the box when it is the highest so far ($803B = its top). Otherwise, if its base (+$0B) is below the box's top, it is a hit: $803B = $FF and $8036 = its top. In both cases $8037 = IX, $8039 = 0 and $8035 = its type byte. Called from $E15B, $E16E, $E181 and $E193.

The 24-bit state of the generator at $E472: $E46F is the low byte and $E471 the high. The tape loads it as $380000. Besides the generator, 23 instructions elsewhere read one of the three bytes directly as a random value: eight read $E46F, seven $E470 and eight $E471, among them $D49F, $D534 and $D5FE in the code that creates objects.

The game's random number generator. It shifts the 24-bit value at $E46F-$E471 left by one bit, puts bit 7 XOR bit 5 of the new $E471 into bit 0, and returns the new low byte in A. The bit that leaves the top is lost, so 23 bits carry the state, and each call brings in a single new bit: a result is the one before it shifted left with a new bottom bit. From the tape's $380000 the first results are $01, $02, $05, $0B, $16, $2C, $58, $B0, $60, $C0, $80 and then ten zeros. The low 23 bits return to their starting value after 7,864,305 calls, which is 15 * (2^19 - 1), and a state of zero would stay zero. Six callers: $7A30, $D438, $D491, $D52A, $D7BC and $E764.

The worm's width table: 34 bytes falling from $FF to $12, the longer a section the smaller the factor. $AC61, the only reference, indexes it with the high byte of the sum of two magnitudes, the absolute values of the words at $8033 and $8035 (plus the byte at $8003 on the pass where the counter at $8067 runs out), held to a maximum of $1E, and scales both magnitudes by the byte it reads, over 256, through $A8DB. So entries 0 to 30 can be read and the last three, $14, $13 and $12 at $E4AB-$E4AD, cannot.

Address of the next byte of the sound script being played. $7585 loads it with $E4C2 for a new game, $E511 with $E4B2 for the menu and $E4FC with whatever its caller passes; $E9E8 reads through it and moves it on. It holds $E4B2 on the tape, and $0000 after a script has run to its end.

The number of calls of $E9E8 left before the sound script moves to its next byte; 0 means that no script is playing, which is what $E4F7 tests. It is set to 1 whenever a script is started, reloaded from $E4B1 at each step and zeroed at $EA15 when a script ends.

How many buffer copies each sound script byte lasts. Every store that starts a script writes $0101 across $E4B0 and $E4B1 ($758B, $E503, $E50B), so this is always 1, one byte to a copy. It is read only at $E9FF.

The sound script that the menu loads at $E50E: $07, $0A and the $00 that closes it. A script is a run of values for $8055, one for each call of $E9E8, closed by $00 and a word that is either the address of the script to carry on with or $0000 to stop. This one clicks the speaker every 7th pixel row of one buffer copy (18 clicks) and every 10th of the next (12), and so on round.
Link word of the menu's sound script: $E4B2, its own start, so it repeats for as long as it stays loaded. On the menu and in the key redefiner a byte is used each time a page is drawn.

Sound script $02, $09, $04, $0B, $06, $0D, $08, $0F and the closing $00: two rising runs interleaved. It is started through $E4FC, without the test for a script already playing, by $7815, which the code at $77A7-$77CD reaches when each of the four bytes $7F5A, $7F6A, $7F7A and $7F8A is between 1 and $80.

Link word $E4B7: the script at $E4B7 goes back to its own start, so once begun it runs until $E508 or $757F loads another, and every start asked for through $E4F7 in between finds the counter at 1 and does nothing.

The sound script $7582 loads when a game starts: 28 values and the closing $00. They are $13, $02, $11, $03, $0F, $04, $0E, $05, $0D, $06, $0C, $07, $0C, $08, $0B, $09, $0A, then $11 three times, $03, and $1E seven times: a falling run and a rising run interleaved until they meet, then a tail.
Link word $0000 after the game-start script: the high byte is zero, so $EA15 zeroes the counter and the script stops, leaving $0000 in the pointer at $E4AE.
Sound script $0E, $0E, $0E, $1E and the closing $00: four buffer copies with 9, 9, 9 and 4 clicks. It is started through $E4F7, so only when nothing else is playing, from $9E8B, $A5F0 and $A601.
Link word $0000: the script at $E4E1 plays once and stops.

Sound script $1A, $1A, $1A and the closing $00, three buffer copies of 4 clicks each. Its one start is the $E4F7 call at $D87B, in the branch of the type-$F3 handler taken when the record has met a type-$F1 record and its own +$08 is $0E.
Link word $0000: the script at $E4E8 plays once and stops.
Sound script $14, $18, $19, $0B, $08, $06 and the closing $00. Its one start is the $E4F7 call at $7863, in the code that ends a game, so it plays only if no other script is running at that moment.
Link word $E4EE: the script at $E4EE repeats from its own start until the menu at $E508 loads $E4B2 in its place.

Starts the sound script at DE unless one is already playing: it returns with nothing changed when the counter at $E4B0 is not zero, and otherwise falls into $E4FC. A script whose link word points back at itself never lets the counter reach zero, so after $E4B7 or $E4EE has started nothing can be started through here until the menu or a new game loads another script. Called from $7863, $9E8B, $A5F0, $A601 and $D87B.

Starts the sound script at DE whatever is playing: it stores DE in $E4AE and $0101 in $E4B0/$E4B1, so the script's first byte is taken by the next call of $E9E8. Called directly only from $7818; $E4F7 falls into it.

The opening menu, and where every game ends up. It loads the sound script at $E4B2 with counter and reload 1, draws message $86, the menu page, through $E930, and jumps to the tune at $E69F. That never returns: the keys are polled by $E51C after every note, and its two jumps are the only way out. Five references: $7F40 after the first screen, $7699 when the abort control (bit 7 of $8057) is down in play, $7899 and $78C6 at the end of a game, and $E57F when the key redefiner's EXIT row is chosen. It does not set the stack pointer itself.

The menu's key test, called by the tone loop at $E791 after every note of the tune. Through $7BE8 it tests key number $23, the 0 key, and if it is down jumps to $757F to start a game; then $24, the 1 key, which jumps to the key redefiner at $E544; then $1C, the 2 key, which flips the byte at $E868 between $0D and $0E (XOR 3) to turn the Kempston joystick on or off, redraws the menu page with $E930 and waits at $E5B2 until no key is down. With none of the three down it returns to the tune. The two jumps leave the tune's return addresses on the stack; both destinations load SP afresh.

The key redefiner page. It resets SP to $F000, puts a space in the marker of the EXIT row ($E8F3) and starts at row 0, keeping the row number in $8034. For the current row it writes '>' into the row's first byte, whose address comes from $E5BB, and draws message $87 through $E930. Then it polls two keys with $7BE8. SPACE (key $20) blanks the marker and moves to the next row, going from row 8 back to row 0; the page is redrawn at every step and there is no wait for the key to be released, so a held key steps on as fast as the page redraws. ENTER (key $21) on row 8, EXIT, jumps to the menu at $E508. ENTER on rows 0 to 7 writes $88 into the row's key slot, its eighth byte, redraws the page so that three solid blocks show there, waits at $E5B2 for every key to be released and takes the next key pressed from $7B8B. That key's number goes into the control table at $7BE0, in the slot that the eight bytes at $7BD8 give for the row (2, 1, 5, 4, 7, 6, 3, 0), and its display code from the 40-byte table at $7BB0 goes into the row's key slot. Any of the 40 keys is accepted, SPACE and ENTER among them, and nothing stops two controls sharing a key. Entered only from $E529.

Waits until no key is down: it reads port $FE with A = 0, which selects all eight half-rows at once, and loops while any of the five key bits reads 0. Called from $E540 after the Kempston option has been toggled and from $E590 before the redefiner reads a new key.

Returns HL = $E89B + 11 * A, the first byte of row A of the key redefiner's nine rows inside message $87, which it steps through 11 bytes at a time (the ninth row, EXIT, is 10 bytes long), with D = 0 and E = 11 * A. Called from $E550, $E564 and $E582.

Pitch table of the menu tune: twelve pairs of bytes, one pair for each semitone of an octave, read by $E716. The first byte of a pair is the delay count for half a cycle in octave 1, falling from $BE to $65 a semitone at a time; the second is a quarter of the number of half-cycles to play, rising from $19 to $2F, so that every note lasts about the same time (the twelve products lie between 4,650 and 4,815).

Ten addresses, the tune's scripts numbered $A0 to $A9: $E5F8, $E5FD, $E606, $E60F, $E618, $E61F, $E628, $E660, $E685 and $E68E. $E6B6 indexes the table with twice the element byte less $A0 and does not check the range.

Tune script $A0, the whole tune: $A6, $A6, $A7, $A7 and the $FF that ends every script. A script is a list of one-byte elements. $00-$27 is a note, twelve to the octave over four octaves; $28-$4F the same notes at half length; $50-$9F a note reached by a slide up from the semitone below; $A0-$A9 plays another script and comes back; $C8 would play the element after it as noise. One pass of this script plays 450 elements and takes about 194 million T-states, 55 seconds, and $E69F repeats it without end.
Tune script $A1, eight notes and $FF: $0C, $18, $07, $1B, $0C, $1F, $07, $1B. Script $A6 plays it four times, in two pairs.
Tune script $A2, eight notes and $FF: $0B, $1A, $06, $1E, $0A, $19, $05, $1D. Script $A6 plays it twice, each time after a pair of $A1.
Tune script $A3, eight notes and $FF: $0E, $1D, $07, $20, $0E, $24, $07, $20. Script $A6 plays it twice in succession.
Tune script $A4, six elements and $FF: $11, $4B, $48, $0C, $4B, $48. $4B and $48 are notes $23 and $20 at half length. Script $A6 plays it four times, in two pairs.
Tune script $A5, eight notes and $FF: $0B, $1A, $06, $1E, $0B, $1F, $06, $1E. Script $A6 plays it twice in succession, after its pair of $A3.

Tune script $A6, the first half of the tune: 55 elements and $FF, which call scripts $A1 to $A5 fourteen times in all between notes of its own. Its own elements include the runs $35-$3A and $34, $36, $37, $38 of half-length notes and the slide notes $6F and $74. Script $A0 plays it twice.

Tune script $A7, the second half of the tune: 36 elements and $FF. It opens with $A8 twice and $A9, plays 32 elements of its own, the last three of them the slide note $6F, and closes with $A9 again. Script $A0 plays it twice.
Tune script $A8, eight notes and $FF: $07, $1F, $0C, $1B, $07, $1D, $0C, $1A. Script $A7 plays it twice at its start.

Tune script $A9, sixteen elements and $FF: $0C, $18, $05, $1E, $0C, $19, $05, $1F, $07, $1D, $0C, $18, $07 and three of the slide note $6A. Script $A7 plays it twice. Its $FF at $E69E is the last byte of the tune.

The menu's idle loop: it stores 0, a NOP, in the patched opcode at $E75D, plays tune script $A0 through $E6AB and starts again, without end. Reached from the menu at $E519. The only ways out are the two jumps in $E51C, which the tone loop calls after each note.

Plays one element of the tune, in A. For $A0 or more, A less $A0 picks one of the ten script addresses at $E5E4 and each byte of that script is played by a recursive call, up to its $FF; a $C8 inside a script flips the opcode at $E75D between NOP and CCF (XOR $3F) around the element after it, which makes the tone loop move the speaker at random for that element, but no script on the tape holds a $C8. Below $28 the element is a note and goes straight to $E745. $28-$4F is the note A less $28 with its half-cycle count halved. $50-$9F is a slide: the note one semitone below A less $50 for $5A half-cycles, then the note itself for its own count less $5A; the three used, $6A, $6F and $74, are notes 26, 31 and 36, whose counts are well above $5A. Called from $E6A5 and from itself at $E6D2 and $E6E1.

Looks up note A for the tone loop. A divided by 12 is the octave and the remainder picks a pair of bytes from the table at $E5CC. It returns HL = the delay count for half a cycle and DE = the number of half-cycles: in octave 0 twice the first byte and twice the second, in octave 1 the first byte and four times the second, and for each octave above that the delay halved again and the count doubled. Note 12 gives HL = $BE and DE = $64. Called from $E6F2, $E6FF, $E70A and $E745.
Plays note A at full length: it calls $E716 and falls into the tone loop at $E748. Reached only from $E6E9, for elements below $28.

The beeper. HL = the delay count for half a cycle and DE = the number of half-cycles. It takes 4 off HL to allow for its own overhead and, for each half-cycle, runs the delay as OUT ($FE),A inside a DJNZ, once for each unit left in HL, with A still holding the value last sent: bits 0-2 are 1, so the border stays blue. With the opcode at $E75D a NOP, every half-cycle then flips bits 3 to 7 of A, taking the speaker and MIC bits between $01 and $F9. Counted in T-states without memory contention, note 12 is 100 half-cycles about 4,600 apart, close to 380 Hz, and every full-length note lasts about 0.13 s. Entered from $E745 for a plain note and from $E6F9, $E705 and $E713.

One byte of the tone loop that other code rewrites: $00, a NOP, stored at $E6A0, or $3F, a CCF, which the $C8 element switches on and off at $E6CC and $E6DB. It follows an SCF. As a NOP it leaves the carry set and the speaker is flipped on every half-cycle. As a CCF it clears the carry, $E472 is called and the flip is left out when bit 0 of the random byte is 1, which makes noise. The rest of the loop follows from here. A counter in A', 7 at first and afterwards 9 less the high byte of four times the delay count, marks every few half-cycles; on those marks, once fewer than 45 half-cycles remain, the delay count goes up by one, so each note sags in pitch as it ends. When DE runs out the loop calls $E51C to poll the menu keys, and returns. A delay count whose low byte reaches 0 on the way up gives one half-cycle of twice the length, because the DJNZ then runs 256 times more than it should; that happens once in each of notes 7 and 8.

Ten addresses, the messages the printer at $E95D reaches as codes $80 to $89: $E7A9 twice ('<SPACE>'), $E7B1 ('<SYM SHIFT>'), $E7BD ('<CAPS SHIFT>'), $E7CA ('<ENTER>'), $E7D2 ('ER......'), $E7DB (the menu page), $E882 (the key redefiner page), $E92C (three solid blocks) and $7CE0, the text of the forgery warning. $E961 indexes the table with twice the low seven bits of the code. $86 and $87 are the only codes passed to $E930; $81 to $85 and $88 occur inside messages or come from the key name table at $7BB0. Inside a message $80 is the cursor command, so the first word cannot be reached from text, and nothing asks for $89: the forgery screen prints its text with its own routine at $7CB3.

'<SPACE>', messages $80 and $81: both of the first two table words point here. $81 is the display code of key $20 in the table at $7BB0, the default in the BLAST row's key slot at $E8A2, and the key named in the first help line at $E903.
$00, the end of '<SPACE>'.
'<SYM SHIFT>', message $82, the display code of key $18 in the table at $7BB0.
$00, the end of '<SYM SHIFT>'.
'<CAPS SHIFT>', message $83, the display code of key $27 in the table at $7BB0.
$00, the end of '<CAPS SHIFT>'.
'<ENTER>', message $84, the display code of key $21 in the table at $7BB0 and the key named in the second help line at $E918.
$00, the end of '<ENTER>'.

'ER......', message $85: the ending shared by the eight control names of the key redefiner, each of which stores only its stem (BLAST, BURP, FAST, SLOW, RIGHT, LEFT, BOUNC, ABORT), with six full stops that lead across to the key.
$00, the end of message $85.
Message $86, the menu page, starts here with five control bytes: $FE $0F sets the attribute to $0F, white ink on blue paper, and $80 $04 $F2 puts the cursor at $F204, pixel row 16, column 4.
The title, 24 characters: 'FAT WORM', two spaces, 'BLOWS A SPARKY'. It is printed in white from column 4 on pixel rows 16 to 23.
$80 $24 $F2: the cursor goes to $F224, pixel row 17, column 4, one pixel row below the start of the title.
24 underline characters (code $5F). Printed one pixel row lower than the title, their bottom line falls on pixel row 24, just under the title's cells, and rules it off.
$FE $0C sets the attribute to $0C, green ink on blue, and $80 $04 $F5 puts the cursor at $F504, pixel row 40, column 4.
'BY JULIAN G TODD', 16 characters, the first of the two green lines.
$80 $04 $F6: the cursor goes to $F604, pixel row 48, column 4.
The copyright line, 21 characters: code $7F, the copyright sign in the Spectrum's character set, and 'DURELL SOFTWARE 1986'.
$FE $0E sets the attribute to $0E, yellow ink on blue, and $80 $03 $F8 puts the cursor at $F803, pixel row 64, column 3.
17 characters: '1', three spaces and 'REDEFINE KEYS'. The 1 key is tested at $E524.
$80 $83 $FB: the cursor goes to $FB83, pixel row 92, column 3. The START GAME line is stored before the KEMPSTON line although it is printed lower down the screen.
14 characters: '0', three spaces and 'START GAME'. The 0 key is tested at $E51C.
$FE, the attribute command for the KEMPSTON JOYSTICK line; its operand is the byte at $E868.

The attribute of the menu's KEMPSTON JOYSTICK line, which doubles as the joystick switch. $0D, cyan ink, as on the tape, is off; $0E, yellow like the other two options, is on. The 2 key on the menu flips it with XOR 3 at $E533-$E538, and the control reader at $7C2A reads the Kempston port $1F only when it finds $0E here.
$80 $43 $F9: the cursor goes to $F943, pixel row 74, column 3.
21 characters: '2', three spaces and 'KEMPSTON JOYSTICK', printed in whichever attribute $E868 holds. The 2 key is tested at $E52C.
$00, the end of message $86.
Message $87, the key redefiner page, starts here: $FE $0F sets white ink on blue and $80 $07 $F1 puts the cursor at $F107, pixel row 8, column 7.
The page's title, 15 characters: 'KEY', three spaces and 'REDEFINER'.

$FE $0D sets the attribute to $0D, cyan ink on blue, and $80 $06 $F3 puts the cursor at $F306, pixel row 24, column 6, for the first of the nine rows. The rows that follow are 10 pixel rows apart, so most of them do not start on a character row.

Row 0 of the key redefiner: its marker byte, '>' on the selected row and a space on the others (written at $E553 and $E567), and the stem BLAST. With message $85 after it the line reads BLASTER. This is also the base of the nine-row table that $E5BB indexes. The row is printed at pixel row 24, column 6.
Code $85 in the BLAST row: the printer inserts message $85, 'ER......', here.

The key slot of the BLAST row, its eighth byte: the display code of the key, $81 on the tape, which prints as '<SPACE>' (key number $20 in the control table at $7BE2, bit 5 of $8057 in play). The redefiner writes $88 here while it waits for a key and then the new key's code from $7BB0.
$80 $46 $F4: the cursor goes to $F446, pixel row 34, column 6, for the BURP row.
