Row 8 of the key redefiner: its marker byte and EXIT, with no key slot. $E549 puts a space in the marker each time the redefiner is entered, because leaving through this row leaves '>' in it. ENTER on this row goes back to the menu ($E57F). Printed at pixel row 104, column 6.
$FE $4B sets the attribute to $4B, BRIGHT with magenta ink on blue paper, and $80 $03 $FE puts the cursor at $FE03, pixel row 112, column 3.
'PRESS ', the start of the first help line.
Code $81 in the first help line: the printer inserts message $81, '<SPACE>'.
' TO ADVANCE', which completes 'PRESS <SPACE> TO ADVANCE'.

$80 $01 $FF: the cursor goes to $FF01, pixel row 120, column 1, the last character row of the buffer. The printer also colours the cell below each character, and below row 15 that wraps to row 0, so this line leaves the attribute $4B in columns 1 to 31 of the top row of the screen.
'PRESS ', the start of the second help line.
Code $84 in the second help line: the printer inserts message $84, '<ENTER>'.
' TO CHANGE OR EXIT', which completes 'PRESS <ENTER> TO CHANGE OR EXIT', 31 characters from column 1.
$00, the end of message $87.

Message $88: three bytes of character code $01 and a closing $00. The printer takes the glyph for code $01 from $3C08 in the ROM, below the font, where the 48K ROM holds eight bytes of $FF, so the message draws three solid blocks. $E588 writes $88 into a row's key slot to show them while the redefiner waits for the new key.

Draws a text page; A = the message number. It first sets each of the 512 attribute bytes $5800-$59FF, the top sixteen character rows, to its own ink on blue paper (AND 7, OR 8), which also clears BRIGHT and FLASH. Then it zeroes the frame buffer $F000-$FFFF, prints the message into the buffer with $E95D and copies the buffer to the screen with $E9E8, which also takes one byte of the sound script. The bottom eight rows, the panel, are not touched. Called with $86 from $E516 and $E53D and with $87 from $E557 and $E58D.

Where the next character goes, as an address in the frame buffer: $F000 + 32 * pixel row + column, so a line can start on any pixel row, not only on a character row. The $80 command in a message sets it ($E979) and each character moves it on by one ($E9E1). It holds $F000 on the tape.
The attribute byte written with each character. The $FE command in a message sets it ($E987) and $E9B3 reads it. It holds $0F on the tape.

The text printer. With bit 7 of A set it prints a message: the low seven bits pick an address from the table at $E795 and the bytes there are read up to a $00. $80 is followed by a two-byte cursor address for $E95A, $FE by an attribute for $E95C, and every other byte is printed by a recursive call, so a code of $81 or more inside a message inserts another message. With bit 7 clear it prints the character A at the cursor. The cursor is an address in the frame buffer; from it the routine works out the attribute cell (bits 8-11 are the character row, bits 0-4 the column) and writes the attribute there and in the cell below, wrapping from row 15 to row 0, because a character need not start on a cell boundary. The glyph is the eight bytes at $3C00 + 8 * A in the ROM, which is the ROM font for codes $20 to $7F. Each byte is ORed with itself shifted one pixel right, which thickens every stroke, and XORed into the buffer on eight successive pixel rows, 32 bytes apart. The cursor then moves one byte on, so the bold characters are still eight pixels wide. Called from $E953 and from itself at $E98E.

The stack pointer, kept here while SP is used to move data: by the buffer copy at $E9E8 (saved at $EA21, restored at $EAA3), by the buffer clear at $EAA9 (restored at $EAF0) and by the routine at $D37D (restored at $D3E5).

Copies the frame buffer to the screen and makes the frame's sound. First the sound script: if the counter at $E4B0 is not 0 it is decremented and the byte at the script pointer $E4AE goes into $8055; when the counter reaches 0 the pointer moves on, the counter is reloaded from $E4B1, and if the next byte is $00 the pointer is replaced by the word after it, a zero high byte there stopping the script. Then the copy. SP is saved at $E9E6 and set to $F000, and 2,048 POPs read the buffer two bytes at a time, 16 POPs to a pixel row, while HL steps through the first two thirds of the display file, $4000-$4FFF, in its own order: eight pixel rows $100 apart, then the next character row, then the second third. Buffer byte $F000 + 32 * y + x lands on pixel row y (0 to 127), column x; the bottom third and the attributes are not written. After each row a counter loaded from $8055 is decremented, and when it reaches 0 it is reloaded and A, 1 at the start, has bits 3-7 flipped and is sent to port $FE. With n in $8055 that is one click every n rows: 128 / n of them, rounded down, for n from 1 to 128, and none for 0 or for more than 128. Interrupts are off throughout the game, so nothing else uses the stack meanwhile. Called from $766B in every frame and from $78EA, $790A, $7920, $D336 and $E956.
A lone $C9, a RET, after the RET that ends $E9E8. No instruction refers to this address and nothing falls into it; what it is left over from is not established.

Starts a new frame in the buffer. SP is saved at $E9E6 and set to $0000, and 2,048 pushes of $FFFF fill the buffer from $FFFF down to $F000, 16 pushes to a pixel row, so all 256 by 128 pixels start set. After each row a counter loaded from $8056 is decremented and at 0 is reloaded, with bits 3-7 of A (1 at the start) flipped and sent to port $FE, just as the copy at $E9E8 does with $8055: 128 / n clicks for n from 1 to 128 and none otherwise. A row here takes about a third of the time a row of the copy takes, so the same value gives a higher note. With SP restored it calls $EB2B for each of the nine six-byte records at $8069, $806F, $8075, $807B, $8081, $8087, $808D, $8093 and $8099, which the code at $ADD2-$AE3B fills in for the three-by-three block of squares around the one the view is centred in. Called from $7665 in every frame and from $78D3, $7904 and $791A.

Draws the floor of one board square into the buffer. HL = a six-byte record: the x and y of the square's corner in buffer pixels, as signed words, and the square's address, or 0 where the board has no square. It stores x and y in $801B and $801D and each plus 256 in $801F and $8025. For a missing square it sets $80BE to $00FF and calls $8E13, which clears the part of the buffer the square covers; the 0 it writes to $80B4 beforehand is overwritten by the first instruction of $8E13. For a real square it scatters dots: the address goes through $B350 (HL * 1509 + 41) to seed a sequence, the low three bits of the first value plus 7 give the number of dots, 7 to 14, and each later value gives one dot at x plus its low byte and y plus its high byte, cleared through $B9F2 when it lies inside the buffer. The dots depend only on the square's address, so they keep their places on the board as it scrolls. Called nine times by $EAA9.

The head of the display list: the address of the first record to draw. A link whose high byte is 0 ends the list. $AAF9 stores 0 here at the start of each frame's build; the insertion at $B008, the drawing walk at $B300 and the search for the surface under a point at $9A89 all start from this word. The tape image holds $EB8D, the address of the leftover record below, which the game never links.
Thirteen zero bytes between the list's head word and the leftover record at $EB8D. No instruction names them, and the recorded sessions neither read nor wrote them.

Fifteen bytes in the shape of a display-list record, left in the image: link 0, a box from -8 to 8 both ways, top height $0C, bottom height $0A and type $FF, which is drawn as nothing. The image's head word at $EB7E points at it. Two instructions load its address, LD HL at $AAF3 and LD IX at $AED8, and each is overwritten by the instruction after it: records are allocated from $EB9C, 15 bytes on. The end-of-game code at $7841-$785B addresses the worm's records one slot low, so it writes this record's type ($EB9B) and source pointer ($EB97-$EB98), and nothing reads them.

The routine that made the master tape. The game never runs it: its only reference is the JP at $757C, and no instruction or stored word in the image names $757C. It disables interrupts, sets the stack to $F000 and walks the board's records from $6464 in 7-byte steps: a record with $F7 in its byte +6 is given a handler address in its bytes +4 and +5, chosen by the code it finds in +5 ($FF: $BD6F, $FE: $BD90, $FD: $BDD1, $FC: $BE07, $0C: left alone, anything else: $BED1); a zero byte ends a group and $FF ends the walk. From $EBF0 it builds the 256-byte bit-reversal table at $6200, then the seven pages of shifted values at $5B00-$61FF. At $EC5B it loads IX with $4000 and DE with $BF68, pushes $EFD8 and jumps to $FA6B, the turbo save routine: 49,000 bytes from $4000 go to tape, and the save returns into the entry stub. The tape therefore holds the tables and the handler addresses already built, and at $EFFE the word $EFD8 that this routine pushed. In play the display list is written over it: the worm's four records are at $EB9C, $EBAB, $EBBA and $EBC9, and the records of the board and of the objects follow them.

Where the loader hands over. The tape's loader pushes $EFD8 before it reads the block and returns here when the block ends, whether or not the load succeeded: its error exits use the same return. Two NOPs, then DI, the stack to $F000, the bitmap $4000-$57FF cleared with LDIR, the 768 attribute bytes from $5800 set to $0E (yellow ink on blue paper), the border set to blue with OUT ($FE), and a jump to $7C92. Interrupts are not enabled again anywhere in the game. In play the stack grows down over this code; the recorded sessions wrote as far down as $EFE8.

The picture of the bottom panel as loaded: 2,048 bytes of bitmap for the lowest third of the screen (the insert map's frame, the row of lights and the counter window), in the screen's own layout for that third. $7F30 copies it to $5000-$57FF once, on the way from the first screen to the menu, and nothing reads it again: from the first frame of play $F000-$FFFF is the frame buffer for the top two thirds of the screen.
The second half of the bottom panel's bitmap, $F400-$F7FF: the same block that starts at $F000, copied to the screen by the same LDIR at $7F39.

The bottom panel's colours: 256 attribute bytes, eight rows of 32 cells, which $7F3B-$7F3E copy to $5A00-$5AFF after the bitmap. $F8FF is the last byte of the picture; the frame buffer covers these addresses in play.

The entry of the tape utility the author saved the game with. It is not the game's code and the game never calls it. Called from BASIC, it steps the interpreter past the USR that called it and reads the next character of the line with RST $18: the tokens for SAVE ($F8), LOAD ($EF), VERIFY ($D6) and MERGE ($D5) select $1AE0, $1AE1, $1AE2 or $1AE3 in BC, and anything else jumps to the ROM's 'Nonsense in BASIC' report at $1C8A. $FA60 then stores BC in the system variable at $5C74 and jumps to $FBAB, in the utility's copy of the ROM's cassette code. That copy fills $FA67-$FF43: the ROM's $04C2-$099E moved up by $F5A5, with its internal calls and jumps repointed into the copy and its timing constants changed to save and load faster than the ROM does.
Ten characters between the utility's two pieces of code: the copyright sign (code $7F in the machine's character set), then ' 1983 NMS'. Nothing reads them.

The four token tests at $FA40-$FA51 arrive here with BC holding $1AE0 plus 0 to 3. It stores BC in the system variable at $5C74 and jumps to $FBAB, one byte into the copy of the ROM routine that handles SAVE, LOAD, VERIFY and MERGE (the ROM's $0605, here at $FBAA).
